# Podcast websites, built and run for you

Spotify, Apple, and YouTube own the pages your show appears on. I give the show a home it owns: a website on your domain, generated from your RSS feed, with a real page for every episode and a daily job that keeps it current without anyone touching it.

## Why a show needs one

Search engines and AI assistants read text. A feed full of audio gives them almost nothing to work with, and the episode pages the platforms generate are thin and identical. A page per episode, carrying the full transcript, turns every hour you've recorded into something a person can find by searching for what you talked about. The platform pages also belong to the platform, and a platform can shut down a directory overnight, the way Google Podcasts closed in 2024.

## What I deliver
- A generator, written in Python with OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, that reads your feed and writes the whole site as static HTML.
- Episode pages at permanent addresses, each with cover art, a player that streams from your host, the show notes, a transcript, and a glossary when an episode calls for one.
- Search titles and descriptions for every episode, drafted with AI and reviewed by hand, and alt text for every cover.
- PodcastSeries and PodcastEpisode structured data, a sitemap, an llms.txt file, and an RSS feed of the site.
- A 1,200 by 630 share card for every episode, carrying the cover and the episode title, so links posted to social platforms show in full.
- An archive, an about page with every place to listen, and room for written articles alongside the episodes.

## The daily job

A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow runs every morning. It adds new episodes, collects transcripts that arrive days late, rebuilds, and commits only when something changed. It refuses to publish when the feed looks broken, for example when the feed suddenly lists far fewer episodes than the site already has. When the audio stays with your host, every play still counts there.

## Ownership, start to finish

The domain and the repository are registered to you. Shows that already publish through Spotify, Apple, or another host can keep doing exactly that; the site clones their feed and adds a page for each new episode. Shows that want full ownership can go further: the site publishes the RSS feed the directories read, and the audio lives in storage on the show's own domain, such as Cloudflare R2, which charges nothing for downloads. The nightly check can run at any hour, or several times a day around release.

## Running costs

GitHub Pages hosts the site and Cloudflare handles DNS. Neither charges for a site like this, so the domain is the only bill unless you host your own audio, where R2 bills for storage past its free allowance. Nothing on the server needs patching, because nothing runs on the server.

## After launch

Most shows want more than a mirror of the feed. Common additions are corrections to an episode's notes, photos, links to the things discussed, and articles grown out of episodes that drew a response. Articles go through the same fact-check I describe on [fact-checked writing in your voice](https://gerriscorp.com/services/editorial/).

## Want to build it yourself?

The full method is free in my guide to [building a podcast website with Codex or Claude Code on GitHub Pages](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-website/). For getting episodes found once the site exists, see [podcast SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-seo/).

## Engagement

A build from an existing feed is a fixed-scope project, quoted after a call about your feed and your goals. Additions after launch are quoted as a fixed fee or covered under [ongoing support](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ongoing-support/). Terms are on [Work With Me](https://gerriscorp.com/work-with-me/).

# Multi-location and connected businesses

A parent brand with several locations. Sister companies sharing an owner, a building, or a phone number. Stores in neighboring towns competing with each other in Google. These businesses confuse search engines and AI assistants unless their identities are untangled deliberately.

## Common problems
- Search engines can't tell the parent brand from its original location, so the wrong one shows up.
- Location pages that repeat the same copy with a city name swapped in.
- Google Business Profiles that link to the home page instead of the matching location page.
- Sister businesses with conflicting names, addresses, or phone numbers across the web, or duplicate listings.
- Structured data that describes every location as the same business, or several businesses as one.
- Several related sites and domains, some redirecting, some not, competing for the same searches.

## What I do

### Entity architecture

A clear map of who is who: the parent organization, each location, each sister business, and how they relate. Then structured data that states it, using organization and local business types with parent and branch relationships, so search engines and AI systems describe each one correctly.

### Location pages that earn their place

One page per real location, with the address, hours, services, staff, directions, and local details that make it useful, linked from the matching Google Business Profile. Service-area pages where the business travels to customers, written for that area instead of cloned.

### Consistency everywhere

Names, addresses, phone numbers, and categories aligned across websites, profiles, and directories, with duplicates found and resolved.

### Connected businesses kept distinct

Separate content, FAQs, and structured data for each business, even when they share an owner and an office. A plumbing company and a foundation repair company with the same owner need different answers to different questions.

### Multi-site cleanup

Old domains, duplicate sites, and inconsistent domain versions consolidated with 301 redirects, and Search Console history preserved for each property.

### Seasonal planning

For seasonal businesses, risky changes such as category edits that can trigger reverification happen in the off-season, and a change freeze covers the peak.

## How it starts

A paid diagnostic maps every site, profile, and listing the business controls, finds the conflicts, and ranks the fixes. Implementation follows in the order that protects existing rankings, visibility, and reviews first.

## Common questions

### Should each location have its own website?

Usually one site with a strong page per location works best, because the locations share the brand's authority. Separate sites make sense for genuinely separate businesses.

### Can you fix suspended or duplicate profiles too?

Yes, as part of the same engagement. See [Google Business Profile hard cases](https://gerriscorp.com/services/google-business-profile/).

# Reputation and perception management

For founders, executives, and families who need privacy and a defensible public record at the same time.

Your reputation is whatever comes up when someone searches your name, and increasingly whatever an AI assistant says when someone asks about you. Both draw on the same sources: your own pages and profiles, news coverage, public records, data broker listings, and whatever else the web holds. Perception management means knowing what's in that record, removing what shouldn't be public, and making sure accurate information is what people and machines find first.

## What I do

### Audit the record

A full picture of what search engines and the major AI assistants say about you or your company, across names, spellings, and related searches, with the sources behind each result and answer.

### Remove what shouldn't be public

Personal information removed from data broker and people-search sites, removal requests through Google's "Results about you" tool for contact details in search results, and use of state privacy rights where they apply, including California's new Delete Request and Opt-out Platform. The [guide to removing your personal information](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/personal-information-removal/) explains how each works.

### Strengthen what's accurate

Pages you control, consistent facts across them, and structured data that tells search engines and AI systems who you are. Strong, accurate pages are what push weaker or outdated results down.

### Correct AI answers

When an assistant gets you wrong, I trace the answer to its sources and fix or outweigh them, then retest on a schedule.

### Monitor and report

Monthly reporting on search results, AI answers, new broker listings, and anything that needs attention, with fast response when something new appears.

## Working with your other advisors

This work plugs into security, legal, and family office teams, and the disciplines strengthen each other: they watch for threats, and I keep the public record accurate and the private information private.

## Background

I've done this work for more than twenty years, starting at New Media Strategies, where online reputation management grew up as a practice, and including high-end reputation and executive privacy work at Reputation.com.

## Common questions

### Is this work confidential?

Completely. I name none of my reputation clients, and I'm happy to sign a nondisclosure agreement before the first conversation.

### How is reputation work structured?

It starts with a paid audit, then usually continues as a monthly retainer billed in advance, because the record changes and data brokers relist people constantly.

### Can negative articles be removed?

Removal depends on the source and the law. Some content qualifies for removal under platform policies or privacy rules; most legitimate news coverage doesn't. Where removal isn't available, accurate and stronger pages change what people see first.

# Google Business Profile hard cases

Suspensions, failed video verifications, profiles that are live in public and stuck in the dashboard, and access problems across managed profiles.

A Google Business Profile is often the first thing a local customer sees, and when it's suspended or stuck, calls and visits drop at once. Google handles these cases through automated systems, an appeals process, and a support queue that moves at its own pace. The cases I take are the hard ones: repeated suspensions, verification loops, duplicate or split profiles, and accounts where one problem has spread to every profile they manage.

## Advisory work, priced for the effort

I take on Google Business Profile cases as paid advisory engagements or as part of an ongoing SEO or reputation retainer. Each stage is scoped in writing, so the work is defined before it starts.

## Stage one: a written diagnostic

A review of the profile, its history, the account and its other profiles, the business's documentation, and Google's guidelines, delivered as a written findings report:
- What most likely triggered the problem, based on the evidence available.
- What documentation exists and what's missing.
- Whether an appeal or reverification is viable, and what it would involve.
- What to fix first, whether or not you hire me for the next stage.

## Stage two: remediation and appeal

When there's a viable path, a separately scoped engagement covers compliance fixes to the profile and website, the appeal, and correspondence with Google, with agreed limits on profiles, appeal rounds, and hours. I build appeals like a legal brief: the strongest verifiable document first, nothing that exposes private information, and only claims the paperwork supports. Further rounds are agreed and paid separately.

## What I need from you

Truthful documentation, access to the profile and account, and prompt answers to Google's requests. Google makes every reinstatement decision, on its own schedule.

## Prevention

Most suspensions trace back to a mismatch between the profile and reality: an address that's really a service area, a name with extra keywords, a category that doesn't fit, or information that differs from the website. Fixing those before Google notices is far cheaper than an appeal, and it fits naturally into [ongoing support](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ongoing-support/).

## Local search beyond the profile

A profile is only as strong as the website and listings behind it. Consistent name, address, and phone details across directories, location and service pages that match the profile, and reviews answered promptly all support local visibility.

## Common questions

### How long does reinstatement take?

Google's appeal reviews take anywhere from days to several weeks, and complex cases take longer. The diagnostic itself is delivered within a week of receiving access and documents.

### Do you manage profiles that aren't suspended?

Yes, as part of local SEO within [ongoing support](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ongoing-support/) or a broader SEO engagement.

# Email authentication and DNS

Unglamorous plumbing that decides whether your email arrives and whether your domains keep their value.

Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo have required authenticated email, and Microsoft's Outlook.com followed in May 2025 for high-volume senders. Mail that fails authentication lands in spam or bounces. At the same time, DNS is where websites, email, and verification records all live, so a careless change for a website move can quietly break email. I handle both with an inventory first and a change list second.

## Email authentication
- **SPF** listing every service allowed to send as your domain, within the ten-lookup limit.
- **DKIM** signing for your mailbox provider and every sending service: newsletters, CRM, invoicing, help desk.
- **DMARC** starting at monitoring, reading the aggregate reports to find every legitimate sender, then tightening to quarantine and reject.
- Alignment, one-click unsubscribe headers for bulk mail, and spam-rate monitoring in Google Postmaster Tools.

The [SPF, DKIM, and DMARC guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-authentication/) explains each record and the current requirements.

## Deliverability

When mail goes missing, I trace it: authentication results in message headers, DMARC reports, blocklists, sending reputation, and content. Then I fix everything the domain owner controls: authentication, DNS, the sending setup, and the separation of marketing mail from business mail. Getting a domain off a blocklist or rebuilding its standing with Gmail and Microsoft is decided by those operators, on their schedule; for that stage I document the fixes for their review processes, and bring in a deliverability specialist when a case needs one.

## DNS and domains
- A complete DNS inventory before any change, so nothing breaks by accident.
- Moves between DNS providers, such as Cloudflare, Squarespace, GoDaddy, and Route 53, without downtime.
- Website moves that change only the web records and leave mail exactly where it is.
- Domain consolidation, including internationalized domains, with 301 redirects that carry search equity to the right place.
- Verification records for Google, Microsoft, and other services kept intact and documented.

## How an engagement runs
1. A complete export of every DNS record, and a list of every service that sends mail as your domain.
2. A written change plan: what changes, what stays, and in what order.
3. The changes, made in a quiet period with time-to-live values lowered first.
4. Verification with test messages, header analysis, and DMARC reports.
5. A record of the final configuration, so the next person who touches DNS knows what everything does.

## Domains you own but don't use

Old brand names, typo domains, and defensive registrations need attention too. Parked domains get spoofed for phishing, so they need SPF and DMARC records that reject all mail, and any that still attract visitors or links should redirect to the right place on your main site.

## Common questions

### How long does DMARC take to set up?

The records take minutes. Moving safely from monitoring to enforcement usually takes a few weeks of reading reports, because every legitimate sender has to be found and authenticated first.

### Will changing DNS take my site or email offline?

Not when it's planned. I copy every record, lower time-to-live values ahead of the change, and verify mail and web after the switch.

**Related:** [SPF, DKIM, and DMARC explained](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-authentication/) · [Site speed and Cloudflare](https://gerriscorp.com/services/site-speed/) · [Website migrations](https://gerriscorp.com/services/migrations/)

# Guides

Plain explanations of the problems I'm hired to fix, written for 2026 and kept up to date. Each one stands on its own, and each ends with how I handle the problem for clients.

# How to fact check a confident AI answer about SEO before you act on it

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

I asked an AI search assistant whether ending every page title with a pipe and the company name hurts a website. The answer came back polished, cited, and full of percentages. When I pushed my own opinion back at it, it declared that opinion “100% true” and invented psychology to support it. The recommendation itself was reasonable. A good share of the evidence was not. This is the routine I use to separate the two before anything reaches a client's site.

## Turn the answer into a list of claims

Paste the answer into a document and give every sentence that asserts a fact its own line. In this exchange the list read: titles are cut off after about 60 characters; Google rewrites more than 75 percent of titles; Google strips pipes and brand names; Google displays the site name on its own; repeated suffixes cause duplication penalties and dilute relevance; searchers read a pipe as a sign of automated spam.

A sound recommendation can rest on claims that are half wrong. Grading each line separately stops a good conclusion from carrying bad evidence into your report.

## Grade every claim by where it comes from

Each line goes into one of four bins: the platform's own documentation, an independent study with a published method, a vendor test, or nothing traceable. Here is how this exchange graded out.
| Claim | What I found |
| --- | --- |
| Titles are cut off at about 60 characters | Google's documentation sets no maximum length and says the displayed title is shortened to fit the device. Sixty characters is an industry habit, not a Google limit. |
| Google rewrites over 75 percent of titles | I could not trace that figure to a primary dataset about pipes or brand names. The best documented study I found, by Zyppy, measured 61.6 percent of 80,959 titles on 2,370 sites, using desktop results from early 2022. Titles longer than 70 characters were rewritten 99.9 percent of the time. |
| Google strips pipes | The same study found pipes removed or replaced in 41.0 percent of titles that used them, often swapped for a dash. Dashes were removed 19.7 percent of the time. |
| Google strips brand names | The study names missing or superfluous brand names as a rewrite trigger and gives no percentage. Google says it may omit a site name that repeats the one already shown. |
| Google shows the site name separately | Supported by Google's documentation. |
| Repeated suffixes cause penalties or crawling problems | Nothing traceable. Google warns that boilerplate titles make results hard to tell apart, which is about usefulness to searchers, not a penalty. |
| Searchers read a pipe as spam | Nothing traceable. I found no study measuring that reaction. |

## Follow every number back to its population

A statistic describes the set of things someone counted, at a particular time, in a particular way. Ask who measured it, when, on which device, and what exactly was counted. A rewrite rate for all titles says nothing specific about pipes. A desktop sample from early 2022 may not describe mobile results today. When an assistant cannot show where a number came from, or the source measures something else, drop the number and keep the point in plain words.

## Distrust agreement that grows when you push

The clearest warning in this exchange came after I shared my own view. The follow-up adopted my wording, raised its certainty, and added mechanisms nobody had measured. An assistant that grows more confident because you sounded confident is reflecting you back at yourself. Open a fresh conversation and ask the opposite question: what is the case for keeping the company name in every title? If the answer flips that easily, the evidence was never doing the work.

## Settle it with your own data

For title changes, the deciding evidence sits in your own Search Console. Change one group of pages, leave a comparable group untouched, and compare clicks and click-through rate across several weeks. A controlled result from your own site outranks any general statistic, accurate or invented. My guide to [diagnosing a Google traffic drop in Search Console](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/traffic-drop/) covers lining changes up with dates, and the one on [measuring AI citations, referrals, and leads](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/measure-ai-search/) applies the same discipline to AI search reporting.

## What survived the check

After grading, the defensible advice fit in a few lines: write a specific title for each page, include the company name where it helps someone recognize or choose the result, keep titles concise, and measure the change. Dropping a repeated suffix remains a legitimate editorial call. It simply has to be presented as judgment backed by a test, never as escape from a penalty that does not exist.

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com)

# How to measure AI search citations, referrals, and actual leads

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 12, 2026

An AI answer mentions your business. Someone sends a screenshot. Another person asks whether revenue has increased. Those are three different observations, and a useful report keeps them separate. I would build a small measurement routine around citations, identifiable visits, and business outcomes, with a note explaining what each source can and cannot see.

## Define the outcome before choosing a dashboard

A citation is a reference to a page in an answer. A mention names the business and might provide no link. A referral is a visit with an identifiable source. A lead is a business event, such as an inquiry or completed booking. None of those measures is interchangeable with the others.

Choose the question the report needs to answer. If the goal is correcting inaccurate descriptions, an answer log may be the best instrument. If the goal is qualified inquiries, analytics and the inquiry record matter more. If the goal is finding which articles become sources, provider citation reporting deserves attention.

I would avoid combining these into an invented visibility score. A score can hide a rise in mentions alongside a fall in meaningful visits. Show the underlying observations and let the reader understand the tradeoffs.

## Read Bing's citation reporting within its boundaries

Bing Webmaster Tools provides an AI Performance report for Microsoft Copilot, Bing, and selected partner experiences. Microsoft's June 2026 update added preview capabilities for intent, topic, citation share, and period comparisons. These are provider observations, not a census of every AI product.

Review the cited pages and the retrieval queries associated with them. A grounding query reflects the system's search for supporting material; do not present it as a verbatim customer question. Topic and intent groupings can suggest editorial questions worth investigating, but their labels are not a substitute for reading the actual pages.

Microsoft defines citation share around the citations for a particular grounding query. It is not traffic share or a content quality score. When reporting a change, retain the dates and scope of the comparison. A movement may reflect demand, system changes, or other sources as well as your own revisions.

## Build a separate view of identifiable visits

In GA4, examine session source and medium alongside the landing page. Start with the referring domains that actually appear in your own data rather than copying an enormous list from a marketing article. Check whether visits from an assistant are being grouped with referrals or another channel.

Google Analytics lets a property use custom channel groups while leaving its default channel definitions intact. A custom group can make recognized AI referrals easier to review. Document the matching rules and check for overlap with existing categories before using the group in a recurring report.

Source information is incomplete. Apps, browser privacy settings, and links that do not pass a referrer can obscure where a visit began. A visit without source information is not automatically an AI visit. Report the identifiable portion as such, and resist estimating the rest from a guess.

For links you control in a campaign, consistent tagging can help attribution. You cannot assume that an assistant will preserve tags or that every visitor will follow the cited link. Keep citation totals and session totals in separate columns.

## Keep Google's reporting distinct

Google documents traffic from its AI search features within the Search Console Performance report's Web search type. That aggregate is not a dedicated citation inventory. Do not label a change in all Google impressions as a measured change in AI citations.

Use page and query comparisons to locate changes in search performance, then investigate them. A title revision, a changed canonical, seasonality, or an indexing issue may matter. A chart moving after a publishing change establishes timing; it does not prove the change caused the movement.

## Create a repeatable answer log

A manual check is useful when its conditions are saved. Choose a short list of genuine customer questions and preserve the exact wording. Record the product, mode, date, relevant account or location context, answer summary, cited addresses, and factual inaccuracies.

Repeat the same questions on a schedule, with a consistent procedure. If you change the prompt halfway through, label that as a new test. Keep unexpected or unfavorable answers in the record rather than retaining only flattering screenshots.

A practical observation log might contain these fields:
- **Question identifier:** a stable label linked to the saved wording.
- **Experience tested:** the provider and the relevant search mode.
- **Observed answer:** the claim being checked and whether it is accurate.
- **Source addresses:** the pages actually linked in that response.
- **Follow-up:** the correction, page improvement, or further test required.

This is a sample of answers under recorded conditions. It cannot establish your universal position across all users, prompts, and products. The purpose is to detect patterns and factual problems you can act on.

## Connect the observations to inquiries

Define a small set of meaningful business events. A contact submission may count; a button click alone may not. Test that the event fires when the action succeeds, and check whether duplicate events inflate the count. Compare the analytics record with actual received inquiries before presenting a conversion total.

An optional “How did you hear about this business?” field can add context, but self reported answers have their own limits. A customer may recall an assistant while the final visit came through a branded search. Preserve both observations without forcing them into one source label.

A hypothetical monthly report could list cited pages, identifiable assistant referrals, qualified inquiries from those visits, and unresolved attribution questions. Keep small counts visible. One additional lead can produce a dramatic percentage change when the previous total was tiny.

## Review the evidence before commissioning more content

Ask which pages are repeatedly useful, which questions remain unanswered, and whether the cited explanation is accurate. Improve a specific weakness and record the release date. Compare an appropriate later period, while acknowledging other changes that occurred during it.

The report should end with a decision: repair a factual error, improve a relevant article, investigate tracking, or leave a useful page alone. For the publication side of that process, use [the IndexNow and AI search release workflow](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/indexnow-ai-search/). If the tracking itself needs work, see [analytics setup and repair](https://gerriscorp.com/services/analytics/).

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Citation gap analysis: finding the sources AI cites instead of you

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

A citation gap is a page that AI assistants cite when they answer your buyers' questions, which names your competitors and leaves you out. Finding them is mechanical: ask the questions, collect every cited URL, sort the sources by type, and mark the ones where a competitor appears and you don't. The result is a ranked list of places to be, and it replaces guessing about which publications "AI trusts" with the actual pages it used.

## Collect the sources, not only the answers

Start with a fixed set of buyer questions and run them with web search turned on. The answer text tells you who was named. The citations tell you why. OpenAI's API returns two lists for a web search answer: the URLs cited inline, and, on request, every source the model consulted, which is usually longer. Claude returns the cited URL with each passage it draws from a search result. Keep both lists for every answer, with the date and the engine.

Bing Webmaster Tools now reports how often your own pages are cited in Copilot answers and lets you compare that citation share against other sites. That is the one place a search engine shows citation counts directly, and it covers only your side of the gap. The question set covers the rest.

## Sort every source by type

A pile of URLs becomes useful once each one carries a label. I use seven:
- marketplace and directory listings (freelance platforms, agency directories, review sites)
- "best of" roundups and ranked lists
- practitioner guides written by third parties
- vendor and tool company blogs
- trade press and news
- forums and communities
- competitors' own sites

The labels decide the remedy. A listing gap is closed with a complete, current profile. A roundup gap is an editorial pitch. A practitioner-guide gap is closed by writing the better answer yourself and by giving the writers of those guides a reason to cite you. A competitor's own page that keeps getting cited is a content benchmark: read it and work out what it answers that your page doesn't.

## Mark the gaps and rank them

For each source, record which names it mentions. A source that names two of your competitors and not you is a gap. Rank the gaps by how many questions cited the source, then by how reachable it is. A directory you can join this afternoon outranks a national publication that might cover you next year, even though the publication carries more weight.

## What a real run turned up

In October 2026 I ran sixteen buyer questions about my own services through Claude with web search. On the hiring questions, the names came from marketplace listing pages, an agency directory, and three "best consultants" lists. On a question about recovering from a traffic drop, the answer named four well-known practitioners, and it found them through three recovery guides written by other people, none of them the practitioners' own pages. On the how-to questions, vendor blogs outnumbered practitioners' guides.

My own gaps were plain. I was absent from the roundups that supplied the hiring names, and none of my guides was among the sources cited for the how-to questions. The answers that did name me rested almost entirely on pages I wrote, and the assistant said so. That sets the work: listings and roundups first, because they are reachable, and third-party coverage over the following months.

## Closing a gap without buying your way in

Some roundups sell placement. A paid inclusion is an endorsement relationship, and the FTC's Endorsement Guides require a clear disclosure of any material connection between an advertiser and the person recommending it. An undisclosed paid placement is a legal problem before it is an SEO one, and a ranked list that discloses payment carries little weight with readers or with AI systems that read the disclosure. Pitch the editors on evidence instead: a specific result, a public case study, a quote they can use. I wrote separately about why [ranking yourself first in your own list](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/self-ranking-lists/) stopped working.

## Rerun it and watch the list move

Run the same questions monthly. A gap is closed when the source names you and the answers start to cite it beside your name. Sources drop out of the answers on their own as the assistants find newer pages, so pull the list fresh each month. Pair this with a log of identifiable referral visits, as described in my guide to [measuring AI search](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/measure-ai-search/), so the report shows outcomes as well as presence.

## Where I fit

I run citation gap analyses for companies and as a specialist on agency teams: the question set, the source collection, the ranked gap list, and the pitches or pages that close each gap. # How to write a content brief for pages AI search will quote

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

A content brief is a one-page instruction that settles a page's question, its answer, its evidence, and its limits before anyone writes a sentence. For AI search the brief carries more weight than it used to, because answer engines lift single passages out of a page and repeat them without the context around them. A page built from a good brief answers in its first lines, supports every claim, and stays inside its own question. I learned the discipline as an executive editor running a staff of writers, and it is the same job now with a new kind of reader.

## The question, word for word

Every brief starts with one question, written the way a buyer asks it. Take the wording from Search Console queries, sales call notes, or the questions in an AI visibility question set. "How do I fix Crawled, currently not indexed" is a brief. "Indexing issues" is a topic, and a page written from a topic answers nothing in particular.

Under the question, name who asks it and what they will decide after reading. A developer deciding whether a template is at fault needs a different page from a marketing director deciding whether to hire help, even when they type the same words.

## The answer, written by the expert first

The person who knows the subject writes the answer in two or three sentences before the writer starts. This is the passage an AI system is most likely to lift, so it has to stand alone: it names the thing, gives the answer, and includes the number or condition that makes it true. A writer can polish it. A writer working without it will produce a careful introduction that circles the answer for three paragraphs.

Google's guidance on helpful content asks whether a page provides original information and substantial value beyond what other pages offer. The expert's answer is where that originality lives: the threshold from your own projects, the failure you have seen five times, the step everyone skips.

## The evidence list

List every claim the page will make that a reader could doubt, and the source for each one: a vendor's documentation page, your own data with its date and sample, a public record. Writers open every source before citing it, and the brief says so. Answer engines cross-check, and a confident sentence with no support behind it is the sentence they drop or contradict.

Mark which evidence is first-party. Data from your own client work, anonymized, is the material no competitor can copy, and it is what turns a page into a source other pages cite.

## The sections, each one self-contained

Outline the sections as questions the reader will ask next, in the order they ask them. Each section opens with its own answer and makes sense if it is the only part quoted. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may run several related searches across subtopics to build a response, so a section that answers a sub-question cleanly can be the passage selected for that sub-search.

## The limits

A brief says what the page does not cover and where that material lives instead, with the link. This is how a site avoids two pages answering the same question, and it keeps each page short enough to finish. When the limit points to a page that doesn't exist yet, the brief has found the next brief.

## The links, title, and description

List the internal links the page must carry: up to the hub page for the subject, across to the pages a reader needs next, and from two or three existing pages that should now point to this one. Draft the title and meta description in the brief, inside the site's limits, because Google often uses the description for the snippet when it describes the page better than the page's own text. Structured data, where the page uses it, must match what the visible page says; Google's AI features guidance asks for exactly that.

## The review before publishing

Before a page goes live, someone other than the writer checks it against the brief: the answer is in the first lines, every claim has its source, the limits held, and every link resolves. AI drafting tools speed up the writing and change none of this. Google's guidance on generative AI content judges the result by its accuracy, quality, and relevance, and so does every reader who decides whether to trust you.

## Where I fit

I write briefs for clients' writers and agencies' content teams, supply the expert answer and the evidence list from the technical side, and review drafts before they publish. If your content team is producing pages that rank but never get quoted, [send me two of them](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/) and I'll show you what the brief was missing. For the source side of the same problem, see my guide to [citation gap analysis](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/citation-gap-analysis/).

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Your public GitHub README is a source AI search reads

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

If your website is built from a public GitHub repository, its README file is a public page, and AI assistants with web search read it. In October 2026 I asked Claude what gerriscorp.com was. Its answer quoted this site's own repository, and it described the site as a preview that hadn't launched, because the README still carried the setup notes I wrote before launch. The site had been live for nine days. The fix took ten minutes.

## Why a README gets read

GitHub shows a repository's README on its front page, so the file is public web content like any other. When an assistant searches for a site or a company and the repository ranks for that name, the README is often the most direct description it can find: who built the site, what it is for, and what state it is in. Developers write READMEs for other developers, in the present tense, and then stop updating them. An assistant can't tell a launch checklist from a status report.

Static sites on GitHub Pages, Netlify, and Vercel all tend to sit in public repositories. Agencies, open-source projects, and companies with developer documentation have the same exposure: every public repository that names the company is a page that can describe it.

## What to put at the top

Open the README with two sentences for the reader who arrived from a search: what the repository builds, the live address, and the date it went live. Then say where to learn about the company itself. Mine now begins: "This repository builds https://gerriscorp.com, live since October 5, 2026. For what Gerris Corp does and who runs it, read the site; this file only explains how the site is built."

Below that, write for developers as before. Rewrite any section that describes a past state as current: "the site starts as a noindexed preview" becomes a short "Live" section with the date.

## Keep it current on the same schedule as the site

Treat the README as a page of the site. When the site's status, name, address, or ownership changes, the README changes in the same commit. A check in the build can enforce it: fail when the README mentions "preview" or "staging" while the site is set to live. My build scripts already check titles, descriptions, and links on every run, and the README is one more file to check.

## Check every repository that names you

The live site's repository is rarely the only one. Old prototypes, a redesign that never shipped, a fork a contractor made, and a project from a previous company name can all sit in public accounts with READMEs describing a state of affairs that ended years ago. Search GitHub for the company name and the domain. An archived repository stays public and readable; archiving only freezes it. For each one that describes a past state, either add a first line that says so and links the current site, or make it private if nothing in it needs to stay public.

## Keep confidential material out of it

A public README is public. Client names, internal hostnames, credentials, and notes about how a client relationship works belong in a private file. I keep a separate briefing file for each of my sites, listed in the repository's ignore file so it never reaches GitHub. If a public README already contains something private, edit it and treat the old version as exposed, since the history is public too. GitHub's documentation on repository visibility explains what changing a repository to private does and doesn't hide.

## Check what the assistants say

Ask an assistant with web search to describe your company and your site, then read the sources it cites. If a repository appears among them, read its README the way a stranger would. Google's guidance for its AI features applies here as everywhere: the content the systems can find is the content they use. My guide to [citation gap analysis](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/citation-gap-analysis/) covers checking sources systematically, and [giving your SEO repository access](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/repository-access/) covers working in the repository itself.

## Where I fit

I audit the public sources that describe a company, repositories included, and fix what they say. If your site is built from a public repository, [send me the link](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/) and I'll tell you what an assistant would learn from it.

# Speculation rules: make the next page open instantly in Chrome

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 14, 2026

Speculation rules are a short block of JSON in a script tag that tells Chrome and Edge which links to load before the reader clicks them. When the reader does click, the page is already in memory and opens at once. I added one rule to every site I run in October 2026. It costs nothing in browsers that don't support it, and on a static site it takes about five minutes.

## Prefetch or prerender

A prefetch downloads the next page's HTML and holds it in memory without rendering it. A prerender goes further: Chrome's documentation says the page behaves as if it had been opened in an invisible background tab, then is shown when the reader arrives. Prerender is faster still and uses more memory and bandwidth, and it runs the page's scripts before anyone sees the page.

I use prefetch. It removes the network wait, which is most of the delay on a static site, and it runs no scripts early, so analytics, consent tools, and anything else that should only run for a real visit behave exactly as before. Prerender suits sites whose pages are heavy to render and whose scripts are built to handle it. Chrome also caps how much it will speculate: its documentation allows up to 50 immediate prefetches and 10 immediate prerenders per page, so a rule that matches every link on a long page cannot flood the network.

## Choose the eagerness

Eagerness sets how early Chrome acts on a rule. The four levels, from Chrome's documentation:
- **immediate:** as soon as the rule is seen.
- **eager:** on desktop, when the pointer rests on a link for 10 milliseconds; on mobile, shortly after a link enters the viewport.
- **moderate:** on desktop, when the pointer rests on a link for 200 milliseconds, or on pointer down if that comes first; on mobile, using viewport heuristics after the reader stops scrolling.
- **conservative:** on pointer or touch down, the default for rules that match links on the page.

Moderate is the setting I use. A 200-millisecond hover is a good signal of intent, and it fetches few pages the reader never opens.

## The rule I use

```
<script type="speculationrules">
{"prefetch": [{"where": {"and": [
  {"href_matches": "/*"},
  {"not": {"href_matches": ["/*.md", "/*.txt", "/*.xml"]}}
]}, "eagerness": "moderate"}]}
</script>
```

It matches every same-site link and excludes the files no reader opens in a browser: Markdown copies, llms.txt, and XML feeds and sitemaps. Exclude anything with side effects as well. A logout link, an "add to cart" URL, or any GET request that changes state must never be prefetched. On a static site there are none; on an application, list them.

## Check that it works

Open the site in Chrome, open DevTools, and go to the Application panel. Under background services, the speculative loads view lists the rules Chrome found on the page and the status of each speculation: not triggered, running, ready, or failed, with the reason for any failure. Hover over a link for a moment and watch its entry change. The Network panel shows the prefetch request itself.

Chrome marks speculative requests with a Sec-Purpose request header, set to prefetch for a prefetch. That gives servers and log analysis a way to separate speculative fetches from real visits. A static host serves the page either way. A site that counts visits on the server side should exclude requests carrying that header, so prefetches never inflate the numbers.

## Browser support

Chrome and Edge support speculation rules, with eagerness settings since version 121. Firefox does not support them, and Safari has them behind a flag. Unsupported browsers ignore the script tag, so the rule degrades to an ordinary link.

## What it changes

Lighthouse measures a single page load, so speculation rules leave its scores where they were. What changes is the second page: the reader clicks and the page is already there. That is the part of speed a visitor notices most. In field data, the prefetched page's Largest Contentful Paint starts from a page already in memory, so real-user loading times improve once enough visits have been recorded.

## Where I fit

I add speculation rules as part of a [site speed](https://gerriscorp.com/services/site-speed/) engagement, along with the work Lighthouse does measure: render-blocking resources, image sizes, and third-party scripts. For the measurement side, start with my guide to [Core Web Vitals](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/core-web-vitals/).

# IndexNow, Bing, and a practical AI search workflow for fall 2026

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 12, 2026

A website can publish excellent advice and still have a poor release process. The repository changes, the build finishes, a notification runs, and nobody checks which version reached the public domain. My priority for AI search this fall is making that chain observable. Give each release a clear destination, verify the content there, and keep evidence of what happened afterward.

## Assign a separate job to each part of the system

A sitemap describes the site's intended public inventory. Internal links give visitors and crawlers routes through it. An RSS feed distributes articles to subscribers and other publishing systems. IndexNow sends change notifications to participating engines. None of these substitutes for a page that explains something accurately.

The distinctions matter when a stakeholder asks whether a guide has been “submitted to AI.” There is no single submission step that covers every assistant. Search products can retrieve information through different providers and their own crawlers. IndexNow can support freshness in participating indexes, but it is not a pipeline into every language model.

I would name the checkpoints in a release record: committed, built, deployed, publicly verified, notified, crawled, and indexed. A citation is another observation, not a synonym for any of those states. That vocabulary prevents a green build badge from becoming an unsupported visibility claim.

## Prepare the page before setting up notifications

Choose a permanent address and connect it to the right guide category. Confirm the title describes the question, the introduction supplies an answer, and the author's identity is clear. Check the visible content against the structured data. If a comparison uses numbers, publish the assumptions and the date of the comparison.

Then request the public address directly. It should return the expected page without requiring an editor session. Inspect the canonical and indexing controls, and test important images and downloadable resources. Compare the raw HTML with the rendered page when JavaScript is involved. My [JavaScript visibility guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/) provides a focused diagnostic sequence.

Google's AI search documentation keeps the eligibility requirements within ordinary Search: the page must be indexed and allowed to appear with a snippet. Extra AI specific markup is not required. I would spend the first hour correcting access or content problems before adding another machine readable file.

## Make IndexNow part of the release process

The protocol verifies control of a host through a key file. Publish that file where the submitted key location points, and confirm its contents from the public domain. Submit the final URLs on that host, rather than preview addresses or a development domain. Preserve the verification file through template changes and migrations.

Send notifications for meaningful additions, revisions, or removals. The documentation permits batches of up to 10,000 URLs, but a normal editorial release rarely needs that many. A deployment that changes only a decorative detail does not justify repeatedly announcing the entire archive.

For a static site, the sequence I would implement is:
1. Build the source and validate the generated HTML, sitemap, and feeds.
2. Publish the approved commit to the production host.
3. Wait until the changed public pages match the intended release.
4. Submit the affected URL inventory to IndexNow.
5. Save the response and review engine reporting later.

A successful API response records acceptance, not a completed crawl. A response awaiting key verification also needs follow-up. Record the HTTP status alongside the host, time, and submitted count. If a request fails, inspect the cause before retrying; do not create an endless loop that hides a broken verification file.

## Use Bing Webmaster Tools as a diagnostic instrument

Verify the business domain in Bing Webmaster Tools and review its sitemap and URL inspection information. Look at the exact production address when investigating a missing article. Keep old and new URLs together during a migration so a redirect can be evaluated against its intended destination.

A submission report and an index report answer different questions. If a URL was notified but remains unavailable in search, examine the content, access rules, canonical choice, and engine feedback. Repeated submissions do not fix an incorrect canonical or a page that needs authentication.

I would also retain the existing Google Search Console routine. IndexNow's participant list does not currently include Google. Use the site's Google reports to assess Google discovery and indexing rather than infer success from a Bing notification.

## Give the Guides a feed that another site can actually use

A summary feed is enough for a headline widget. Republishing a Guide needs more: article content, a stable identifier, a source link, reliable dates, and absolute links inside the imported body. A relative image or navigation address that works on the originating website may point somewhere else after import.

The [Gerris Guides RSS feed](https://gerriscorp.com/rss.xml) carries full article content, and the [Atom version](https://gerriscorp.com/feed.xml) provides an alternative. An importer should preserve the original source URL and recognize the same identifier on subsequent runs. Test one article in Plone before enabling automatic ingestion for the whole archive.

Decide whether the destination displays excerpts or republishes complete articles. A full copy deserves visible attribution and a deliberate canonical policy. A feed cannot control the metadata that a separate CMS emits. Check the resulting Plone page, including its links and images, rather than assume feed parsing completed the SEO work.

## Measure the business result independently

For each release, retain a short note of the question it answers, the production URL, the publication date, and the intended reader. Review search visibility and referred traffic against that record. If you test assistant answers, keep the question wording and the linked sources so another person can inspect the observation.

The strongest operational outcome is a process that can distinguish publication failure from indexing delay and editorial weakness. Those require different remedies. Start with one useful Guide, establish the checkpoints, then repeat the process for the next article. For broader release planning, the [website migration checklist](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-checklist/) shows how inventories and verification fit together.

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# How AI assistants decide what to say about your business

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026

When someone asks ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, or Google's AI Overviews about your company, the answer comes from two places: what the model learned in training, and what it finds by searching the web right then. You can influence both, and the second is where most of the action is.

## Two sources of knowledge

### Training data

Every large language model is trained on a huge snapshot of text, much of it crawled from the public web, and that knowledge stops at a training cutoff. What a model "knows" about you from training reflects whatever was public and widely repeated before that date. It changes only when the company trains a new model, so it lags reality by months or years. Older press coverage, Wikipedia, directories, and anything that was repeated often all weigh heavily here.

### Live retrieval

Most assistants now search the web before answering questions about specific businesses, products, and recent events. The assistant turns the question into one or more searches, reads the top results, and writes an answer grounded in those pages, often with citations. This is called retrieval or grounding, and it means a page that ranks well and answers the question clearly can shape the answer within days of being published.

## Which search indexes feed which assistants
- **Google AI Overviews and AI Mode** are built on Google Search's own index, crawled by Googlebot.
- **Gemini** grounds its answers with Google Search.
- **Microsoft Copilot** uses Bing's index.
- **ChatGPT search** uses OpenAI's own crawler, OAI-SearchBot, alongside third-party search providers.
- **Perplexity** runs its own crawler, PerplexityBot, and its own index.
- **Claude** searches the web through a search provider and fetches pages with Anthropic's crawlers.

The practical lesson: being well indexed in both Google and Bing covers most of the AI landscape. Bing Webmaster Tools and IndexNow, which tells Bing and other engines about changed pages within minutes, matter more than they used to.

## The crawlers, and what each one is for
| Company | Training | Search index | Fetches for a user |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | GPTBot | OAI-SearchBot | ChatGPT-User |
| Anthropic | ClaudeBot | Claude-SearchBot | Claude-User |
| Perplexity | (none listed) | PerplexityBot | Perplexity-User |
| Google | Google-Extended (a robots.txt token) | Googlebot | Google's user-triggered fetchers |

You can allow or block each in robots.txt. Blocking a training crawler keeps your future pages out of future models; blocking a search crawler keeps you out of that assistant's live answers. Google-Extended controls whether your content is used for Gemini, and it doesn't affect Google Search or AI Overviews, which follow Googlebot. Check your CDN, too: Cloudflare began blocking many AI crawlers by default on new setups in 2025, which can keep a business out of AI answers without anyone deciding that on purpose.

## What assistants favor when they write an answer
- **Direct answers.** Pages that state the answer plainly near the top, in a sentence that still makes sense when quoted on its own.
- **Self-contained context.** Definitions, dates, locations, and names on the page itself, so the assistant doesn't have to guess.
- **Consistency.** The same facts about you on your site, your profiles, directories, and press. Conflicting facts produce hedged or wrong answers.
- **Third-party confirmation.** Reviews, news coverage, industry directories, and community discussions. Assistants treat what others say about you as evidence.
- **Freshness.** Visible "updated" dates and current information, especially for anything that changes.
- **Readable HTML.** Most AI crawlers fetch the HTML without running JavaScript, so content that appears only after scripts run is invisible to them. The [JavaScript SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/) shows how to check.

## What you can do this quarter
1. Ask the major assistants the ten questions your buyers ask, and write down the answers and the sources cited.
2. Fix your own pages first: one clear page per service or product, with the facts stated plainly and an FAQ section with real answers.
3. Make your facts consistent everywhere: name, description, location, founding date, leadership, services, prices where public.
4. Add schema.org structured data for your organization, people, products, and services, matching the visible page.
5. Check robots.txt and your CDN's bot settings for the AI crawlers you want.
6. Submit your sitemap to Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, and turn on IndexNow.
7. Consider an [llms.txt](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/glossary/#llms-txt) file. It's a proposed convention from 2024 that gives language models a plain summary of your site; adoption by AI companies is still uncertain, and it costs almost nothing.
8. Repeat the same questions in a month and compare.

## Measuring it

AI answers vary with phrasing, location, account history, and time, so a single test proves little. Use a fixed set of prompts, run them on a schedule, and record the answers and citations. Add referral traffic from chatgpt.com, perplexity.ai, gemini.google.com, and copilot.microsoft.com in analytics, and watch which pages they land on.

# When a Customer Asks for the Best, a Machine Answers

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 23, 2026 · Updated October 24, 2026

Somebody in your service area is, right now, asking Google a question like "best [your trade] near me" or "who should I call for [your service]." A year ago they got a list of businesses and made their own shortlist. Today they get a written answer: two or three names, a sentence about each, and a recommendation. If your name is missing from that paragraph, the shortlist was made without you.

The shift is already measured. [Search Engine Land](https://searchengineland.com/google-ai-overviews-nearly-double-commercial-keywords-498078), reporting Semrush's tracking of 400 US desktop commercial keywords, found that Google's AI Overviews appeared for 88% of them in August 2026, nearly double the share in September 2025. Review searches, exactly the "best," "top-rated," and "near me" questions above, moved the furthest. The searches that end in a phone call are the searches the machines took over first.

## What the answer says about a business nobody is tending

An AI answer is only as good as the record it is built from: your website, your Google Business Profile, your listings, and your reviews, reconciled by a system that cannot call you to check. When that record is untended, the answer still arrives, and it arrives wrong in predictable ways:
- **It names a competitor** whose facts happen to agree with each other across sources, because agreement is what the system reads as truth.
- **It describes the business you used to be**, services you dropped, a location you closed, hours you changed, because old listings never die on their own.
- **It blends you with somebody else**: a similarly named business across town or across the country, your details and theirs averaged into a company that does not exist.
- **It leaves you out entirely** on the searches that carry the most money, while happily citing you for trivia.

Each of those is what an untended record produces, automatically, every day.

## Why service businesses sit in the blast radius

Review and recommendation searches are buying searches. The person asking has a problem, a budget, and a short afternoon. For many of them, the machine's paragraph is the whole of their research. A business can have loyal customers, strong reviews, and a good website, and still lose that customer before the first click, because the answer was assembled from a profile nobody has opened in three years and a directory listing nobody claimed.

The good news is that the same mechanism cuts the other way. The answer rewards the business whose record is consistent, complete, and claimed. That is work. It is also, for once, work a smaller business can finish before a bigger competitor bothers to start.

## Check it yourself in ten minutes

Pick the three searches that bring you the most work, such as "best roofer in Arlington" or "emergency plumber near me," and run each one in Google, ChatGPT, and Perplexity. Write down whether you're named, how you're described, and which source each answer cites. Then open your Google Business Profile and compare its name, hours, services, and service area with your website. Every mismatch you find is a fact the machines can read two ways. Google's own guidance says there are no special tricks for AI Overviews: a page has to be indexed and eligible to show a snippet, and the rest is ordinary, accurate SEO.

## What Gerris does about it

The work comes in three fixed pieces, described in full on the [AI visibility service page](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ai-visibility/). The **audit** ($750) runs your money searches through Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Gemini and checks your details everywhere the machines look, ending in a ranked written fix list. The **Claim Sprint** ($1,500) repairs the technical base and adds the claim layer: entity schema, llms.txt, a canonical page that states what the business is, and FAQ markup. **AI Presence, Measured** ($500 a month) reruns the searches monthly and reports what moved.

## Your Google Business Profile is doing more talking than you think

For local and service businesses, the Google Business Profile is one of the primary sources the AI answers are built from. A suspended profile, a duplicate listing, a wrong service area, or a category that undersells you spreads from Maps into every answer the machines give about you. My [profile work](https://gerriscorp.com/services/google-business-profile/), covering service-area configuration, reinstatement support, and cleanup, runs under the same direction as my search work for one reason: your profile, your website, and your listings have to tell one story, because one story is what the machines believe.

## Start with the audit

Find out what the machines say about your business with one fixed-price audit, read it, and decide from evidence. **[Contact Gerris](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/) to start with the audit.**

# How to tell if JavaScript is hiding your content from Google and AI

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026

A page can look complete in a browser and nearly empty to a crawler. When the important content depends on JavaScript, search engines may see less of it, later, and AI crawlers may not see it at all.

## How crawlers handle JavaScript

Googlebot renders pages with an up-to-date version of Chromium, so it can run JavaScript. Rendering happens in a queue after the initial crawl, though, and the renderer behaves like a very patient visitor who never clicks, never types, and never scrolls the way a person does. It loads the page with a tall viewport and takes a snapshot. Content that waits for a click, a real scroll event, or a user action can be missing from that snapshot.

Most AI crawlers are simpler. GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, and similar crawlers generally fetch the HTML the server sends and read it without running JavaScript. If your product details, prices, reviews, or answers exist only after scripts run, those crawlers see a shell.

## Five tests that settle it

### 1. Compare view-source with the rendered page

Open the page, then open view-source. View-source shows the HTML your server sent; the Elements panel in developer tools shows the DOM after JavaScript ran. Search view-source for a sentence from the content you care about. If it's missing, crawlers that don't render can't see it.

### 2. Fetch it from the command line

```
curl -sL https://example.com/products/widget-200 | grep -c "Specifications"
```

A count of zero means the text isn't in the server's HTML.

### 3. Disable JavaScript

Turn off JavaScript in your browser's developer tools and reload. What remains is roughly what a non-rendering crawler gets.

### 4. Ask Google directly

In Search Console, run URL Inspection on the page, click "Test live URL," then "View tested page" and the HTML tab. That's the HTML Google rendered. If your content is missing there, Google doesn't have it.

### 5. Crawl both ways

Crawl a sample of pages in Screaming Frog with JavaScript rendering off, then on, and compare word counts by template. In one diagnosis I ran, category pages yielded thousands of words while flagship product pages yielded 250 to 400 words despite weighing more than a megabyte, which pointed straight at the product template.

## Common causes
- **Client-side rendering.** Single-page apps that send an empty HTML shell and build the page in the browser.
- **Content that loads on scroll or interaction.** Sections rendered only when they enter the viewport after a real scroll, such as Alpine.js `x-if` combined with `x-intersect`, or reviews fetched when a visitor scrolls near them.
- **Content that loads on click.** Tabs and accordions that fetch their content when opened. Tabs that merely hide content already in the HTML are fine.
- **Links without real URLs.** Navigation built with click handlers instead of `<a href>` links, which crawlers can't follow.
- **Infinite scroll without paginated URLs.** Products beyond the first batch never get a crawlable link.
- **Metadata changed by JavaScript.** Titles, canonical tags, or robots directives rewritten after load, so the raw HTML and the rendered page disagree.
- **Blocked resources.** JavaScript or CSS files disallowed in robots.txt, which prevents Google from rendering the page properly.

## Fixes
- **Render on the server.** Server-side rendering or static generation puts the content in the initial HTML. Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, Astro, and similar frameworks do this well when pages are configured for it.
- **Keep content in the HTML and hide it with CSS.** In Alpine.js, `x-show` keeps an element in the DOM and only toggles visibility, while `x-if` removes it entirely until the condition is true. Use animation as progressive enhancement on content that's already present.
- **Use real links and paginated URLs** for navigation and long lists.
- **Put titles, canonicals, and structured data in the server's HTML**, and keep them unchanged after load.
- **Avoid dynamic rendering** as a long-term answer. Google describes serving crawlers a separately rendered version as a workaround, and server rendering is the durable fix.

## Writing the ticket

Developers fix these problems fastest with evidence: the affected template, example URLs, the word count with and without rendering, the Search Console live test result, and a testable definition of done, such as "a curl of the product URL returns the specification table." There's a [sample ticket on the developers page](https://gerriscorp.com/services/developers/).

I diagnose rendering problems as part of [technical SEO forensics](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-seo/).

# React hydration errors and what they mean for SEO

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

If your browser console on a React or Next.js site shows "Minified React error #418," the page has a hydration error. It rarely stops Google from indexing the content, so it's easy to leave alone. It still costs you layout stability, responsiveness, and trustworthy analytics, and it usually points at a markup fault worth fixing at the source.

## What hydration is

A server rendered React page arrives as finished HTML, so visitors and crawlers see content immediately. Then React loads in the browser and "attaches" itself to that HTML, wiring up buttons, menus, and forms. React calls this hydration: it turns the server's HTML snapshot into an interactive app.

For that to work, the HTML React expects to find has to match what the server sent. React's documentation says it expects the rendered content to be identical, and that you should treat mismatches as bugs and fix them.

## What error #418 means

Production builds of React strip long error messages to save bytes and print a number instead. React's error page decodes #418 as: hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client, and as a result the tree will be regenerated on the client. In plain terms, React gave up on the server's HTML for that part of the page and built it again in the browser.

## What it means for search

Google crawls the server's response first, and server rendering means the content is already in that HTML. Google's JavaScript SEO documentation still recommends server-side or pre-rendering for exactly that reason: it's faster for users and crawlers, and not every bot runs JavaScript. A hydration error happens after that HTML is delivered, so the words on the page usually still reach the index.

The costs show up elsewhere:
- **Layout shift.** When React throws away server markup and re-renders, elements can jump, which counts against Cumulative Layout Shift.
- **Slower interaction.** Rebuilding part of the page on the main thread can delay the response to the visitor's first tap or click, which shows up in Interaction to Next Paint.
- **Broken widgets.** Components in the rebuilt section lose whatever state they had, so a menu, carousel, or form can reset or stop responding.
- **Messy analytics.** Tags that fire on load can fire twice, or against elements that have since been replaced.

Head tags are a separate concern. In Next.js, metadata set with `generateMetadata` or a `metadata` export is resolved on the server and sent as HTML, so titles and canonicals don't depend on hydration succeeding.

## The usual causes

React's own list covers most of what I find on real sites:
- **Invalid nesting.** A `div` inside a `p`, or a link inside a link. The browser's HTML parser rearranges invalid nesting as it reads the page, so the DOM no longer matches the tree React rendered on the server.
- **Unbalanced HTML from a CMS.** Rich text injected with `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` that contains a stray closing tag or an unclosed element. The browser repairs it on the way in, and React finds a different structure from the one it expected.
- **Dates and locales.** A date formatted on the server in one time zone or locale and on the client in another.
- **Random values.** IDs or keys generated with `Math.random()` or `Date.now()`, which differ between the two renders.
- **Browser checks during render.** A branch like `typeof window !== 'undefined'` that renders one thing on the server and another in the browser.
- **Browser extensions.** Extensions that edit the page before React loads. These show up only for some visitors and aren't yours to fix, which is why it's worth reproducing in a clean browser profile first.

## Finding them across a whole site

The browser console shows you one page at a time, and hydration errors often live on a handful of templates or on pages whose CMS content happens to contain bad markup. Spot checking misses them. I script headless Chrome with Playwright to load every URL in the sitemap or the crawl, collect each console error with the URL it came from, and group the results by template. A few hundred pages run in minutes.

The production build tells you only that a mismatch happened. To see where, run the same page against a development build, where React warns about each mismatch with its full message instead of a number. Once the list is grouped, the cause for each template is usually obvious within a few minutes of reading.

## Fixing them at the source
- **Correct the nesting** in the component, using a `div` or `span` where a paragraph can't legally contain the child.
- **Repair the content** that carries unbalanced HTML, and sanitize rich text on the way into the CMS or at render time.
- **Make server and client agree** on dates by fixing the time zone and locale, and generate IDs with React's `useId` rather than random numbers.
- **Move browser only logic** into an effect that runs after hydration.
- **Silence only the unavoidable.** React offers `suppressHydrationWarning` for a single element whose text must differ, such as a timestamp. Use it on that element and nowhere else.

Then stop the problem coming back. A small check in the build that parses every rendered page and fails on unbalanced tags or invalid nesting catches the CMS content that would have caused the next one.

I find and fix these as part of [SEO engineering](https://gerriscorp.com/services/seo-engineering/) and [rendering diagnosis](https://gerriscorp.com/services/crawler-visibility/). For the wider rendering picture, see the [JavaScript SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/) and [Core Web Vitals](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/core-web-vitals/).
