# How to give an outside SEO safe access to your code repository

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

On a site built with Next.js, React, or a headless CMS, the search problems live in the code, so the person fixing them needs to see it. Granting that access is a small, routine job when you set it up in the right order. Here is the order I ask clients to follow, and the reasons behind each step.

## Why an SEO asks for the repository at all

A crawl tells me that 900 pages share a title. The repository tells me which component writes it, which data it reads, and whether a fix will reach every route that uses it. Without the code, I write a ticket describing the symptom and your developer goes looking for the cause. With it, the ticket names the file, or arrives as a pull request ready for review. Read access alone usually cuts the time from finding to fix by a wide margin.

## Invite them to one repository, as an outside collaborator

On GitHub, a consultant belongs outside your organization's membership. Add them as an outside collaborator on the one repository that builds the website, rather than as an organization member who inherits base permissions across everything you own. Your other repositories, your internal tools, and your infrastructure code stay out of view. If the site is split across a frontend and a content repository, add them to both and nothing else.

## Start with the Read role

GitHub's repository roles, from least access to most, are Read, Triage, Write, Maintain, and Admin. GitHub's own guidance is to pick the role that fits each person's function without giving them more access than they need.
- **Read** is GitHub's role for people who view or discuss a project without changing it. That covers the whole diagnostic phase.
- **Triage** adds managing issues and pull requests without write access, which suits a consultant who files tickets in your tracker.
- **Write** is for contributors who push to the project, which an SEO needs only once they start making changes themselves.
- **Maintain** and **Admin** are for your own team. An outside SEO never needs either.

GitLab has its own set: Guest, Reporter, Developer, Maintainer, and Owner, ordered from fewest permissions to most, plus specialized Planner and Security Manager roles. Reporter is the usual starting point for an outside reviewer there, and Developer is roughly the equivalent of GitHub's Write.

## Grant Write only after main is protected

Before anyone outside your team can push, make sure nobody can push straight to your main branch. On GitHub, a ruleset or a branch protection rule controls who can push to a branch and can require reviews on pull requests before they merge. GitHub's documentation notes that when both a ruleset and a protection rule apply to the same branch, all the rules apply, and the most restrictive version of each wins.

With that in place, Write access becomes safe: the consultant can create branches and open pull requests, and every change still waits for one of your people to approve it. Nothing they write reaches production without your review.

## Use deploy previews to see each change before merge

Netlify builds a Deploy Preview for pull requests in a connected GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or Azure DevOps repository, and Vercel creates a preview deployment for every push to a non-production branch and every pull request. Each preview gets its own URL. Your team can click through the change, and I can check what a crawler will see on it: titles, canonicals, structured data, status codes, and rendered content. Netlify adds an `X-Robots-Tag: noindex` header to its previews, which asks search engines to leave them out of results. For anything sensitive, Netlify recommends password protection on top.

## Keep secrets out of the repository

API keys, database passwords, and tokens belong in your host's environment variables, never in a committed file. Anyone you give read access can read every file and its history, so a key committed two years ago and deleted since is still visible to them. Two habits protect you:
- **Turn on push protection.** GitHub's push protection is a secret scanning feature that blocks pushes containing recognized credentials before they reach the repository, from the command line, the web interface, and the API.
- **Rotate anything that ever leaked.** If secret scanning finds an old key in the history, revoke it and issue a new one before you invite anyone in.

An SEO needs no production credentials to do this work. If someone asks for them, ask why.

## The CMS only option

Some teams can't open the codebase, for contractual or security reasons. That still leaves plenty of room. Give the consultant an editor role in the CMS for content, titles, and descriptions, Search Console access, and the preview URLs. They write tickets with the evidence and the acceptance criteria, and your developer makes the code changes. It's slower, and it works.

## Remove access when the engagement ends

Put the end date in your own calendar on the day you grant access. When the work finishes, remove the outside collaborator from the repository, take them out of Search Console and the hosting dashboard, and revoke any deploy keys or tokens created for the engagement.

## A checklist for the day you say yes
1. Invite the consultant as an outside collaborator on the website repository only.
2. Assign Read on GitHub, or Reporter on GitLab.
3. Confirm deploy previews are switched on for pull requests.
4. Check that push protection or secret scanning is enabled and the history is clean.
5. Add a ruleset or branch protection requiring a reviewed pull request on main.
6. Move to Write, or Developer, only once that rule is in place.
7. Set a reminder to remove every grant at the end date.

This is the setup I ask for at the start of an [SEO engineering](https://gerriscorp.com/services/seo-engineering/) engagement. For how I work once I'm in, see [developer specs and QA](https://gerriscorp.com/services/developers/) and the guide to [working safely with AI coding assistants](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-coding-assistants/).

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com)

If your company hires through Upwork, you'll find me [there as well](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

# A Next.js SEO checklist for the App Router

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

Next.js gives you everything a search engine needs, as code: metadata, sitemaps, robots rules, redirects, and status codes. Every one of them can also be left at a default that quietly hurts you. This is the list I work through on every Next.js site, in the order I check it.

## 1. Every route sets its own title and description

In the App Router, metadata comes from a `metadata` object or a `generateMetadata` function exported from a layout or page. Static pages can use the object. Pages built from data, such as products, posts, and locations, need `generateMetadata` so each URL gets its own title and description from its own record.

Both exports work only in Server Components, which keeps the tags in the server's HTML. If a page needs client-side features, keep `page.tsx` as a Server Component and move the interactive parts into a child component.

## 2. The title template does what you meant

A `title.template` in the root layout, such as `'%s | Brand'`, adds a suffix to every child page's title, and `title.default` fills in for pages that set none. That's convenient, and it's also how a site ends up with 2,000 pages titled with the brand name alone. Crawl the site and sort titles by frequency: any title used more than a few times is a page that fell through to the default.

## 3. Canonicals are set per route, with a metadataBase

Set `metadataBase` once in the root layout, then give each route `alternates.canonical`. Next.js combines the two into a full URL. Check the output on routes with query strings and on paginated lists, where a template canonical copied from the parent layout can point every page at page one.

## 4. You know what crawlers receive when metadata streams

When `generateMetadata` waits on request time data, Next.js can stream the page first and append the metadata tags to the body once they resolve. It does that for crawlers it expects to run JavaScript, such as Googlebot, and blocks rendering to put the tags in the head for a list of HTML limited bots, including Bingbot, social preview bots, and several others. GPTBot, ClaudeBot, and PerplexityBot are absent from the default list in the Next.js source. If AI crawler visibility matters to you, fetch your key pages with those user agents and check where the title and canonical land. The `htmlLimitedBots` option in the Next.js config lets you add them, at some cost in response time.

## 5. The sitemap is generated, complete, and honest

An `app/sitemap.ts` file that returns an array of URLs produces `/sitemap.xml`. Generate it from the same data source as the routes, include only canonical, indexable URLs that return 200, and set `lastModified` from the content's real update date rather than the build time. Large sites can split into several sitemaps. Compare the sitemap with a crawl: every URL in one should be in the other.

## 6. robots.ts says what you mean, for each crawler

An `app/robots.ts` file generates `/robots.txt`, with rules per user agent and a sitemap line. Decide deliberately about AI crawlers, and make sure preview and staging deployments disallow everything while production allows what you intend. A single environment variable deciding which robots file ships is a common source of a production site that tells every crawler to stay out.

## 7. Redirects are permanent where you mean permanent

Redirects in `next.config.js` take a `source`, a `destination`, and a `permanent` flag. With `permanent: true` Next.js returns a 308, the permanent status that tells browsers and search engines to remember the move. With `false` it returns a 307, a temporary redirect that nothing caches. A migration map written with `permanent: false` tells search engines to keep the old URLs. Check every rule's flag, and test the map against a crawl of the old site.

## 8. Missing pages return a real 404

Calling `notFound()` renders the not-found page, returns a 404, and adds a noindex tag. One catch: if the check runs inside a Suspense boundary after the response has started streaming, the status is already sent, so the page keeps its 200 and relies on the noindex tag. Run the existence check before streaming begins on routes where a real 404 matters, such as products and posts that get deleted. Then crawl a list of deliberately broken URLs and confirm the status codes.

## 9. JSON-LD is rendered in the component

The Next.js recommendation is a plain `<script type="application/ld+json">` in the layout or page, built from the same data as the visible content. Escape the `<` character in the JSON, as the Next.js guide shows, so content from a CMS can't inject script. Validate a sample from each template with the Rich Results Test or the Schema Markup Validator.

## 10. Navigation uses real links

The `Link` component extends the HTML anchor element, so it produces an `<a href>` that crawlers can follow. Navigation built from buttons with `router.push` in a click handler produces no link at all. Search the codebase for click handlers that navigate, and crawl with JavaScript rendering off to see which pages are reachable from plain HTML.

## 11. The rendered page matches the server page

Finally, compare the raw HTML with the rendered DOM on each template, and run the pages in headless Chrome to collect console errors. Hydration mismatches, content that loads only after interaction, and client-side redirects all show up here. The [guide to React hydration errors](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/hydration-errors/) covers the most common fault.

## Make the checklist permanent

Every item above can become an automated check in the build, so a future change can't undo it. That's the subject of [adding SEO tests to your website's build](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/seo-build-checks/).

I work through this list, and fix what it finds, as part of [SEO engineering](https://gerriscorp.com/services/seo-engineering/) for Next.js and React sites. If you're bringing me into your repository, start with [how to give an outside SEO safe access](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/repository-access/).

# How to add SEO regression tests to your website's build

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

Most SEO damage on a coded website arrives in an ordinary pull request. Someone refactors a layout, and the canonical tag disappears from 4,000 pages. A content import runs, and every description is blank. Nobody notices for a month, because nobody was looking. A short set of automated checks, run on every build, looks every time. Here is what to test and how to wire it in.

## Where the checks run

Continuous integration runs your tests automatically whenever code is pushed. On GitHub Actions, the results appear on the pull request itself, so a reviewer sees a failed check before anyone merges. SEO tests belong in the same place as the unit tests your developers already run: they're just tests whose subject is the built HTML.

The simplest pattern is to build the site, then run a script over the output. A static or prerendered site produces a folder of HTML files to read directly. A server rendered site can be started in the CI job and fetched page by page from a list of representative URLs, one per template.

## The checks worth having

### Titles and descriptions
- Every page has exactly one title element and one meta description, and neither is empty.
- No two pages share a title or a description. Google's documentation asks for distinct titles on every page and warns against repeated or boilerplate text, and it says the same of descriptions.
- Lengths stay inside a range you choose. Google sets no length limit and truncates to fit the device, so the range is a house style. Mine is 50 to 60 characters for titles and 140 to 160 for descriptions, and the build enforces it.

### Indexing signals
- Every indexable page carries exactly one canonical tag, pointing at its own production URL.
- No production page carries a noindex, unless it's on an explicit allow list.
- robots.txt in the production build allows what you expect and lists the sitemap.

### Sitemap agreement
- Every URL in the sitemap exists in the build and returns 200.
- Every indexable page in the build appears in the sitemap.

### Structured data
- Every JSON-LD block parses as valid JSON.
- Each template emits the types it should, such as Product on product pages and Article on posts.
- Key values match the visible page. Google's guidelines say structured data should represent the main content of the page and describe content the user can see, so a price or a name in the JSON-LD that differs from the page is a real fault.

### Headings and markup
- Exactly one H1 per page.
- The HTML parses with balanced tags and no invalid nesting, which also heads off a class of React hydration errors.

### Links
- Every internal link points at a page that exists in the build.
- No internal link points at a URL that redirects, so links go straight to the final address.

## A minimal example

A check doesn't need a framework. This Python sketch reads every built page and fails the build on a missing or duplicate title:

```
import pathlib, re, sys
seen, problems = {}, []
for page in pathlib.Path("out").rglob("*.html"):
    html = page.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    titles = re.findall(r"<title>(.*?)</title>", html, re.S)
    if len(titles) != 1:
        problems.append(f"{page}: {len(titles)} title elements")
        continue
    seen.setdefault(titles[0].strip(), []).append(str(page))
for title, pages in seen.items():
    if len(pages) > 1:
        problems.append(f"duplicate title {title!r}: {pages}")
print("\n".join(problems))
sys.exit(1 if problems else 0)
```

Add a step to the CI workflow that runs it after the build. A nonzero exit fails the check, and the message names the page and the rule, so the developer can fix it without asking anyone. For anything beyond a sketch, use a real HTML parser in place of regular expressions.

## Checks that guard the writing, too

Build checks can protect content as well as markup. This site's build compares the text of every page with every other page and fails when two pages share more than 15% of their six-word phrases, or when a sentence of ten or more words appears on two pages. That keeps near-duplicate pages from creeping in as the site grows. A similar rule suits any site that publishes many pages from a shared template, such as location or category pages.

## Rolling it out without blocking everyone
1. **Start in report only mode.** Run the checks and print the results without failing the build, and fix the existing backlog.
2. **Turn on failure one rule at a time,** starting with the ones that cost the most when they break: canonicals, noindex, and robots.txt.
3. **Keep messages specific.** "Missing canonical on /products/blue-widget/" gets fixed in a minute. "SEO check failed" gets the check switched off.
4. **Make the rules a file in the repository,** reviewed like code, so changing a threshold is a decision someone signs off.

## What tests can't tell you

Build checks prove the HTML you ship meets your rules. They can't tell you how Google ranks it, whether a title persuades anyone to click, or what an AI assistant says about you. Pair them with a crawl of the live site after each release and with Search Console, and keep a person reading the pages.

I write these checks into client repositories as part of [SEO engineering](https://gerriscorp.com/services/seo-engineering/). For the Next.js specifics they should cover, see the [Next.js SEO checklist](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/nextjs-seo/), and for safe repository setup, [giving an outside SEO access](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/repository-access/).

# Traffic fell after a site migration: how to find what broke and get it back

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

The new site launched, and organic traffic dropped and stayed down. Some dip is normal while Google recrawls. A drop that's still there after a month has a cause, and it's almost always one of a short list. Here is the recovery routine I run, in the order that finds the money fastest.

## First, separate normal turbulence from real loss

Google says to expect ranking fluctuations during any significant move, and that for a medium sized site it can take a few weeks or more before the new URLs gradually replace the old ones in results, longer for large sites. So the first question is shape. A dip that's recovering week over week is the move settling. A cliff that hasn't moved, or losses concentrated in one section, is a fault.

In Search Console, compare the four weeks after launch with the four weeks before, and look at pages rather than totals. Sort by lost clicks. The top twenty URLs usually account for most of the loss, and they tell you where to dig.

## Rebuild the list of old URLs

Every recovery starts with the URL inventory the migration should have started with. If nobody kept one, rebuild it from every source you can reach:
- The Search Console Performance report for the months before launch, exported by page.
- Analytics landing pages for the same period.
- The old XML sitemaps, from a backup or from the Wayback Machine.
- A backlink tool's list of linked URLs on your domain.
- Server logs, if the old host kept them.

Merge them and remove duplicates. This list, weighted by the traffic and links each URL carried, is what you'll test.

## Test every old URL's redirect

Screaming Frog's own migration guide describes the method. Switch to list mode, turn on Always Follow Redirects under Config > Spider > Advanced, upload the old URLs, and crawl them. The All Redirects export then shows each old address, the final address it lands on, the type of each hop, and whether a chain or a loop is involved.

Read the export for these failures, in this order:
1. **404s and soft 404s.** Old URLs with no redirect at all. On a big site these are usually whole patterns, such as an old category path or a dropped file extension.
2. **Redirects to the home page or a generic category.** Google treats a redirect to an unrelated page much like a missing page, and the old URL's value doesn't carry over.
3. **Temporary redirects.** Google's documentation says a permanent redirect shows the new target in results, while a temporary one keeps showing the source. A migration built on 302s or 307s is telling Google to keep the old URLs.
4. **Chains and loops.** Each extra hop slows crawling, and loops never resolve.
5. **JavaScript and meta refresh redirects.** Google ranks server-side redirects as the most reliable way to signal a move. Anything else should be replaced with one.

## Compare old pages with their new versions

A redirect that lands on the right URL still loses traffic if the new page is weaker. If you have a crawl from before launch, compare it with a crawl of the new site in Screaming Frog's comparison mode, using URL Mapping to pair old and new addresses. Without one, archived copies of the top pages will do. Check each pair for:
- Titles, descriptions, and H1s that were rewritten, shortened, or replaced with a template default.
- Body copy cut down, split across tabs, or moved behind a script.
- Structured data that existed before and doesn't now.
- Internal links that used to point at the page and no longer do, which shows up as greater crawl depth.
- Canonical tags pointing at staging, at the old domain, or at the wrong page.
- A noindex or a robots.txt rule carried over from the staging site.

## Check that Google can see the new site the way you think

Use URL Inspection on a sample of the top lost URLs and their new equivalents. Look at Google's chosen canonical, the indexing status, and the rendered page. Check the old sitemap and the new one in the Sitemaps report: Google's guidance is to submit both during a move, and to expect the indexed count on the old one to fall as the new one rises. If the old URLs still show as indexed weeks later, Google isn't following your redirects as you intended.

For a move to a new domain, confirm the Change of Address request went in from the old property. Google's help is specific about when it applies: a move between domains or subdomains. HTTP to HTTPS, www to non-www, and path changes within one site don't use it.

## Fix in order of value

Recovery work goes fastest when it follows the money. Fix the redirects for the twenty URLs that lost the most first, then the patterns that cover hundreds of URLs at once, then content and template gaps on the pages that matter, then the long tail. Keep every redirect in place: Google recommends at least a year, and longer is better for people following old links.

After each round of fixes, run the list crawl again and confirm the failures are gone, then watch the affected pages in Search Console. Recovered pages usually come back over weeks, as Google recrawls them. I make no promise about full recovery, because rankings also move for reasons unrelated to the migration, but a site whose old URLs all resolve cleanly to equal or better pages has removed every cause it controls.

## Keep the evidence

Write down what you found, what you fixed, and when, with the before-and-after crawl exports. If traffic doesn't come back in the expected window, that record is what lets the next person separate a migration fault from an algorithm update or a seasonal dip.

I handle this as part of [website migration SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/services/migrations/), and for inherited projects that went badly, [project rescue](https://gerriscorp.com/services/rescue/). To prevent the next one, use the [website migration checklist](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-checklist/) and the [tools I use for a website migration](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-tools/).

# The SEO tools for a website migration, and the job each one does

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

No single product migrates a website for you. A migration is a handful of jobs, and each has a tool that does it well: an inventory, a redirect map, a pre-launch comparison, a launch day test, and weeks of watching. Here is the kit I use, matched to the job, with the free options where they exist.

## Job 1: list every URL that matters

The inventory is the foundation, and it comes from several tools at once, since no single source sees everything.
- **A crawler.** Screaming Frog SEO Spider, Sitebulb, or a similar desktop crawler finds every URL linked from the site. Screaming Frog's free version stops at 500 URLs; a licence removes the limit.
- **Google Search Console.** The Performance report, exported by page over the last twelve to sixteen months, lists the URLs that actually earn impressions, including ones no longer linked from anywhere.
- **Analytics.** Landing pages from GA4 or whatever you run, for the URLs people arrive on from every channel.
- **A backlink tool.** Ahrefs, Semrush, or Majestic for the URLs other sites link to, which carry value even if they earn no traffic.
- **The XML sitemaps** and, if you can get them, **server logs.**

Merge them into one spreadsheet with a row per URL and columns for clicks, links, and sessions. That's the list everything else is tested against.

## Job 2: build and store the redirect map

The map pairs each old URL with its closest new equivalent. A spreadsheet is fine for drafting. The finished map belongs wherever the new site serves redirects: the server configuration, the host's redirect rules file on Netlify, Vercel, or Cloudflare, or the framework's own configuration. In Next.js, for example, redirects live in `next.config.js`, and each rule's `permanent` flag decides between a 308 and a 307. Keeping the map in version control means it gets reviewed, and nobody loses it.

For large sites, pattern rules cover whole sections in one line, and exceptions handle the pages that don't fit the pattern. Test the patterns before launch, because one bad regex can redirect thousands of pages to the wrong place.

## Job 3: compare staging with the live site

Before launch, crawl both the live site and the staging site with the same settings, then compare them. Screaming Frog's crawl comparison does this with URL Mapping, which uses a regex to pair the staging hostname's URLs with the live ones. You see, template by template, which titles, descriptions, headings, canonicals, structured data, and internal links changed. It needs a licence and database storage mode.

Check the staging site's robots.txt and meta robots tags at the same time. Staging is supposed to be blocked from search. Production isn't, and the block coming across at launch is one of the most common migration disasters.

## Job 4: test every redirect on launch day

Once the redirects are live, crawl the old URL list in Screaming Frog's list mode with Always Follow Redirects switched on, as Screaming Frog's migration guide describes. The All Redirects report shows each old URL, where it finally lands, and every hop in between, so you can spot 404s, chains, loops, and temporary redirects in minutes. Run it again a day later, after caches have cleared.

For a quick spot check without a crawler, `curl -sI` on the command line shows the status code and the Location header for any single URL.

## Job 5: tell Google, then watch
- **Search Console sitemaps.** Google's site move guidance is to submit the sitemaps for both the old and new URLs, then watch the indexed count move from one to the other. Warnings that the old URLs redirect are expected.
- **The Change of Address tool,** for moves from one domain or subdomain to another, used after the redirects are in place. It doesn't apply to HTTP to HTTPS, www changes, or path changes within one site.
- **URL Inspection,** on a sample of important old and new URLs, to see Google's chosen canonical and indexing status.
- **The Performance report with a date comparison,** by page, to catch any section that loses more than the expected dip.
- **Bing Webmaster Tools,** the equivalent for Bing, which also supplies results to other search and AI products.
- **Server logs,** which Google also recommends checking during a move, to confirm Googlebot is crawling the new URLs and to catch error codes your crawler missed.

## Job 6: prove the move held

A few weeks after launch, crawl the new site again and compare it with the pre-launch staging crawl, and rerun the old URL list. Anything that drifted, such as a redirect someone edited or a template change that dropped schema, shows up as a difference. If the numbers have fallen and stayed down, the [migration recovery guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-recovery/) covers what to do next.

## What a tool can't do

Every tool above reports facts. None of them decides which new page is the right home for an old one, whether a thin page should be merged or kept, or which redirect rule is safe on a site with forty thousand URLs. That judgment is the migration work itself, and it's why the inventory and the map deserve the most time.

I run migrations with this kit as [website migration SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/services/migrations/). For the full sequence, follow the [website migration checklist](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-checklist/), and for redirect rules in depth, see [301 redirects explained](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/301-redirects/).

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Diagnosing Core Web Vitals with MCP and an AI coding assistant

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026 · Updated October 15, 2026

Fixing a slow page used to mean running a test, reading a waterfall, opening the code, and going back and forth between the three. With the Model Context Protocol, an AI coding assistant such as Claude Code can drive Chrome, record a performance trace, read the result, and open the component responsible, all in one session. Here is how I set it up, what each piece does, and where a person still has to check the work.

OpenAI Codex and Claude Code are my primary coding assistants for repository work. This guide keeps a Claude Code command as a concrete setup example; choose your assistant and follow its current MCP documentation before connecting browser tools.

## The three numbers you're chasing

Core Web Vitals measure loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. Google's web.dev thresholds for a good experience are a Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less, and a Cumulative Layout Shift of 0.1 or less, measured at the 75th percentile of page loads on mobile and desktop separately. A page passes when it meets all three. The [Core Web Vitals guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/core-web-vitals/) explains each metric and its usual causes; this guide is about the tooling.

## What MCP adds

MCP is a standard way for an AI assistant to call outside tools. An MCP server wraps a tool, such as a browser or a crawler, and the assistant can ask it to do things and read back the results. In Claude Code, you register a server with `claude mcp add`, and its tools become available in the session. The assistant still needs you to tell it what to look at and to check its conclusions, but the tedious loop of test, read, and search the code collapses into one conversation.

## Chrome DevTools MCP: lab traces on demand

Google's Chrome DevTools MCP server gives an assistant control of a real Chrome browser and the DevTools performance panel. Its documented setup for Claude Code is a single command:

```
claude mcp add chrome-devtools --scope user npx chrome-devtools-mcp@latest
```

The tools that matter for Core Web Vitals:
- **performance_start_trace** and **performance_stop_trace** record a trace, optionally reloading the page and bypassing the cache to measure a cold load. The tool is described as finding frontend performance issues and Core Web Vitals.
- **performance_analyze_insight** opens a specific finding from the trace, such as the LCP breakdown, which shows where the time before the largest element appeared actually went.
- **emulate** throttles the CPU and network, with presets from Slow 3G to Fast 4G, and sets a mobile viewport, so a fast desktop doesn't hide a slow phone experience.
- **list_console_messages** and **list_network_requests** show errors and the heaviest resources.
- **lighthouse_audit** runs Lighthouse for accessibility, SEO, and best practices. Its documentation notes that it excludes performance, which is what the trace tools are for.

Two settings are worth knowing. The performance tools can send the traced URL to Google's CrUX API to show real-user data beside the lab result; the `--no-performance-crux` flag turns that off. And Google collects usage statistics from the server by default, which `--no-usage-statistics` disables.

## Real-user data: CrUX, and a change to PageSpeed Insights

A lab trace shows one load on one machine. Search uses field data from real Chrome users, collected in the Chrome UX Report. The CrUX API returns that data for a page or a whole origin, with a Google Cloud API key set up for it.

One change to plan around: Google's PageSpeed Insights API documentation says Google plans to stop including CrUX real-user data in that API, and recommends the CrUX API or the CrUX History API instead. Any script or dashboard that pulls field data from PageSpeed Insights should move now.

## Screaming Frog: every template, not one page

Traces are for depth. For breadth, Screaming Frog's PageSpeed Insights integration, under Configuration > API Access > PageSpeed Insights, pulls Lighthouse metrics and opportunities for every URL during a crawl. It can also run Lighthouse locally, which avoids the API's daily query limit but has no CrUX data.

Screaming Frog version 24 also runs as an MCP server, so an assistant can start crawls and read reports and bulk exports directly. It's a paid licence feature and needs database storage mode. Optional tools let the assistant run Node.js scripts, and they're off until you enable them in the MCP server settings.

The combination is where the time savings live: crawl every URL, group the slow ones by template, trace one representative page per template, and fix the template once.

## A working session, step by step
1. **Start from field data.** Check the Core Web Vitals report in Search Console or the CrUX API to see which metric fails and on which group of pages.
2. **Pick representative URLs,** one per failing template.
3. **Trace each on emulated mobile.** Ask the assistant to throttle to a mid-range phone and record a cold load.
4. **Read the insight, then the code.** For a slow LCP, the breakdown shows whether the time goes to the server, to fetching the hero image, or to rendering. With the repository open, the assistant can find the component that loads the image and propose a change, such as preloading it or removing its lazy loading.
5. **Test on a preview.** Trace the same page on the branch's preview deployment and compare.
6. **Confirm in the field.** CrUX data is a rolling 28-day window, so real-user numbers improve gradually after release.

## Where to keep a hand on the wheel
- **Lab is not field.** A trace on a developer's machine, even throttled, is one sample. Treat it as a diagnosis and judge the outcome by field data.
- **Check every proposed fix.** An assistant can suggest deferring a script that the page needs, or a preload that competes with the real LCP image. Measure before and after.
- **Mind what the browser can see.** The DevTools server's own documentation warns that it exposes the browser's content to the assistant. Use a separate browser profile, never one signed in to anything sensitive.
- **INP needs interaction.** A page load trace says little about responsiveness. Have the assistant click, type, and open menus during a trace, and compare with field INP.

This is how I run speed work on code based sites as part of [site speed and Core Web Vitals](https://gerriscorp.com/services/site-speed/) and [SEO engineering](https://gerriscorp.com/services/seo-engineering/). For the habits that keep an AI assistant safe in a client codebase, see [using AI coding assistants on a business website](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-coding-assistants/).

# How to get your email off a blocklist and back into the inbox

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 13, 2026

Your invoices are bouncing, or your newsletter vanished into spam, and somebody says you're "blacklisted." Recovery is a procedure anyone can follow: find the actual problem, fix it, ask for removal through the front door, and then send mail people want for long enough that the filters change their minds. Here is the sequence.

## First, the scam to avoid

Spamhaus, the most consequential blocklist operator, is blunt about it: there is never any charge or fee to remove a Spamhaus listing, any offer to remove one for a fee is a scam, and no third party can influence or speed up a removal. Anyone promising to make a listing disappear for a price is selling the thing you can do yourself for free, or nothing at all.

## Step 1: find out what's actually blocked

"Blacklisted" covers several different problems, and the fix depends on which one you have.
- **Read the bounce.** A rejected message comes back with an error code and usually a sentence naming the reason and often the list. Keep a copy. That text is your most specific evidence.
- **Check the sending IP and the domain.** Spamhaus's IP and Domain Reputation Checker covers its lists, and multi list lookup tools such as MXToolbox check the rest at once. Note whether the listing is on your *domain* or on the *IP address* that sent the mail; on a shared email service, that IP belongs to the provider, and so does the fix.
- **Check the mailbox providers' own views.** Google Postmaster Tools shows Gmail's spam rate, reputation, authentication, and delivery errors for your domain. Microsoft's Smart Network Data Services shows Outlook.com's view of IP addresses you control. These aren't public lists, and they often matter more than the lists do.

## Domain blocklists are a different animal

Most talk about blocklists is about IP addresses. A second family lists *domains* that show up inside spam messages, and SURBL is the best known. A listing there can hurt any email that merely links to you, your own signature included, wherever a spam filter consults it. SURBL's ABUSE list covers abuse and spam sites.

You can check these lists yourself with a DNS lookup, with two traps to know about. First, query the domain with the list's zone added, such as `example.com.multi.surbl.org`: no answer means not listed, and an answer in 127.0.0.x means listed, with the last number telling you which list. SURBL documents 64 as its ABUSE list. Second, the big public resolvers are often refused: SURBL answers 127.0.0.1 when your access is blocked, and Spamhaus answers 127.255.255.254, so those replies tell you nothing about your domain. Always look up the list's published test entry alongside your own, such as `test.surbl.org`; if the test entry doesn't come back listed, your result isn't real. The TXT record for a listed domain usually states which list it's on.

## Step 2: fix the cause before you ask for anything

Every operator says the same thing in different words: the problem must be identified and corrected first. Spamhaus's documentation for its fastest list notes that it will let you remove an IP, then list it again at once if the problem is still detected. The usual causes:
1. **A compromised account or website.** A hacked mailbox or a form on the website relaying spam. Change passwords, turn on two factor authentication, lock down the form with a CAPTCHA, and check for anything that sends mail you didn't write.
2. **A bad list.** Purchased, scraped, or years old, full of dead addresses and spam traps. Stop sending to it. Keep only people who asked to hear from you and have engaged recently.
3. **Missing authentication.** Google and Yahoo both require SPF or DKIM at a minimum for everyone, plus valid forward and reverse DNS for sending IPs, and bulk senders need SPF, DKIM, and DMARC together, aligned with the From domain. Since May 2025 Outlook.com enforces the same for domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day.
4. **No easy way out.** Google requires marketing mail from bulk senders to support one click unsubscribe and to show a visible unsubscribe link. People who can't leave press "report spam" instead, and complaints are what sink you.
5. **Marketing on the business domain.** When a newsletter's complaints land on the same domain as your invoices, the invoices suffer. Move bulk mail to a separate subdomain and sending service.

## Step 3: request removal, once, with the evidence
- **Spamhaus:** start from its IP and Domain Reputation Checker and follow the removal link for the specific list. Self-service removals are limited, so use them only after the fix.
- **Barracuda:** its removal form asks for the IP, your contact details, and a reason. It says valid requests are usually handled within 12 hours, and that repeat requests are ignored.
- **Microsoft:** the Outlook.com postmaster site is the starting point, with troubleshooting for mail that Outlook.com blocks or sends to junk.
- **Gmail:** no list to be removed from. Google's guidelines say senders who don't follow its practices may not be considered for deliverability mitigations, so meeting every requirement comes first.
- **If the listing is on your provider's IP,** contact the provider. They control that address and its removal.

Write each request the way you'd write an appeal: what happened, what you changed, and the date you changed it. One clear request beats five vague ones.

## Step 4: rebuild slowly

Removal from a list only stops the blocking. Reputation with Gmail and Microsoft recovers from behavior over time. Send only to your most engaged recipients at first, at a steady, modest volume, and raise it gradually over several weeks while you watch Postmaster Tools. Google asks senders to keep the spam rate it reports below 0.1% and never to reach 0.3%; Yahoo's limit for all senders is the same 0.3%. A spike during the rebuild is the signal to slow down.

## What money really buys, and when to start fresh

Big senders do recover faster, and money is part of the reason: dedicated sending IPs they control and warm up themselves, account managers at their email platforms, paid certification programs, and staff who watch these dashboards daily. All of it shortens the feedback loop; the filters still judge the mail itself. A small sender reaches the same result on the same rules, more slowly.

Sometimes the practical answer is a fresh start: business mail stays on the main domain once it's clean, and marketing moves to a new subdomain on a reputable sending service, built up from scratch with a clean list. A new address can't carry a bad list or a hacked form forward, so fix those first or the new domain will end up in the same place.

## Keep it from happening again
- Read your DMARC aggregate reports, or have a tool summarize them, so spoofing and misconfigured senders show up early.
- Watch Postmaster Tools monthly, and sign up for feedback loops such as Microsoft's Junk Email Reporting Program and Yahoo's Complaint Feedback Loop.
- Remove bounces and long silent addresses after every campaign.
- Lock down every form on the site that can send email.
- Give any domain that never sends mail a reject DMARC policy and an SPF record that allows nothing, so nobody can borrow its name. My [email authentication guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-authentication/) covers SPF, DKIM, and DMARC.

For how to diagnose missing mail before it becomes a listing, see the [email deliverability guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-deliverability/). I set up authentication and trace delivery problems as part of [email authentication and DNS](https://gerriscorp.com/services/email-and-dns/).

# "Crawled, currently not indexed": what it means and how to fix it

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026

Google visited the page, read it, and decided not to put it in the index, at least for now. It's the most misunderstood status in Search Console, and the fix depends entirely on why Google made that call.

## Where you see it

In Google Search Console, open Indexing, then Pages. The "Why pages aren't indexed" table lists every reason Google has for leaving URLs out. "Crawled, currently not indexed" means Googlebot fetched the URL successfully and chose not to index it. Google gives no specific reason, and the status alone isn't an error. Every large site has some URLs here, and many of them deserve to be.

## How it differs from "Discovered, currently not indexed"

"Discovered, currently not indexed" means Google knows the URL exists and hasn't crawled it yet. That usually points to crawl priority: too many URLs, weak internal linking, a slow server, or a site Google doesn't consider worth crawling quickly. "Crawled, currently not indexed" means Google did crawl the page and judged it not worth indexing. One is about getting Google to look; the other is about what Google saw when it looked.

## Common causes
- **Thin or duplicate content.** Pages that say little, or say nearly the same thing as other pages: tag archives, near-identical location pages, product variants, and boilerplate-heavy templates.
- **Content hidden from the renderer.** The page looks rich to visitors, but Google's rendered HTML holds only the template, because the substance loads on scroll or click. The [JavaScript SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/) shows how to check.
- **Weak signals of importance.** Few internal links, no external links, buried deep in the site.
- **Low-value URL patterns.** Filter and sort parameters, internal search results, and session URLs that multiply without adding anything.
- **Soft 404s and empty states.** Out-of-stock or "no results" pages that return a 200 status.
- **A new or recently changed site.** Google is still deciding, and many URLs move into the index over the following weeks.

## A method that finds the real cause
1. **Export the examples.** Click the status in the report and export the URL list. Search Console shows a sample of up to 1,000 URLs.
2. **Group them by template.** Sort the URLs into page types: product, category, article, location, tag, parameter. A status spread evenly across the site tells a different story than a cluster in one template.
3. **Ask whether each group deserves indexing.** Parameter URLs, tag pages, and near-duplicates are often correctly excluded. Handle those with canonicals, noindex, or by removing the links that create them, and move on.
4. **Inspect the important ones.** For pages that should rank, run URL Inspection, test the live URL, and read the rendered HTML. Is the main content there? Is the canonical the URL you expect? Is the page returning 200?
5. **Compare with pages that are indexed.** Crawl both groups and compare word counts, internal links, duplication, and load time. The difference usually points at the cause.
6. **Check the dates.** Line up when the count started rising with deployments, template changes, migrations, and plugin updates.
7. **Keep other problems separate.** A backlink spike or a redirect error at the same time may be a coincidence. Investigate each on its own track until the data connects them.

## Fixes, by cause
- Thin or duplicate pages: merge them, expand them with real substance, or canonicalize them to the strongest version.
- Hidden content: render it in the server's HTML.
- Weak signals: link to the pages from relevant, indexed pages and from navigation where it makes sense.
- Low-value patterns: stop generating crawlable links to them, and keep them out with canonicals or noindex.
- Soft 404s: return a real 404 or 410, or give the page useful content.

After the fix ships, click "Validate fix" in the report. Validation takes days to weeks, and Google reprocesses pages at its own pace. Request indexing through URL Inspection for a handful of the most important pages.

## When it's a crisis

A sudden rise concentrated in your most valuable template, with a matching traffic drop, is a technical emergency, and it's usually a rendering or template change. A slow, even scatter across low-value pages is housekeeping. Telling the two apart is the first job.

I diagnose indexing problems as part of [technical SEO forensics](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-seo/) and [Search Console cleanup](https://gerriscorp.com/services/search-console/).

# The website migration SEO checklist

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026

Migrations lose traffic for predictable reasons: URLs that weren't mapped, redirects that weren't tested, templates that changed what crawlers see, and nobody watching afterward. This checklist covers each stage.

## Before you start
- Record a baseline: organic sessions and conversions by landing page from analytics, and clicks, impressions, and indexed pages from Search Console. Export them, because you'll compare against them for months.
- Decide the launch window. Avoid your busiest season.
- Make sure Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools are verified for both the old and new sites, and that you'll keep access to the old domain if it's changing.

## Build the URL inventory

Combine every source, because each one misses something:
- A full crawl of the current site.
- Every URL in the XML sitemaps.
- Pages with clicks or impressions in Search Console over the last 16 months.
- Landing pages with traffic in analytics.
- URLs with external backlinks, from Ahrefs, Semrush, or Search Console's Links report.
- Images, PDFs, and other files that rank or receive links.

## Build the redirect map
- Map every old URL to its closest equivalent on the new site with a 301 or 308 permanent redirect.
- Redirect to the most relevant page, never to the home page in bulk. Google treats mass redirects to the home page like soft 404s.
- Make deliberate decisions about pages you're retiring: redirect them to a close substitute, or let them return 404 or 410 if nothing fits.
- Avoid chains. Every old URL should reach its final destination in one hop, including URLs that were already redirecting.
- Keep the map in a spreadsheet: old URL, new URL, status, reason. It's the document every later question goes back to.

## Review the new site before launch
- Crawl staging and compare titles, descriptions, headings, canonicals, and word counts with the old site, template by template.
- Check that the main content is in the server's HTML, so it doesn't depend on JavaScript.
- Check structured data, internal links, image alt text, and hreflang if you have more than one language.
- Test Core Web Vitals on the new templates.
- Keep staging blocked from search with authentication or noindex, and write down exactly how, so it can be removed at launch.

## Launch day
- Remove the staging block, and confirm production robots.txt and meta robots tags allow crawling.
- Test the redirect map in bulk against the live site: status codes, single hops, correct destinations.
- Submit the new XML sitemaps. Keep a sitemap of the old URLs available for a few weeks so Google recrawls them and discovers the redirects faster.
- For a domain change, use Google's Change of Address tool in Search Console and Bing's Site Move tool.
- Confirm analytics and tag tracking work on every template.
- If DNS changes, confirm that mail records were left untouched and email still arrives.

## The weeks after
- Watch Search Console daily for the first two weeks: page indexing, crawl stats, and 404s.
- Compare organic landing pages with the baseline, and investigate every important page that lost traffic.
- Fix redirect gaps as they appear in 404 reports and server logs.
- Update internal links that still point at old URLs.
- Ask the most valuable sites linking to you to update their links.
- Keep the redirects in place for at least a year, and ideally indefinitely.

## Special cases

### HTTP to HTTPS and www changes

Pick one canonical host and protocol, redirect every other combination to it in a single hop, and update canonicals, sitemaps, and internal links to match.

### Merging several sites into one

Map each old site's pages to their best home on the new one, and keep every old domain registered and redirecting. Old domains carry links for years.

### Moving to a JavaScript framework

Check that the new templates render their content on the server. A migration from a traditional CMS to a client-rendered app is a common way to lose content from Google and AI crawlers. See the [JavaScript SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/).

## What to expect

A well-run migration often shows some fluctuation for a few weeks while Google reprocesses the site, then settles. Domain changes take longer than platform changes on the same domain. A drop that deepens after the first month, or that's concentrated in one template, means something specific went wrong, and it's worth diagnosing rather than waiting out.

I run this process as a [website migration SEO service](https://gerriscorp.com/services/migrations/), before launch or after it. The kit is in [SEO tools for a website migration](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-tools/), and if traffic has already fallen, start with [migration recovery](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-recovery/).

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# SPF, DKIM, and DMARC for every domain that sends email

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026

Three DNS records decide whether mail from your domain is trusted. Since 2024, the largest mailbox providers require them, and mail without them increasingly lands in spam or bounces.

## The current requirements

Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require every sender to authenticate mail with SPF or DKIM, to have valid forward and reverse DNS for sending servers, and to keep spam complaint rates low. Bulk senders, those sending around 5,000 or more messages a day to Gmail accounts, must also have SPF, DKIM, and a DMARC policy, align the visible From domain with SPF or DKIM, offer one-click unsubscribe on marketing mail, and keep the spam rate reported in Google Postmaster Tools below 0.3%. Since May 2025, Microsoft's Outlook.com has required SPF, DKIM, and DMARC from senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to its consumer addresses.

Even small businesses are affected, because a newsletter tool, CRM, invoicing system, or help desk sending as your domain counts as a sender.

## SPF: who may send

SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record on your domain listing the servers and services allowed to send mail as you.

```
example.com.  TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com include:sendgrid.net ~all"
```
- Publish exactly one SPF record per domain. Two records break SPF.
- SPF allows at most ten DNS lookups. Each `include` counts, and nested includes count too. Too many services can push you over.
- `~all` (soft fail) is the common ending; `-all` (fail) is stricter. With DMARC in place, either works.

## DKIM: a signature on every message

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) signs each message with a private key; receivers check the signature against a public key published in DNS under a selector.

```
google._domainkey.example.com.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkq..."
```
- Every service that sends as your domain needs its own DKIM setup, usually a TXT or CNAME record the service provides.
- Use 2048-bit keys where the service offers them.
- DKIM survives forwarding better than SPF, which makes it the more reliable of the two for DMARC alignment.

## DMARC: the policy that ties them together

DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance) tells receivers what to do when a message claiming to be from your domain fails authentication, and asks them to send you reports.

```
_dmarc.example.com.  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@example.com"
```
- A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM passes and the domain it passed for aligns with the visible From address.
- `p=none` monitors only, `p=quarantine` sends failures to spam, and `p=reject` refuses them.
- `rua` sets where daily aggregate reports go. They're XML files listing every source that sent mail as your domain and whether it passed.

## Reaching enforcement safely
1. Inventory every service that sends mail as your domain.
2. Set up SPF and DKIM for each.
3. Publish DMARC at `p=none` with reporting, and read the reports for two to four weeks, using a report viewer to make them readable.
4. Fix every legitimate source that fails.
5. Move to `p=quarantine`, optionally with `pct` below 100 to phase it in, and keep reading reports.
6. Move to `p=reject` once failures are only spoofing.

Enforcement is what stops criminals sending invoices and password resets in your name. It also unlocks BIMI, which can show your logo next to your mail in supporting inboxes when combined with a verified mark certificate.

## Common mistakes
- Two SPF records after a new service is added, which invalidates both.
- A sending service set up without DKIM, so its mail fails DMARC once enforcement begins.
- DMARC reports sent to a mailbox nobody reads.
- Jumping straight to `p=reject` and blocking legitimate invoices or password resets.
- Mail records lost during a DNS provider change because only the web records were copied.

## Domains that don't send mail

Parked and secondary domains get spoofed too. Protect them with an SPF record of `v=spf1 -all`, a DMARC record at `p=reject`, and no MX records if they receive no mail.

## Changing DNS without breaking mail

Website moves, CDN setups, and DNS provider changes are when mail records get lost. Export every record first, recreate them exactly, keep MX, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC untouched unless they're the point of the change, and send test messages afterward. Header analyzers show exactly which checks passed.

I set this up and troubleshoot deliverability as [email authentication and DNS](https://gerriscorp.com/services/email-and-dns/) work.

## Want me to handle this for you?

# How to remove your personal information from data brokers and search

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026

Your home address, phone numbers, relatives, and age are probably for sale on dozens of people-search sites. Removing them is tedious and never permanent, and it's still worth doing, especially for executives, public figures, and anyone with a reason to be careful.

## Where the information comes from

Data brokers compile profiles from public records such as property deeds, voter files, court records, and business filings, combined with marketing data, social media, and other brokers. People-search sites such as Spokeo, Whitepages, BeenVerified, Radaris, and many others sell access to those profiles, and search engines index the result pages, which is how your address ends up in Google results for your name.

## Opting out, site by site
- Most people-search sites have an opt-out form, usually linked from the footer as "Do not sell," "Opt out," or "Privacy."
- Search each site for every version of your name, past and current addresses, and relatives' listings that include you.
- Use a dedicated email address for opt-out requests, since many sites require confirmation by email.
- Keep a log of each site, the date, and the confirmation. Listings reappear when brokers refresh their data, so the work repeats every few months.
- Commercial removal services automate much of this for a subscription. They cover the major sites well and the long tail less well.

## Google's "Results about you"

Google's Results about you tool lets you request removal of search results that show your phone number, email address, or home address, and it can alert you when new results with your contact information appear. Removal from Google doesn't delete the page from the website itself, so pair it with an opt-out at the source. Google also has separate removal policies for doxxing, non-consensual explicit images, and certain other harmful content.

## Your legal rights

### California's Delete Act and DROP

California's Delete Act created the Delete Request and Opt-out Platform, known as DROP, run by the California Privacy Protection Agency. Since January 2026, California residents can submit one request that goes to every registered data broker, and brokers must begin processing those requests in August 2026 and keep checking for new ones on a regular schedule. It's the most significant change to data broker removal in years.

### Other states

California, Vermont, Texas, and Oregon require data brokers to register, which makes the industry easier to identify. A growing number of state privacy laws give residents a right to delete personal information held by businesses, with exceptions, so check what your state provides.

### Outside the US

In the European Union and the United Kingdom, data protection law gives a right to erasure, and search engines handle delisting requests for results about you that are inaccurate, inadequate, or no longer relevant.

## What removal can't do

Public records themselves usually stay public, though some states let certain people, such as judges, law enforcement officers, and domestic violence survivors, shield their addresses. Legitimate news coverage is rarely removable. Where removal isn't available, the practical answer is a stronger, accurate public record that ranks above what you can't remove.

## Protecting the people around you

Broker profiles link relatives, so a spouse's or parent's listing can expose your address even after your own is removed. For executives and public figures, the work should cover the household, old addresses, and any properties held in a personal name. Consider holding new property in a trust or entity where that's appropriate, and use a mailing address that isn't your home for registrations and subscriptions.

## Keeping it clean

Brokers refresh their data from public records and other brokers constantly, so removed listings come back. A quarterly sweep across all the major sites catches relistings early, and monitoring tools, including Results about you, flag new appearances between sweeps.

## A sensible routine
1. Search your name, with and without your city, in Google and Bing, and on the largest people-search sites.
2. Opt out of every listing you find, and log each request.
3. Set up Results about you, and use DROP if you're a California resident.
4. Repeat every three months.
5. For families and executives, cover spouses, children, and older addresses as well.

I handle this for clients as part of [reputation and perception management](https://gerriscorp.com/services/reputation/).

# How to diagnose a Google traffic drop in Search Console

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 6, 2026

Organic traffic fell and everyone wants an answer by Friday. The answer is almost always findable, and it comes from narrowing the drop down until only one explanation fits. This is the order I work in.

## 1. Confirm the drop is real

Start by ruling out measurement. Analytics can fall while search traffic is fine.
- Compare Google Analytics with Search Console clicks over the same dates. If Search Console is flat and analytics fell, the problem is tracking: a broken tag, a new consent banner, a site redesign that dropped the snippet from some templates.
- Check that the date ranges match in length and in days of the week. A Monday-to-Sunday week compared with a Thursday-to-Wednesday week shows a false drop on a business site.
- Compare with the same period last year. Many businesses fall every summer or every January, and that's seasonality.

One reporting change to know about: in September 2025 Google stopped supporting a parameter that rank-tracking tools used to load a hundred results at a time. Desktop impressions fell sharply for many sites and average position appeared to improve, with no change in clicks. A drop in impressions alone from that month is usually that.

## 2. Read clicks, impressions, CTR, and position together
| Pattern | Likely meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Impressions and clicks both fell, position fell | Rankings dropped: an algorithm update, a technical problem, or stronger competition |
| Impressions steady, clicks and CTR fell | The results page changed: an AI Overview, more ads, a new feature above you, or a rewritten title |
| Impressions fell, position steady | Fewer people are searching: seasonality, a news cycle ending, or a product falling out of fashion |
| Everything fell to near zero | The site is blocked, deindexed, or under a manual action |

## 3. Find where the loss is

Use the Compare option in the Performance report, then sort each tab by the change in clicks.
- **Pages.** Is the loss spread across the site, or concentrated in one section or template? A drop in one template points to something technical about that template.
- **Queries.** Separate branded searches from everything else with a regular expression filter on the brand name. Branded loss means fewer people are looking for the business; unbranded loss means rankings.
- **Countries and devices.** A drop on mobile alone suggests a mobile rendering or speed problem. A drop in one country suggests hreflang, a local competitor, or a regional update.
- **Search appearance and search type.** Lost rich results, or lost image and video traffic, show up here.

## 4. Line it up with dates

Find the first day of the decline as precisely as the daily data allows, then check what happened that week.
- **Google's Search Status Dashboard** lists confirmed core updates, spam updates, and incidents with start and end dates.
- **Your own changes.** Deploys, plugin and theme updates, CMS upgrades, migrations, CDN or security changes, new consent tools, and changes to robots.txt or redirects. Ask the developers for the deploy log.
- **Outside events.** A competitor's launch, a press story, a product recall.

## 5. Check the technical reports
- **Security and Manual actions.** One look, and either there's a notice or there isn't.
- **Page indexing.** A rise in "Crawled, currently not indexed," "Excluded by noindex," "Blocked by robots.txt," or "Duplicate, Google chose different canonical" that starts on the same date is a strong lead.
- **Crawl stats.** Under Settings: host status problems, a spike in server errors, slower response times, or a sudden change in crawl volume.
- **URL Inspection.** Run a live test on a page that lost traffic and read the rendered HTML. Content missing from Google's render is a common, invisible cause. The [JavaScript SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/) has the tests.

## 6. Separate the problems

Drops often have more than one cause at once: a core update lands the same month a redesign broke a template, or a backlink spam spike shows up beside a redirect error. Treat each candidate as its own hypothesis and test it against the data separately. When the evidence for each one points to different pages or different dates, they're different problems, and each gets its own fix.

## 7. Write it down

The deliverable is a short document: the size and start date of the drop, where it is concentrated, the cause, the evidence for it, the explanations that were ruled out and why, and the fix with tickets the developers can act on. Then mark the fix's ship date and watch the same report, filtered the same way, over the following weeks.

## Questions about traffic drops

### How fast does traffic recover after a fix?

A technical fix such as an unblocked template often recovers within weeks, as Google recrawls. Losses from a core update usually move only when Google runs a later update, after the content has improved.

### How far back does Search Console go?

Sixteen months. For longer history, set up the bulk export to BigQuery now, because it only collects data from the day it starts.

Finding the cause of lost traffic is the core of [technical SEO forensics](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-seo/). See also the [indexing recovery case study](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/indexing-recovery/), and if the drop followed a relaunch, [recovering traffic after a site migration](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/migration-recovery/).

# When two problems hit at once, keep them on separate tracks

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

The hardest traffic losses to fix are the ones with two causes. Everyone wants one story, so the evidence for both gets poured into the same bucket, a single explanation forms, and the fix that follows repairs half the damage or none of it. I run every overlapping cause as its own investigation, with its own evidence and its own test, and I connect them only when the data does.

## Why one story feels right and fails

A single explanation is satisfying. It fits on one slide, it gives the team one thing to do, and it lets everyone stop worrying. When a site loses traffic in the same season that a spam link spike shows up in a backlink tool, the spike becomes the villain within a day, because it is visible, dated, and blamable on strangers.

The trouble is what happens next. The team ships the fix for the story it chose, waits six weeks, and reads the result. If the other cause was the bigger one, traffic keeps sliding and the fix looks like it failed, so a good fix gets abandoned. If both causes ease at the same time, the fix gets credit for a recovery it didn't produce, and the real cause returns with the next release. Either way the business pays for weeks of waiting and learns the wrong lesson.

## Signs you have more than one problem

Nobody announces that a drop has two causes. These are the patterns that tell me to split the work before anyone writes a ticket:
- **The decline has two shapes.** A slow slope across months plus a sudden step on one date is almost never one cause.
- **The losing pages don't share a template.** When product pages and the homepage both fall, one mechanism rarely explains both.
- **The dates don't line up.** If one page group started falling in February and another in April, an April event can't explain February.
- **Brand and nonbrand queries move differently.** Branded searches respond to reputation, links, and redirects; product and category searches respond to content, rendering, and indexing.
- **The first fix moved one metric and not the others.** That is the clearest sign of all, and the most often ignored.

## Open a track for each candidate cause

A track is a written hypothesis with four parts: what I think is happening, the evidence that supports it, the test that would prove it wrong, and the person who can fix it. Writing the disproof test first matters most. A hypothesis with no way to fail is a belief, and beliefs are how one story swallows two problems.

Each track gets its own page in the working document and its own heading in the report. Findings get filed under the track they support. A finding that seems to support both goes in a third place, marked as unassigned, until something decides it.

## Give each track its own evidence

Different causes leave fingerprints in different places, so each track gets the evidence that can actually speak to it:
- **Template problems** show up in a crawl. I compare what a crawler extracts from each page type with what a person sees in the browser. A product page that weighs over a megabyte but yields three hundred words of text to the crawler is a template problem, whatever else is going on.
- **Indexing problems** show up in Search Console's Page indexing report and in URL Inspection, grouped by template rather than read one URL at a time.
- **Date driven problems** show up when the Performance report is segmented by page group and query type and laid against a calendar of releases, migrations, confirmed Google updates, and changes to redirects or hosting.
- **Link and reputation problems** show up in the Links report and in third party backlink data, read for timing and pattern rather than for alarming totals.

Segmentation is where most blended stories fall apart. A sitewide traffic line hides everything. The same data split into homepage, category, product, and editorial pages, and then into branded and unbranded queries, usually shows two or three distinct curves, each with its own start date.

## Join the tracks only on proof

Two problems can be connected, and sometimes one causes the other. A redirect error can send link equity to the wrong place and depress branded rankings. A rendering failure can strip internal links and starve deeper pages of crawl attention. When that happens, I merge the tracks. What I need before merging is a shared mechanism, the same affected URLs, or the same date with a plausible path from one to the other. Coincidence in the same month is not enough, and neither is the fact that both problems are bad.

## A worked example

An ecommerce client lost a large share of organic sessions over several months. Two things were visibly wrong. Product templates mounted their specifications, FAQs, and reviews only when a shopper scrolled them into view, so crawlers received a heading, an image, a few bullets, and a price. Separately, in April, the backlink tools showed several hundred new spam links against a baseline of a few dozen, around the same weeks that homepage traffic and branded searches fell.

The tempting story was the spam. It was dated, it was dramatic, and it blamed someone outside the building. Split into tracks, the evidence told a different and more useful story. The rendering track was confirmed by crawl extraction on every major product page, by the template code itself, and by a cluster of clean product URLs sitting in "Crawled, currently not indexed." The April track explained the homepage and the brand queries, and it pointed at a redirect and URL handling issue as much as at the links. Neither track explained the other's pages. They went to different people as different tickets: server rendering to the developers, the redirect handling and the link review to me.

## Sequence the fixes so you can read the result

When two fixes ship in the same week, nobody can say afterward which one worked. Where the business can afford it, I ship them apart, with the larger or better proven fix first, and I annotate every release date in the reporting. Where both have to ship at once, I measure each against the page group and query segment it was meant to move, so a recovery in product pages counts for the rendering fix and a recovery in branded queries counts for the redirect fix.

Each fix gets an acceptance check on the live site before anyone waits for traffic: a plain fetch of a product page that returns the specifications, a redirect test that returns one hop to the right destination. Traffic takes weeks to respond. Whether the fix shipped correctly takes minutes to verify, and there is no reason to spend six weeks waiting on a fix that never deployed.

## What the owner hears

The written report keeps the tracks separate all the way to the summary. Leadership gets one paragraph per problem: what it is, what it costs, who fixes it, and how anyone will know it worked. Engineers get the technical evidence, also by track. Nobody gets a single blended villain, because a single villain is the most expensive thing a diagnosis can produce.

## How I handle this for clients

This is the core of my [technical SEO forensics](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-seo/) work. Every engagement starts with a paid diagnostic that ends in a cause per track, the evidence behind each, and a prioritized plan with an owner for every item. When the cause turns out to be content the crawler never sees, that track becomes [crawler visibility](https://gerriscorp.com/services/crawler-visibility/) work; when it becomes a ticket for your team, it gets a [developer spec with acceptance criteria](https://gerriscorp.com/services/developers/). For the single cause version of the method, start with [diagnosing a traffic drop in Search Console](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/traffic-drop/).
