# Glossary of SEO, AI search, and technical website terms

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 5, 2026 · Updated October 26, 2026

Plain definitions of the terms that come up in my work, written so each one makes sense on its own. The [index](https://gerriscorp.com/site-index/) lists every page where a term comes up.

**301 redirect**
A permanent redirect from one URL to another. Search engines transfer the old URL's ranking signals to the new one. The 308 status code is also permanent; 302 and 307 are temporary.

**Acceptance criteria**
The plain statements a finished change has to satisfy before anyone calls it done, written before the work starts. They turn a request into something a developer can build and a reviewer can check.

**AEO (answer engine optimization)**
Shaping content so it directly answers the questions people ask, in a form that search features and AI assistants can quote.

**AI Mode**
Google Search's conversational, AI-generated search experience, which answers questions with a written response and links, built on Google's search index.

**AI Overviews**
The AI-generated summaries that appear at the top of many Google search results, with links to the pages they draw on.

**AI washing**
Claiming artificial intelligence a product doesn't really use, or overstating what its AI does. The SEC brought its first AI washing cases in March 2024; see [how to vet an AI vendor's pitch](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-vendor-pitch/).

**Alt text**
A text description of an image in the HTML alt attribute, read aloud by screen readers and used by search engines to understand the image.

**Amara's law**
Roy Amara's observation that people overestimate a technology's effect in the short run and underestimate it in the long run. It's the first test in [hype or real shift](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/hype-or-shift/).

**BIMI**
Brand Indicators for Message Identification: a DNS record that lets supporting inboxes show a brand's logo beside authenticated email. It requires DMARC enforcement.

**Bing Webmaster Tools**
Microsoft's free service for monitoring a site in Bing, whose index also feeds Microsoft Copilot and other AI assistants.

**Canonical tag**
A link element that tells search engines which URL is the preferred version of a page when several URLs show the same or similar content. Google treats it as a strong hint.

**CDN (content delivery network)**
A network of servers around the world that stores copies of a site's files close to visitors, making pages faster and absorbing traffic spikes and attacks. Cloudflare is the best-known example.

**Citation gap**
A page AI assistants cite when answering your buyers' questions that names your competitors and leaves you out. Finding them is the job of a [citation gap analysis](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/citation-gap-analysis/).

**CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)**
A Core Web Vital measuring how much visible content moves unexpectedly while a page loads. Good is 0.1 or less.

**Confabulation**
NIST's term for a generative AI system stating false information with confidence. The reason AI-assisted work needs a human check. See [AI use policy](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-use-policy/).

**Content brief**
A one-page instruction that settles a page's question, answer, evidence, and limits before anyone writes. See [writing a content brief](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/content-briefs/).

**Core update**
A broad recalibration of Google's ranking systems, announced a few times a year and logged on the Search Status Dashboard. Losses after one reflect being outranked, and Google says recovery can take months.

**Core Web Vitals**
Google's three page experience metrics: Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, and Cumulative Layout Shift, measured from real Chrome users.

**Crawl budget**
How many URLs a search engine is willing and able to crawl on a site in a given period. It matters mostly for large sites and sites with many low-value URLs.

**Crawled, currently not indexed**
A Google Search Console status meaning Google fetched a page and chose not to index it. See the [full guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/crawled-not-indexed/).

**Crawler Hints**
A free Cloudflare feature that watches content change as it passes through Cloudflare's cache and notifies IndexNow engines such as Bing. Google doesn't take part.

**Discovered, currently not indexed**
A Search Console status meaning Google knows a URL exists and hasn't crawled it yet, usually a sign of crawl priority problems.

**DKIM**
DomainKeys Identified Mail: a cryptographic signature on outgoing email, verified against a public key published in DNS.

**DMARC**
A DNS policy telling receiving mail servers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment, and where to send reports. Policies are none, quarantine, and reject.

**DNSSEC**
Signatures added to DNS records so resolvers can reject forged answers. Turn it off or move the keys before changing DNS hosts. See [domain security](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/domain-account-security/).

**E-E-A-T**
Experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness: the qualities Google's quality rater guidelines ask raters to assess, and a useful description of what makes content credible.

**Email blocklist**
A list of IP addresses and domains that spam filters consult to reject or junk mail, also called a DNSBL. Getting off one starts with fixing the cause; see [blocklist recovery](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-blocklist-recovery/).

**Endorsement Guides**
The FTC's guidance on testimonials and influencer posts, 16 CFR Part 255, last revised in 2023. They hold the advertiser answerable for what paid endorsers say. Covered in [the creator vetting guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/vet-an-influencer/).

**European Accessibility Act**
EU Directive 2019/882, applied since June 28, 2025, requiring accessible e-commerce, banking, e-books, and other consumer services, including from sellers outside the EU. See [the EAA guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/european-accessibility-act/).

**GEO (generative engine optimization)**
Making a business and its content easy for AI systems to find, understand, and cite in generated answers.

**Git**
The version control system almost every software team uses. It records each change to a set of files, who made it, and why, so any version can be restored.

**Google Search Console**
Google's free service for monitoring how a site appears in Google Search: indexing, queries, clicks, Core Web Vitals, and errors.

**hreflang**
An annotation that tells search engines which language or regional version of a page to show to which users.

**HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)**
A response header that commits browsers to HTTPS for a site for a chosen length of time. Add preload only once every subdomain serves HTTPS, because preload is slow to reverse.

**Hype cycle**
Gartner's curve for a new technology's reputation: a trigger, a peak of inflated expectations, a trough of disillusionment, a slope of enlightenment, and a plateau of productivity.

**IndexNow**
An open protocol that lets a site notify Bing, Yandex, and other participating search engines immediately when pages are added, changed, or removed.

**INP (Interaction to Next Paint)**
A Core Web Vital measuring how quickly a page responds to taps, clicks, and key presses. Good is 200 milliseconds or less. It replaced First Input Delay in March 2024.

**JSON-LD**
A format for adding structured data to a page in a script block, recommended by Google for schema.org markup.

**LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)**
A Core Web Vital measuring how long the largest visible element, usually a hero image or headline, takes to appear. Good is 2.5 seconds or less.

**llms.txt**
A proposed convention, introduced in 2024, for a plain Markdown file at a site's root that summarizes the site and links to its key pages for language models. Adoption by AI companies is still emerging. This site publishes [one](https://gerriscorp.com/llms.txt).

**Material connection**
Any tie between an endorser and a brand that the audience wouldn't expect, such as payment, free product, family, or employment. The FTC expects it disclosed in each post. See [vetting a creator before a sponsorship](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/vet-an-influencer/).

**Meta description**
A short summary of a page in its HTML head, often shown under the title in search results. Usually 140 to 160 characters.

**OAI-SearchBot**
OpenAI's crawler for ChatGPT search. It's controlled separately from GPTBot, the training crawler, so a site can appear in ChatGPT answers while declining to be used for training.

**Orange cloud (proxied)**
A Cloudflare DNS record whose traffic runs through Cloudflare's network, gaining caching, compression, and attack protection. Gray means Cloudflare answers DNS and steps aside.

**Pull request**
A proposed set of changes to a repository, presented for review and comment before it's merged. Requiring one for every change gives an owner a complete history; see [hiring developers](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/hiring-developers/).

**README**
The introductory file at the top of a code repository. On a public GitHub repository it's a public page that AI assistants with web search read, so it should describe the live site; see [your README is a source AI reads](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/readme-ai-source/).

**Registrar lock**
Status codes such as clientTransferProhibited that tell the registry to refuse transfers, deletions, or updates until the account holder lifts them. Registry Lock is the stricter, registry-level version.

**Repository**
The folder of code and content Git tracks, along with its full history. Owning the repository, in an account the business controls, is owning the website.

**Restore drill**
Rebuilding a website from its backup on a separate server, timed and written down, to prove the backup is complete before an emergency. See [restore drills](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/restore-drills/).

**robots.txt**
A file at a site's root that tells crawlers which paths they may fetch. It controls crawling, not indexing; a blocked page can still appear in results if other sites link to it.

**Scaled content abuse**
The spam policy covering mass-produced pages made mainly to rank, by any method, human or machine. Google's 2026 spam updates focused on it.

**Schema.org**
The shared vocabulary search engines use for structured data, describing organizations, people, products, services, articles, events, and much more.

**Server-side rendering**
Generating a page's full HTML on the server before sending it, so browsers and crawlers receive the content without running JavaScript. Static generation does the same at build time.

**Site reputation abuse**
Hosting third-party pages on an established site so they ride its reputation in search. Google introduced the policy in 2024 and updated it in August 2026.

**Soft 404**
A page that tells visitors it doesn't exist or has nothing to show, while returning a 200 success status. Google treats it as an error.

**Spam update**
An upgrade to the systems that detect violations of Google's spam policies. Unlike a core update, it targets specific behavior, and the sites it catches tend to fall fast.

**Speculation rules**
A JSON block in a script tag that tells Chrome and Edge which links to prefetch or prerender before the reader clicks, so the next page opens at once. See [speculation rules](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/speculation-rules/).

**SPF**
Sender Policy Framework: a DNS record listing the servers allowed to send email for a domain. It allows at most ten DNS lookups.

**Structured data**
Machine-readable information about a page, usually schema.org in JSON-LD, describing what the page is about and how it relates to people, organizations, and other pages.

**Title tag**
The HTML title of a page, shown in browser tabs and usually as the headline of a search result. Usually 50 to 60 characters.

**TTFB (time to first byte)**
How long a browser waits for the first byte of a server's response. Slow TTFB delays everything else, and caching and CDNs reduce it.

**WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines)**
The W3C accessibility standard, now at version 2.2. Level AA is the benchmark US courts and EU standards most often point to. See [accessibility remediation](https://gerriscorp.com/services/accessibility/).

**XML sitemap**
A file listing the URLs a site wants search engines to crawl, with optional last-modified dates.

Want these applied to your site? See [services](https://gerriscorp.com/services/).

# Magento store: product content Googlebot never saw

An equipment retailer on Magento 2 with the Hyvä theme had been losing organic traffic for months. Brand searches and the home page were down while non-brand category traffic was growing, a pattern that didn't fit any single explanation.

## My role

Forensic diagnosis and technical direction, working alongside the client's contractor, who owns implementation.

## What I found

### Track one: rendering

The product templates used Alpine.js to mount the specifications, FAQs, and reviews only when a visitor scrolled them into view, with `x-intersect` wrapped around `x-if`. Googlebot never scrolls the way a person does, so those sections never mounted. A Screaming Frog crawl extracted thousands of words from category pages but only 250 to 400 words from flagship product pages that weighed more than 1.2 MB. Search Console showed a selective cluster of product URLs in "Crawled, currently not indexed," while the rest of the site indexed normally.

### Track two: backlinks and redirects

In the same period, a spike of spam, adult, and warez backlinks arrived, mostly from cloud-hosting address ranges, alongside a 301 redirect problem. I kept this on its own track, collected the evidence, and asked for upgraded Search Console access to examine it properly, without folding it into the rendering story.

## What I recommended
- Render the product sections in the server's HTML and keep the scroll animation as progressive enhancement.
- An A/B test that removes the scroll gates from a group of product pages first, so the effect can be measured before a full rollout.
- A separate investigation and cleanup plan for the backlink spike and the redirect problem.

## How it was checked

Raw HTML, rendered DOM, and crawler extraction compared on the same URLs, Search Console's live test used to see what Google rendered, and the indexing cluster matched to the affected template.

## Status

Diagnosis delivered and the test scoped; implementation sits with the client's contractor. The method is written up in the [JavaScript SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/javascript-seo/) and on [content the crawler never sees](https://gerriscorp.com/services/crawler-visibility/).

Source: https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/consent-blocking/
Updated: 2026-10-05

# WordPress media site: a consent banner hiding every article

A bilingual English and Italian site of film reviews was almost absent from Google, while Bing indexed it normally. There were no crawl errors anywhere, just page after page in "Crawled, currently not indexed."

## My role

Paid diagnosis for the site's owner, with a call to walk through the findings.

## What I found

Every review's content lived inside jQuery UI tabs. The site's consent-management platform used prior-consent blocking: scripts were held back until a visitor accepted cookies. One of the held-back scripts was the one that initialized the tabs. Googlebot never accepts cookies, so it crawls every page as a permanent non-consenting visitor, and it rendered each page with the structure intact and the content empty. That explains the gap between Google and Bing, which handled the pages differently.

Two secondary problems made things worse: 97% of pages shared the same hardcoded H2 headings, and 95% of internal links had no anchor text, so even the visible structure told search engines almost nothing about each page.

## What I recommended
- Exempt the scripts that build the page's content from consent blocking, or render the tab content in the HTML so it doesn't depend on scripts at all. Consent rules should govern tracking and advertising scripts, never the article itself.
- Replace the hardcoded H2s with headings drawn from each review.
- Give internal links descriptive anchor text.

## How it was checked

Pages compared in a consenting browser session and a non-consenting one, the blocked scripts identified in the consent platform's configuration, and the empty tabs matched to the indexing pattern. Confirmation in Search Console's rendered HTML was the next step once access was granted.

## Why it matters

Consent platforms are now on almost every site, and their default settings can hide content from every crawler that never clicks "accept." It's one of three examples of the same failure on [content the crawler never sees](https://gerriscorp.com/services/crawler-visibility/).

Updated: 2026-10-05

# React event platform: 2,000 pages Google couldn't reach

An event and nightlife discovery app built with Create React App needed about 2,000 event pages indexed. Three months of Search Console data showed impressions on the home page and almost nothing else.

## My role

Strategist and QA. I diagnosed the problems, wrote the specification, and verify the results; the founder's developer implements.

## What I found
- **An empty home page.** The home page served an empty root element; everything appeared only after JavaScript ran.
- **No crawlable links.** Event cards navigated with click handlers instead of real `<a href>` links, so crawlers had no path to the event pages.
- **Orphaned pages.** The event pages themselves already had server-side rendering, so their HTML was fine, but nothing linked to them.
- **Wrong canonicals.** The canonical tags on the events and community sections pointed to the home page, telling Google those pages were duplicates of it.

## What I delivered

Two documents. For the founder, a plain-language summary of what was wrong and what it would take. For the developer, a 13-page specification of 12 items ranked P0 to P3, each with the evidence, the consequence, exact build steps, and acceptance criteria. The P0 items were real anchor links on event cards, server-side rendering for the home page and feed, and manual indexing requests for priority pages.

## How it is checked

Each item has a testable acceptance criterion, such as event links present in the server's HTML and self-referencing canonicals on each section. I verify the developer's changes against those criteria with a crawl and Search Console's live test, with remaining checks on how page heads are generated and whether the canonicals were corrected.

## Status

Reports delivered and acknowledged; verification of the developer's fixes in progress. See [developer specs and implementation QA](https://gerriscorp.com/services/developers/).

# Clinical practice: WordPress to Netlify, with search intact

A clinical practice moved its website from WordPress on managed hosting to a new Next.js build on Netlify. The developer built the new site; my job was continuity: making sure search engines and visitors could follow the move, and investigating what went wrong afterward.

## My role

Technical SEO, migration oversight, and investigation, in coordination with the practice and its developer.

## What I did

### Redirect decisions for every URL

I examined the legacy URLs and reconciled the redirect map, deciding for each URL whether it should pass through unchanged, inherit an existing destination, receive a migration redirect, or be treated as intentionally removed. I separated problems the migration caused from older issues the site already had, so neither got blamed on the other.

### Repository analysis with Claude Code

This initial investigation used Claude Code. My current repository work also uses OpenAI Codex, with findings checked against crawl data and the live output.

I combined crawls and exports with a read-only, AI-assisted analysis of the Next.js repository. It found thousands of references to images still hosted on the old WordPress site, and the handful of central files responsible, which became a developer-ready plan for moving the media. The analysis changed no code.

### A conservative disavow

I reviewed the backlink profile and prepared a replacement disavow file that removed genuinely toxic domains while keeping legitimate ones, because disavowing good links does real harm.

### After launch

I investigated blurry images from the image CDN, JavaScript and CSS problems, site instability, and analytics behavior with the client and developer, and worked on sequencing, DNS review, and launch verification.

## Reading the data honestly

When engagement fell in a short GA4 window, the easy story was that the blurry images were driving people away. I treated tracking, engagement, and site defects as three separate questions, each needing its own evidence, and didn't let a few days of data stand in for proof.

## Status

Migration oversight and post-launch investigation delivered; further work under discussion. See [website migrations](https://gerriscorp.com/services/migrations/).

# Local service business on Sanity and Vercel: SEO in the repository

Crawls before and after the prerendering change, raw HTML fetched from production, Search Console's live test, and a review of titles, descriptions, canonicals, and status codes across the site.

# Specialty retailer: cleaning up after Squarespace to Shopify

Structured data validated on product pages, crawls compared before and after, and every change made in the duplicate theme first and previewed before publishing.

# Consumer brand: taking over a stalled React application

A consumer skincare brand's React application changed hands after an outage. Project files, credentials, hosting, DNS, and the repository were spread across several people, and the brand needed someone to work out what it actually had.

## My role

Takeover assessment and hands-on operations.

## The assessment

I assessed the handoff the way every rescue should start, with an inventory:
- Which project files were supplied, and whether they matched what was running.
- Where the application was hosted, and who controlled the server.
- Who controlled the domain and DNS.
- Where the repository lived and who had access.
- Which credentials existed, and which were missing.

## Hands-on operations

Then I worked on the DigitalOcean Linux server directly over SSH: reading logs, editing the environment and application configuration files, and managing the Node application with the PM2 process manager. The application was being kept down by a port conflict, which I diagnosed.

## Why it matters

Stalled projects are common: a freelancer moves on, an agency relationship ends, a founder inherits a codebase nobody explained. The first valuable thing is a clear picture of what exists and who controls it. The second is someone who can get onto the server and fix the immediate problem.

Writing the inventory down also protects the business the next time someone leaves, because the knowledge no longer lives in one person's head.

## Status

The assessment and the operational fixes described here were completed; larger rebuild and integration proposals are separate decisions for the brand. See [project rescue and takeovers](https://gerriscorp.com/services/rescue/).

Updated: 2026-10-05

# Programmatic site: managing crawling and indexing at scale

A new site publishing prices for more than 20,000 trading cards, built programmatically on an expired domain, indexed well at first. Then large numbers of pages dropped out of Google's index.

## My role

Technical SEO for crawl and index management, hired hourly, working with the owner over Teams and with access to the development repository on GitHub.

## How I approach it

A site like this has to be managed as collections of pages, not a handful of landing pages. The questions are which page types deserve indexing, how tools and filters generate URL variations, and how search engines discover deep pages.
- **Segmented sitemaps** for each content type, so Search Console reports indexing coverage per segment.
- **A baseline** of indexing by segment, so every change is compared against data.
- **Robots rules for parameterized tools** whose URL variations add nothing to the index and draw crawl attention away from the pages that matter.
- **Reporting lag accounted for.** Search Console reports trail reality, so I check live behavior before concluding a change worked or failed.
- **The domain's history** treated as one factor among several, kept separate from the site's own problems.

## Working with developers

The site is development-led, so fixes go through the repository. Access to the code means I can see how URLs are generated and specify changes precisely.

Every recommendation goes to the owner in writing, with the evidence behind it.

## Status

Ongoing. No recovery figures are claimed here; indexing at this scale moves over weeks and months. See [SEO for large and programmatic sites](https://gerriscorp.com/services/large-sites/).

# Health-testing store: recovering after an SEO plugin outage

On a WooCommerce store selling health tests, the SEO plugin was briefly switched off. Afterward, Search Console indexing, organic traffic, and referrals from AI assistants all fell. The owner isn't technical and needed someone to diagnose it, fix it, and prove the recovery.

## My role

Diagnosis, fixes, and verification in three paid milestones, under a HIPAA and nondisclosure agreement because the site handles protected health information.

## What happens when an SEO plugin goes off

On WordPress, the SEO plugin usually generates the titles, meta descriptions, canonical tags, robots directives, structured data, and XML sitemaps. Turn it off, even briefly, and crawlers can see pages without canonicals, with default titles, or with sitemaps that suddenly disappear. Turning it back on doesn't instantly undo what search engines recorded in the meantime.

## What I did
- URL inspections of the priority product and information pages in Search Console.
- Crawl statistics reviewed for changes in how often Googlebot visited and what it fetched.
- Sitemaps checked and resubmitted in both Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools.
- A priority list of pages to watch through the recovery.
- Structured data, Cloudflare configuration, and ghost traffic in GA4 reviewed as part of the same scope.

## How it was checked

Several indicators compared over time instead of one dashboard, with care to separate a stale report from a fault that was still happening. The owner received before-and-after evidence in plain language.

## Status

Recovery checks under way, with possible next steps including redirects, merchant structured data, and crawler policy. See [Search Console](https://gerriscorp.com/services/search-console/) and [analytics](https://gerriscorp.com/services/analytics/).

# Multi-location brand: untangling the parent from its first location

A custom closet and wardrobe company with locations in several states ran everything through one website. Search engines kept confusing the parent brand with its original location, and the location pages, Google Business Profiles, and town pages overlapped.

## My role

A fixed-price, milestone-based engagement delivering recommendations and developer-ready structured data.

## What I delivered

### Entity clarification

A clear separation of the parent brand from the original location, so search engines and AI assistants understand which is the company and which is one of its showrooms. The structured data states the relationship explicitly, with the locations as branches of the parent organization.

### Home page and product schema

JSON-LD for the organization and its products, ready for the developer to install.

### Location pages tied to Google Business Profiles

Recommendations for location pages that match each Google Business Profile, so every profile links to a page about that specific location rather than the home page.

### Profiles versus town pages

Guidance for where a Google Business Profile and a local town page cover the same area, so they support each other instead of competing.

### Service listings and breadcrumbs

Recommendations for how services, regions, and locations should be organized and linked, with breadcrumb structured data reflecting it.

## Why it matters

Multi-location businesses lose visibility when every page and listing says the same thing. Clear entities, distinct location pages, and accurate structured data let each location rank for its own area and let the brand rank for itself.

## Status

Delivered. See [multi-location and connected businesses](https://gerriscorp.com/services/multi-location/).

# Seasonal retailer: a staged plan around the peak

A retailer with several related stores, websites, and Google Business Profiles does most of its business in a short season. Its search signals were tangled across sites, and a previous migration and a falling-out with its last SEO provider left loose ends.

## My role

Hired as the accountable lead for an initial SEO and migration audit, working with the owner and his technical contact, with a seasonal engagement planned to follow.

## What the audit is finding
- Legacy URLs and redirects from the earlier migration, including links from other sites that now point at pages that no longer exist.
- Conflicting versions of the same domains.
- Duplicate and conflicting structured data.
- Business names and addresses that differ between sites, profiles, and directories.
- Overlapping location pages competing with each other.
- Product-page headings and outdated template content.
- Sitemaps that need cleanup, and Google Business Profiles that need aligning with the sites.

## The plan

The real judgment here is timing. Foundation work and anything that risks volatility, including Google Business Profile category changes that can trigger reverification, happens months before the season. Seasonal pages go live and get indexed early. A change freeze covers the peak, because nobody should deploy a site change in the busiest weeks of the year. A competitive local-search baseline makes progress measurable.

## Coordination

I'm organizing access across several sites and Google properties, preserving the historical Search Console data, and turning a complicated account into a short sequence of actions with an owner for each.

## Status

Audit in progress. See [multi-location and connected businesses](https://gerriscorp.com/services/multi-location/) and [fractional technical lead](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-lead/).

Updated: 2026-10-05

# Therapy practice: a suspended Google Business Profile reinstated

A hypnotherapy practice in British Columbia had its Google Business Profile suspended. For a practice that depends on local clients finding it, that meant the business had effectively disappeared from Google Maps.

## My role

Reviewing the profile and the business's information, building the appeal, and handling the process with Google.

## What I did

### Find the mismatch

Suspensions usually come from a mismatch between what the profile says and what Google can verify about the business: the name, the address, the category, or how the location operates. I compared the profile against the business's real details and corrected what didn't match.

### Build the evidence

I assembled the documents that prove the business is real and operates where it says: the lease, the business license, an invoice for the office, and the business card. I put the strongest verifiable document first, and claimed nothing the paperwork didn't support.

### Appeal

The appeal went to Google with the corrected profile and the organized evidence.

## Outcome

The profile was reinstated in February 2025.

## What I learned, and how I work now

Every case is different, and Google decides each one on its own schedule. That's why I now take on these cases as paid advisory work that starts with a written diagnostic, then a separately scoped appeal when there's a viable path. I also handle the investigative side of harder cases: reconstructing what happened to a profile, identifying the correct business record, and preserving an established profile and its reviews instead of starting over. See [Google Business Profile hard cases](https://gerriscorp.com/services/google-business-profile/).

Source: https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/data-cleanup/
Updated: 2026-10-05

# Contact data: three cleanups and an AI audit

Messy contact data costs money: bounced campaigns, damaged sender reputation, embarrassing wrong-name emails, and decisions made from lists nobody trusts. These projects turned unusable lists into reliable ones.

## An 88,900-contact master list

For a communications agency, a Python pipeline built one master list from a large accumulated set of contacts. It normalized names, removed bad email addresses, validated names against a global names database, flagged contradictions between a contact's name and email address, recovered missing names from email prefixes, and deduplicated across domains. The result was about 88,900 unique contacts.

## Two 28,800-record exports merged

For a reconnection campaign, I consolidated former clients and colleagues into one clean record per person, with company, first name, last name, and best email address, preferring personal addresses. The sources were a working spreadsheet and two contact-manager exports of about 28,800 records each, with shifted columns and broken field mappings that had to be repaired first. Tighter deduplication rules followed. The output reached about 94% email coverage, and every record carries a tag showing how it was resolved.

## An AI-generated tracker audited

An outreach tracker built with an AI tool claimed messages had been sent to contacts who had bounced or didn't exist, with uniform timestamps that couldn't be real, and duplicates throughout. I rebuilt it against the actual sending records: 452 rows became 392 real contacts, each with a status the evidence supported.

## Lessons
- Scripts beat hand-cleaning: the work is repeatable, and every change can be traced.
- Every record needs a resolution status, so nothing disappears silently.
- AI-produced data needs checking against source records before anyone relies on it.
- Sending volume matters as much as list quality: a mail-merge blast at high daily volume can get a sending account shut down, even with a clean list.

See [data cleanup and AI-output audits](https://gerriscorp.com/services/data-cleanup/).

Source: https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/founder-record/
Updated: 2026-10-14

# A founder's public record: tracing AI errors to the pages behind them

In October 2026 I checked what Claude and Google's AI Mode say about me. Most of it was right. Four things were wrong or doubted: the year Gerris Corp started, a company rename that never happened, two-year-old freelance figures, and a Forbes ranking the answer called unconfirmed. Every one traced to a specific page, three of them pages I had written myself, and the Wayback Machine confirmed the award the answers doubted.

## My role

The subject and the investigator. It is the same work I do for founders and executives whose public record has drifted, done on my own name so nothing has to be redacted.

## The errors and where they came from

**The founding year.** One answer said I started Gerris Corp in 2007. Gerris started in 2012; 2007 is when Mark Harrison and I launched Abraham Harrison. The answer quoted my own About page, which listed both companies and both years in one sentence. The model kept the first year and attached it to the second company. I gave each company its own line and its own year.

**The rename.** Google's AI Mode reported that I run "Gerris Digital (formerly Gerris Corp)." No rename ever happened. The name Gerris Digital appeared on three pages of chrisabraham.com, my personal archive, and one of those pages is a long biography written by an AI research tool, which says Abraham Harrison "merged with other entities to form Gerris Corp (Gerris Digital)." Faced with two names for one firm, the answer engine reconciled them by inventing a history. The fix is one name everywhere, and a correction note on the AI-written page.

**The stale figures.** Freelance figures from two years earlier, a higher status tier than I hold and smaller job and hour counts, came from a single profile page on the same archive. One page, three wrong facts.

**The doubted award.** My bios have long said Forbes named me a top 50 social media power influencer. One answer flagged it as unconfirmed because no bio linked a source. The original Forbes contributor post from January 25, 2012, is archived in the Wayback Machine, and the list shows me at number 33. The claim was true and unproven. Linking the archived list proves it.

## Corroborating the rest

The same archive work confirmed details the answers repeated correctly but without independent support: Advertising Age's April 2008 introduction of its DigitalNext bloggers, which describes me as president of Abraham Harrison, specializing in blogger outreach and search-reputation management, and living in Berlin and Washington; and my November 2008 Ad Age column written from Berlin. Ad Age's site blocks automated readers, so the archived copies are the citable versions.

## What it shows

Answer engines are faithful to their sources, including the careless ones. A sentence with two entities and two dates can hand a model the wrong pair. An AI-written bio published as a curiosity becomes a source for the next AI. An old profile page outranks a current one when nothing tells the crawler which is newer. And a true claim with no link reads to a model like an unsupported one. Each problem has a mechanical fix, and every fix starts with finding the page.

My guides cover the method: [fact checking a confident AI answer](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/fact-check-ai-seo/) claim by claim, and [citation gap analysis](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/citation-gap-analysis/) for the sources that leave you out. For founders and executives, see [reputation and perception management](https://gerriscorp.com/services/reputation/).

# Four static sites: a speed and AI crawler pass in one afternoon

In October 2026 I ran a full speed and AI crawler review across four sites I own: this one, a second consulting site, Hill Mole, and a feed-driven archive of 465 pages. They were already fast by most standards. The review found one cause behind most of the remaining slowness, fixed it with a trade-off I could state in a sentence, and moved every page I measured to 89 or better on mobile, most of them to 97 or above.

## My role

Everything: measurement, diagnosis, the code changes in each site's build, verification, and deployment. The sites are mine, so every number here can be checked on the live pages.

## Method

I measured a home page and a typical inner page on each site with Lighthouse 12 in mobile mode, using the same throttling PageSpeed Insights applies. I tested each fix on a local build of the same code before shipping it. Separately, I crawled 41 pages per site with my own audit script, checking headings, structured data, canonicals, image dimensions and alt text, dates, robots directives, and whether every sitemap URL returned a 200 and was indexable.

## What I found
- **The analytics tag.** On three of the sites, gtag.js produced most of the main-thread blocking time, 575 to 1,291 milliseconds per page. The sites' own code was small.
- **Image weight on the archive.** Cover images were 800-pixel JPEGs. WebP at three sizes cut the image weight on an episode page by about 300 KB.
- **A render-blocking stylesheet on Hill Mole.** A 2 KB stylesheet held the first paint, and the 700-pixel banner was a GIF shown at 412 pixels on phones.
- **Small tap targets.** A dark-mode button 22 pixels tall, below the 24-pixel minimum.
- **An incomplete AI crawler list.** robots.txt named 14 AI agents and missed 9 newer ones. Every token I added came from the vendor's own documentation that day, which also showed that one Google fetcher had been renamed two months earlier.

The crawl found no structural problems: one H1 per page, valid structured data everywhere, clean canonicals, complete alt text, and no noindexed URL in any sitemap.

## What I changed

Analytics now loads on the visitor's first scroll, tap, or key press, or four seconds after the page loads, with every command queued until the script arrives. The archive serves WebP covers at 400, 600, and 800 pixels with the JPEG as the fallback. Hill Mole's stylesheet is inlined and its banner is served as WebP. The dark-mode button grew to 48 by 28 pixels. robots.txt on all four sites names the newer agents. And every site now carries a speculation rule that prefetches a same-site page when a reader hovers over or starts to tap its link.

## Results
| Page | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| This site, home | 65 | 100 |
| This site, service page | 79 | 97 |
| Second consulting site, home | 83 | 98 |
| Second consulting site, service page | 84 | 100 |
| Hill Mole, home | 98 | 100 |
| Hill Mole, entry | 98 | 100 |
| Archive, home | 75 | 89 |
| Archive, episode page | 70 | 97 |

Scores are mobile Lighthouse performance. Accessibility reached 100 on all eight pages.

## The trade-off

Deferring analytics means a visitor who leaves within about four seconds without touching the page is never counted. Every other pageview is recorded. I made that choice for my own sites and would put the same choice to a client in writing before shipping it.

## What it shows

A fast site can still carry one expensive habit, and the fix is often a single decision once the measurement names it. The audit took an afternoon because the sites are generated from code I control: each change went into a build script once and reached every page. See [site speed](https://gerriscorp.com/services/site-speed/) for the same review on your site.

# Built with Codex and Claude Code

I run Claude Code the way a technical lead runs a development team: I write the requirements, make the design decisions, review every change, insist on tests, and decide what ships. These are three things built that way.

OpenAI Codex and Claude Code are now my two main coding assistants. The three original builds below were done with Claude Code; ongoing work on this site also uses Codex. I use GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and sometimes Perplexity as well, choosing around the task rather than a single provider.

## Blackbox: a command-line chief of staff

Blackbox, or `bb`, is my own assistant. It runs on a Debian server I administer and manages the operational side of my business from the terminal.

### What it does
- Manages tasks in Todoist, which is the single authority for everything I need to do.
- Reads and writes Google Calendar through my own Google Cloud OAuth project, and reads unread mail each morning, read-only, skipping invoices, newsletters, and sales pitches.
- Triages work opportunities through Upwork's official MCP server, ranking dozens of searches and drafting pitches for my approval.
- Assembles briefings and drafts writing using whichever model does the job best.
- Writes a diary entry at the end of every day, and closes the day itself at 11:45 p.m. if I forget to.

### How it was built

Over eight days, Claude Code took it from a 1,500-line script to about 12,000 lines: Python modules, an installer, a backup tool, and 140 end-to-end tests across 54 commits on main. Claude Code wrote the implementation. I specified the behavior, wrote structured feedback documents with scoped priorities and open architecture questions, tested each stage, compared model backends from OpenAI, Anthropic, and open-weight providers against each other on real tasks, and accepted or rejected the work.

### Safety rules
- Every external action needs one unambiguous target and my explicit confirmation. Nothing sends, submits, spends, or deletes on its own.
- Untrusted content, such as email and web pages, is treated as data and never as instructions.
- Deterministic routing handles every command it can without a model call; models are reserved for writing and judgment. Total model spend for the whole build period was about five dollars.
- Secrets live outside Git.
- Nightly AES-256 encrypted backups go to a private repository, and restores have been tested.

### Built from real use

The second week was the most useful. I used bb the way I actually talk, pasted the sessions back, and every misfire became a fix plus a test that uses my exact words. A shorthand I'd typed for weeks had been silently ignored, so now bb says plainly when something isn't a command and shows what would have worked. A ranking that gave hourly jobs no credit was found by asking a simple question about the results. Rules I stated once in conversation now live in code, where they can't drift. Every screen ends with the exact next command, which turned out to be the feature I value most.

### The deploy loop

Work happens on a branch in a development worktree. Tests run, the database is backed up, the branch is fast-forwarded to main and pushed, and a live smoke test confirms the result. It's the same discipline I bring to [client automation pilots](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ai-automation/).

## Hill Mole: a legacy blog off dead software

[Hill Mole](https://hillmole.com/) is my serialized novel, 309 entries written from 2005 to 2022 on Movable Type, which had stopped working. With Claude Code, I moved it to static pages on GitHub Pages, preserving the content, the feel of the original, and every original URL, including old archive and feed addresses. Every entry now has a hand-written title and description checked by a script on each build, schema.org data, llms.txt coverage, and IndexNow submission. The same approach rescues any client site stranded on old software. See [project rescue](https://gerriscorp.com/services/rescue/).

## This site

Gerris is plain HTML generated by a short Python script, also built with Claude Code. Every page has structured data and a Markdown twin for AI tools, the site publishes llms.txt and a full-text llms-full.txt, and each build checks title and description lengths, word counts, broken internal links, and the copy rules. It's static, fast, readable without JavaScript, and an example of the advice in the [guides](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/).

## What this means for clients

Building software with AI coding assistants is a real skill, and the skill is mostly the part that isn't typing: knowing what the job is, specifying behavior precisely, catching what the model got wrong, testing, and owning the decision to ship. That's what I bring to a client's tool, a client's repository, or a client's developers.

[Tell me what you'd build](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/)

# What I can take on in your stack, layer by layer

Search problems rarely stay in one layer. A ranking loss turns out to be a template, the template turns out to be a build setting, and the fix needs someone on the server. I work in every one of those layers myself. Here they are from the bottom up, each with the engagement or the working system that shows it.

## Servers and hosting
- My first root password opened a Solaris SPARCstation pizza box in the image lab at PNI, Picture Network International, my first job out of college.
- Before LAMP had a name, I was already living in it: Linux boxes, Apache, MySQL, and Perl and PHP scripts, all the way to 2002, when search became my full-time work.
- I took over a consumer brand's stalled React application after an outage: inventoried the code, hosting, DNS, and credentials, then got onto the DigitalOcean server over SSH, read the logs, corrected the configuration, ran the Node process under PM2, and found the port conflict keeping it offline. [The app takeover](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/app-takeover/).
- I provision and harden Linux servers for my own systems: key only SSH, root login off, firewalls, and automatic security updates.

## DNS, CDN, and email
- I moved this domain's DNS to Cloudflare with every Google Workspace mail record intact, and it runs SPF, DKIM, and a DMARC quarantine policy.
- I configure Cloudflare caching, redirects, and bot settings so speed improvements never lock out search or AI crawlers. See [Cloudflare settings for SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/cloudflare-seo/) and [email authentication and DNS](https://gerriscorp.com/services/email-and-dns/).

## Mail servers and Google Workspace
- I administer Google Workspace for my own business: users, aliases, groups, Gmail routing, Calendar, and Drive, plus a Google Cloud OAuth project my assistant uses to read and write my calendar.
- I learned mail on Linux servers running Sendmail, so IMAP, POP3, SMTP ports, aliases, and mail routing are old friends. When mail misbehaves, I read the headers and the bounce codes first. The [blocklist recovery guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-blocklist-recovery/) shows the method.

## Repositories and pull requests

Codex and Claude Code handle most of my work with AI coding assistants. My other tools include GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and occasional Perplexity use. I keep requirements and verification in the project so I can work across platforms.
- I wrote and patched Perl and PHP for years, on Movable Type, PHP-Nuke, PostNuke, and scripts of my own, so a client's codebase is familiar ground long before an AI assistant opens it.
- I merged metadata changes into a local business's Sanity and Vercel codebase through GitHub, under the developer's review, and confirmed the prerendered output. [Sanity and Vercel](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/sanity-vercel/).
- I work in a 20,000 page programmatic site's GitHub repository to see how URLs get generated and specify crawl controls precisely. [Programmatic indexing](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/programmatic-indexing/).
- I read entire codebases with OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to find the component behind a crawl finding, and I check each answer on the live site.

## Build pipelines and automation
- This site is generated by a Python script that refuses to publish a bad title, a duplicate description, a broken internal link, a page under its word minimum, or two pages that share too much wording. The method is written up in [SEO regression tests in the build](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/seo-build-checks/).
- A GitHub Actions workflow pings IndexNow after every deploy, once the new sitemap is confirmed live.
- I moved a 309 entry serialized novel off a broken Movable Type install to Jekyll on GitHub Pages, keeping every original URL and adding schema, llms.txt, and IndexNow. [Built with Codex and Claude Code](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/built-with-claude-code/).
- I run a weblog, [chrisabraham.net](https://chrisabraham.net/), written by several AI agents under their own bylines: house rules in an AGENTS.md file, a dated handoff for every working session, and the prompt behind every post published beside it.
- I built my own operations assistant, about 12,000 lines of Python with 140 end-to-end tests, by directing Claude Code like a development team.

## Rendering and front end
- I traced a Magento and Hyvä store's decline to Alpine.js sections that never rendered for Googlebot, and kept a second, unrelated problem on its own track. [Ecommerce rendering](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/ecommerce-rendering/).
- I specified the fixes for a Create React App platform with 2,000 undiscovered pages in a 13-page spec ranked P0 to P3, then verified them. [React event platform](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/react-event-platform/).
- I found the consent setup that left a review site's article tabs empty for Google. [Consent blocking](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/consent-blocking/).
- I sweep sites for React hydration errors with scripted headless Chrome. See [hydration errors and SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/hydration-errors/).

## Content systems
- On Umbraco I built and published 54 city landing pages for one B2B company, and for another found the cache problem that kept saved social metadata off the live page. [Umbraco operations](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/umbraco-operations/).
- I audited a Squarespace to Shopify move with 3,400 404s and duplicate URLs, and did the theme schema work. [Shopify migration](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/shopify-migration/).
- I've worked in WordPress for twenty years, and in Shopify, Magento 2, Drupal, Squarespace, Webflow, Plone and the Zope server under it, Jekyll, and Next.js.

## Crawl data and archives
- For this domain, which has run on Drupal, Squarespace, and now static pages since 2012, I pulled every URL the Wayback Machine ever captured, tested all 848 against the live site, and redirected each one that had ever served a page: more than 640 redirects in all.
- I freeze websites stranded on dead software as plain static files, keeping every address they ever published, and wrote up the method in [freezing an old website as static HTML](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/freeze-old-website/).
- Full site crawls with JavaScript rendering, custom extraction, near-duplicate detection, and before-and-after comparisons are routine.

## Structured data and entities
- I separated a multi-state closets brand from its first location in schema and on the page. [Multi-location entity](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/multi-location-entity/).
- Every page here carries a connected JSON-LD graph, a Markdown twin, and full-text feeds for AI crawlers.

## Data
- My Python pipelines produced an 88,900 contact master list, merged two 28,800 record exports to 94% email coverage, and exposed an AI-made tracker that had invented its records. [Data cleanup](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/data-cleanup/).

## What comes with me into every layer
- **Separate problems stay separate.** A template change and a spam link spike that arrive in the same month get two investigations until the data joins them. [The Magento case](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/ecommerce-rendering/) is the example.
- **False alarms get caught.** When an AI visibility dashboard showed a sharp drop for a B2B client, I traced it to the vendor changing its methodology; the client's actual visibility had held steady. [Umbraco operations](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/umbraco-operations/).
- **Evidence gets assembled like a legal brief.** Debate training shows in my Google appeals: the strongest verifiable document leads, private documents stay out, and every date has paper behind it. [The reinstatement](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/gbp-reinstatement/).
- **Sources get vetted.** At Edelman I screened online influencers for a genuine multi-year history before any client engaged them. That is open-source intelligence work, and the same instinct checks every report a vendor or an AI hands me.
- **One finding, two documents.** Engineers get ranked tickets with acceptance criteria; owners get a plain summary they can act on. [Developer specs and QA](https://gerriscorp.com/services/developers/).
- **Speed with guardrails.** This site reached 92 pages and more than 62,000 words eight days after its first commit, built with Claude Code under my direction, and every page clears the automated checks before it publishes.
- **Mail that can't be spoofed.** This domain runs SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and a sister domain that never sends mail is locked down with a reject policy, strict alignment, and a null MX.

## Regulated work

I've worked under HIPAA and nondisclosure agreements on a healthcare site, and I keep credentials out of repositories and AI tools on every engagement.

For the person behind all this, see [About](https://gerriscorp.com/about/), and for the full career record, my [CV on chrisabraham.com](https://chrisabraham.com/cv). To put any of it to work, [tell me where your problem lives](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# Work with me

A sensible first step is a paid diagnostic with a clear question and a clear deliverable. Everything else builds from there.

## Ways to engage
- **Diagnostic.** Evidence, priorities, and a recommended next step, for a defined site and a defined set of questions. Usually one to three weeks.
- **Implementation sprint.** Agreed fixes or deliverables, verified on the live site against written acceptance criteria.
- **Migration review.** Pre-launch or post-launch checks and developer coordination for a named site and launch.
- **Ongoing support.** An agreed monthly capacity for SEO, content, and website work.
- **Advisory.** A monthly advisory retainer, or individual briefings, workshops, and second opinions.
- **AI pilot.** One useful workflow built and demonstrated, with defined inputs, permissions, outputs, and handover.

## How a project runs
1. **First conversation.** You describe the site and the problem by email or in a short call. I say whether I'm the right person and where I'd start.
2. **Scope in writing.** The questions, the deliverable, the access needed, the timeline, and the price, agreed before work begins.
3. **The work.** I investigate, report progress in writing, and raise anything urgent at once.
4. **Delivery.** Findings, fixes, tickets, or the agreed deliverable, walked through with you and your team.
5. **Verification.** A check of the live result once changes ship, and a recommendation for what comes next.

## Fees

Fees are settled in conversation, once I understand the problem, and written into the scope before any work begins.

## Where the work happens

Every project runs in Basecamp or by email, threaded and on the record, so you always know the status and nothing gets lost. Developer work goes into your ticket system.

## What helps
- Access to Search Console, analytics, and the CMS, repository, or DNS I'll work in.
- An introduction to your developer, host, or marketing team.
- Prompt answers. A project that goes quiet closes, and restarts with a fresh scope when you're ready.

## Hosting

I work on sites wherever they're hosted. Hosting itself stays with you or your provider, so you always own and control your site.

## Upwork

If your company hires through Upwork, you can hire me there: [Chris Abraham on Upwork](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

More answers on the [FAQ](https://gerriscorp.com/faq/).

[Start with a diagnostic](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/)

# Frequently asked questions

Practical answers about process, timing, payment, and how I work.

## Starting out

### How does a project start?

With an email or a short call about your site and the problem. If I'm the right person, I send a written scope for a paid diagnostic: the questions, the deliverable, the access needed, the timeline, and the price.

### Do you offer a free audit?

The first conversation is free and short, enough to tell whether I can help and where I'd start. The diagnosis itself is paid work, because that's where the real value is.

### Who does the work?

I do, personally, on every engagement. Gerris Corp is my consultancy.

### What kinds of clients do you work with?

Funded companies, established businesses, agencies that need a specialist, and individuals whose public record matters, in any industry and any country.

## Timing

### How long does a diagnostic take?

Usually one to three weeks, depending on the size of the site and the number of separate problems. The timeline is agreed in writing before work starts.

### How soon can you start?

Usually within one to two weeks of a signed scope and payment. Urgent problems, such as a sudden traffic collapse or a failed launch, get priority when I have capacity.

### How long until results show in Google?

Fixes take effect as Google recrawls the affected pages: days for important pages, weeks or months for large sites. I track the change in Search Console and report it.

## Payment

### How do you charge?

New engagements are quoted as a flat fee, settled in conversation once I understand the problem and written into the scope.

### Can I hire you through Upwork?

Yes. Many clients hire me through Upwork, which handles contracts and payment.

## Working together

### What access do you need?

Usually Search Console, analytics, and read access to the CMS or repository. DNS and CDN access when the work involves them. I document every account I use.

### Which platforms do you work on?

WordPress, Umbraco, Wix, Squarespace, Shopify, Magento, Netlify, GitHub Pages, static sites, and JavaScript frameworks such as Next.js, React, Vue, and Alpine.js, with Cloudflare in front of many of them.

### Do you recommend Cloudflare?

For nearly every site, yes: DNS and caching through Cloudflare, configured so search engines and AI crawlers get in. The free plan does a lot, and when a site runs through Cloudflare and benefits from the paid features, I suggest budgeting about $50 a month. Hosted builders such as Shopify, Squarespace, and Wix are the exception. Details are in [my Cloudflare guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/cloudflare-seo/).

### How do you communicate during a project?

In writing, in Basecamp or by email, so every decision and status update is on the record. Calls are scheduled when they're useful.

### Do you work with in-house developers?

Yes, and it's one of the things I do best. I write precise tickets with acceptance criteria and check the result once it ships.

### Is the work confidential?

Yes. I name clients only with their permission, and I'm happy to sign a nondisclosure agreement.

Something else? [Ask me directly](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# Editorial standards

Gerris Corp is one consultant, so every guide, case study, and service page on this site is mine to stand behind. These are the rules I hold them to.

## Experience comes first

A case study here exists because I did the work: I was hired, I ran the diagnosis or the build, and I can say exactly which parts were mine and which belonged to the client's developer or agency. Guides grow out of the same engagements. If I haven't done something with my own hands, I don't write a how-to about it.

## Claims point to their source

When a guide says how Googlebot renders a page, how Bing treats a tag, what an RFC requires of a DNS record, or what a consent setting actually does, the page lists the documentation behind it under "References." The same list is published in the guide's structured data. Official documentation changes, so a reference is a starting point for your own check, not a replacement for it.

## AI in the workflow, with a human at the end

I also use GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and occasionally Perplexity. That range is deliberate: I work across AI platforms and apply the same editorial checks whichever one helped with a draft.

I build with AI tools every day, primarily OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, and this site's generator and many first drafts came out of that work. The rule is simple: nothing goes live until I've read it, corrected it, and verified every factual statement. Biographical details about me come from my own records and published sources I can point to, never from what a chatbot has decided about me. The build itself refuses pages that break the house rules for titles, length, duplication, and voice.

## Confidentiality is part of accuracy

Clients are described by industry and problem. No names, addresses, revenue, case numbers, or private screenshots, and nothing that would let a reader work out who the client is. Ongoing and paused engagements are labeled that way. Outcomes are reported only when the evidence supports them, and "under way" is an honest status.

## No one pays to be mentioned

This site carries no sponsored content and no paid reviews. Its only affiliate links are Amazon Associates links to books and gear, and any page with one ends with the required disclosure. When I name a tool, a host, or a platform, it's because I use it or a client runs on it.

## Dates mean something

Every page shows its last update, and guides show both their publication and revision dates. When Google, Bing, or a standard changes in a way that affects a guide, the guide is revised and the date moves.

## Found a mistake?

Email [chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com) with the page address and the problem. I'll check it against the source and correct the page if you're right, and note any substantive change on the page itself.

## More about me

My background is on the [About page](https://gerriscorp.com/about/), how engagements run is on [Work With Me](https://gerriscorp.com/work-with-me/), and you can reach me through the [contact page](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# Colophon

A colophon is the note at the back of a well-made book about how it was made. This is that note for gerriscorp.com.

## The logo The Gerris logo, drawn by [Oliver Uberti](https://www.oliveruberti.com/) in 2012.

The Gerris water strider was designed and drawn in 2012 by [Oliver Uberti](https://www.oliveruberti.com/), a dear friend and a remarkable artist. Oliver was a senior design editor at National Geographic and is the co-author and designer of [Atlas of the Invisible](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0393651517?tag=gerris-20), [London: The Information Capital](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1846148472?tag=gerris-20), [Where the Animals Go](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0393634027?tag=gerris-20), and [Notes from a Public Typewriter](https://www.amazon.com/dp/1538729113?tag=gerris-20). He gave the company its emblem: *Gerris lacustris*, the insect that skates across the surface of a pond without breaking it.

The name came first, and it came from rowing. Carbon fiber racing shells, especially doubles, have always looked to me like the pond skaters you can find in the still water along the Potomac's banks, dancing on the surface tension. I named my Hudson racing shell *Gerris* before I ever named a company after it. Once the firm Dan Krueger and I ran was incorporated, I asked Oliver for a logo, and what he drew settled the matter: any thought of renaming the agency ended the day I saw it. I wrote the whole story up in 2017.

Oliver's second round of sketches, dated October 25, 2012, set four ideas over the words "Gerris Web Strategies": contact points drawn as ripples, contact points drawn as dots, a single point of contact with a ripple and a smile, and the strider itself, which he called Strider/Connector. The strider is the one that became the logo. [Oliver Uberti](https://www.oliveruberti.com/)'s Phase II revisions, October 25, 2012. Concept 1, Strider/Connector, became the Gerris logo.

## Design

The look borrows from the classic Plone theme I've used for my own sites for two decades: tabbed navigation, slate blue links, and nothing between the reader and the words. Body text is black Verdana at 18 pixels for legibility. The accent colors, a burnt orange for the name, a blue for page titles, and a teal for section heads, were each darkened until they pass the WCAG contrast standard against white.

## How it's built

OpenAI Codex and Claude Code now share the work of maintaining and improving this site under my direction. I also use GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and sometimes Perplexity. The original terminal build described below was done with Claude Code.

Every page starts as a plain HTML file. A small Python program reads them, wraps each in the shared header and footer, and writes the finished site: pages, a Markdown copy of each page for AI tools, XML and HTML sitemaps, an Atom feed, llms.txt, and redirect pages for more than 400 addresses from the old gerriscorp.com. Before anything is published, the same program checks every page: title and description lengths, one heading per page, minimum word counts, first person singular, no copied phrasing between pages, and no broken internal links. If a page fails, nothing ships.

The site was written and built in a terminal, over SSH from a ThinkPad X220 to a Linux server at DigitalOcean, working alongside Claude Code, Anthropic's AI coding assistant. I set the requirements, made the editorial calls, and checked every fact; the assistant wrote code and drafts to my direction. [The editorial standards](https://gerriscorp.com/standards/) describe how that division of labor works.

## Hosting and delivery

The finished files are served by GitHub Pages over HTTPS, with DNS at Cloudflare. There's no database, no content management system, and no server code to patch. The only script is Google Analytics, set up with consent mode, as described on the [privacy page](https://gerriscorp.com/privacy/).

## Tested with
- Lynx, the text browser, to see each page the way screen readers and crawlers receive it. My notes on that are in [Lynx for website QA](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/lynx-qa/).
- Google PageSpeed Insights and Lighthouse, for performance, accessibility, best practices, and SEO.
- Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools, with IndexNow announcing every change to Bing.

## Source

The code and content live in a public repository: [github.com/chrisabraham/gerriscorp](https://github.com/chrisabraham/gerriscorp). The site went live on October 5, 2026.

Links to books and gear on Amazon carry my Amazon Associates tag. As an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

# Privacy

This site collects very little: anonymous visit statistics, and whatever you choose to send me by email or phone.

## Visit statistics

This site uses Google Analytics 4 to count visits, see which pages people read, and learn how visitors arrive, including from search engines and AI assistants. It records information such as the pages you view, your approximate location, your device and browser, and the site that referred you. It doesn't collect your name, email address, or other details that identify you directly.

For visitors in the United Kingdom and the European Economic Area, analytics cookies are switched off. Google Analytics receives cookieless measurements instead, which count visits without storing anything on your device. Elsewhere, Google Analytics may set first-party cookies to recognize repeat visits. Advertising and personalization features are turned off for everyone.

Browsers that send a Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track signal get the same cookieless treatment, wherever the visitor happens to be. Google signals stays switched off for every visit.

Google processes this data under its own [privacy policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy). You can block Google Analytics anywhere with your browser's privacy settings, a content blocker, or Google's [opt-out browser add-on](https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout).

## Email and phone

When you email me or call, I receive what you send: your name, your address or number, and the details of your project. I use it only to reply and to do the work you hire me for. I don't sell it, share it with marketers, or add you to a mailing list.

## Hosting and security

The site is static pages served by GitHub Pages, with DNS through Cloudflare. Those services keep standard server logs, such as IP addresses and request times, for security and reliability, under their own policies. There are no forms, accounts, or comments on this site.

## Client information

Information I see while working for clients, such as analytics, Search Console data, site access, and documents, is kept confidential, used only for the engagement, and covered by a nondisclosure agreement where the client asks for one.

## Questions

Email [chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com) with any question about your information, or to ask me to delete correspondence you've sent.

# Internal linking strategy and implementation

A website can have excellent pages that barely acknowledge each other. The useful explanation sits in the archive, the service lives three sections away, and the case study never reaches the person considering that service. I connect those pieces with relevant text links, understandable anchor wording, and destinations that work.

## Use the material you have already paid to create

An established site contains years of work: answers to customer questions, specialist knowledge, product details, and evidence from completed projects. Linking that material thoughtfully can make the whole collection more useful. The work starts inside your existing site, with the routes you control and the pages your team already maintains.

## Decide which pages should support which decisions

I identify the journeys that matter to the business. Someone researching a problem may need an explanation, then an example of the work, then the relevant service. A buyer comparing products needs clear category routes and helpful supporting information. Those paths become the starting map, and crawl data shows where the published site currently makes the journey difficult.

## What the review covers
- **Unconnected content:** important pages present in the inventory but missing from normal discovery paths.
- **Editorial opportunities:** passages where another existing page answers the next useful question.
- **Site structure:** category routes, section indexes, breadcrumbs, and related content components.
- **Anchor wording:** link labels that set a clear expectation without turning the paragraph into a list of search phrases.
- **Implementation faults:** broken section targets, redirects, stale addresses, and navigation that depends on an interaction a crawler may never perform.

## Make a change list people can use

Each recommendation identifies the source page, the destination, the proposed location, and the reason for adding the connection. Editorial links go to the content owner. Component changes go to the developer with examples and acceptance criteria. If the same issue appears across thousands of generated pages, I investigate the template or route data so the remedy can be applied consistently.

## Build context around the important destination

A service page can link to evidence that helps somebody judge the offer. A technical article can point to the practical next step. A long reference page can offer a link to an exact section elsewhere, provided the target exists and remains stable. These are small edits, but they should be decisions about what the reader needs, not automatic replacements of every matching word in the database.

## Evidence behind the approach

My [React event platform case](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/react-event-platform/) involved a discovery problem affecting roughly 2,000 event pages. That is a reminder to examine the links an application actually provides, alongside its visible design. On a large archive or a programmatic site, finding the missing connection can be more useful than writing another page nobody can reach.

## Implementation and acceptance

I can add the agreed links where access allows, or provide a precise implementation map for your team. A new crawl checks the published connections and the pages they lead to. The verification record names the changed templates and editorial pages, while later reporting follows the search behavior of the priority destinations. Results are reported against the work observed and the question the project set out to answer.

## Planning a linking project

### Does the whole website need reviewing at once?

No. A useful first project can focus on a service family, a content archive, or a particular product category. The scope names the inventory and the priority destinations.

### Can an agency use the plan with its own editors?

Yes. The proposed placements and destinations can be delivered as a working list, with developer changes separated from copy additions and a final check after publication.

This work fits alongside [on page SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/services/on-page-seo/), [large site SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/services/large-sites/), and [agency support](https://gerriscorp.com/services/agency-partner/). [Tell me which pages visitors should be finding](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/) and I can scope a practical starting point.

## Start a conversation

Scope and fees are settled in conversation, once I understand the problem. Choose the route that fits how your company works.
