# AI workflow testing and acceptance reviews

The demonstration worked. Now somebody needs to find out what happens with an incomplete request, a duplicate record, a failed connection, or an instruction hidden inside a document. I help turn an AI pilot into something your team can judge against written requirements.

## Start with one job

The useful unit is a workflow: turn these meeting notes into draft tasks, reconcile these two exports, or prepare this briefing from these sources. I define the inputs, the expected output, the person who accepts it, and the actions the system may take. That makes the review concrete. The question is whether this tool can do your job within agreed limits, with evidence somebody else can inspect.

## A set of examples your team recognizes

I work with representative examples from the people who will actually use the tool. A good test collection includes ordinary requests, shorthand, missing information, conflicting instructions, repeated submissions, and the cases that have already caused trouble. Sensitive material can be replaced with controlled examples that preserve the behavior being tested. Each case records what a satisfactory result would look like before the tool runs.

## What I check
- **Output quality:** whether names, dates, totals, sources, and record identities match the input.
- **Action boundaries:** whether a draft stays a draft and an action requiring approval waits for it.
- **Failure behavior:** what happens when a service is unavailable, an answer is uncertain, or an input cannot be parsed.
- **Repeated work:** whether retrying an interrupted task creates duplicate records or messages.
- **Traceability:** whether the team can distinguish proposed work, completed work, and work that never happened.

## Experience behind the review

My own command line assistant grew through real use: misread requests became explicit examples in its test suite. The [coding assistant case study](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/built-with-claude-code/) describes that process and the 140 end-to-end tests in the original build. Separately, I checked an AI-generated outreach tracker against actual sending records and found activity the evidence did not support. That work is in the [data cleanup and AI audit case study](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/data-cleanup/). Both experiences inform a simple habit: compare the tool's report with what actually happened.

## Platform agnostic by design

I use OpenAI Codex and Claude Code as my primary coding assistants, alongside GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Grok, and occasional Perplexity use. For this work, the test cases and expected behavior belong to your project. The same collection can help compare a proposed replacement with the version already in use, provided the inputs and acceptance rules stay consistent.

## The handover

You receive the agreed test collection, observed results, evidence of failures, and a prioritized list of changes or unresolved questions. The recommendation can be to proceed within a limited scope, revise the pilot, or gather evidence that was missing. I also identify which checks can become automated regression tests and which still need a person to read the output. A passing result applies to the tested version and conditions.

## Before a pilot review

### Can you review a tool someone else supplied?

Yes, with enough access to exercise the workflow and inspect its records. The scope distinguishes behavior I can observe from implementation details that need the supplier's cooperation.

### Where should a first engagement start?

With a named workflow, a small set of representative tasks, and a paid diagnostic. Implementation or a wider rollout follows only after the findings and next scope are agreed.

The [AI pilot testing guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-pilot-tests/) includes a worksheet you can use yourself. For a review, [send me the workflow and what a good result should accomplish](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/). If you need the tool built as well, see [AI agents and automation](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ai-automation/).

## Start a conversation

Scope and fees are settled in conversation, once I understand the problem. Choose the route that fits how your company works.

# Test an AI pilot with the work it is supposed to do

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 15, 2026

A polished demonstration answers the question the demonstrator prepared. Your working day contains the requests they did not prepare: a missing date, two customers with the same name, a task submitted twice, or a report that sounds finished when the underlying action failed. A pilot needs examples of those situations before anyone can decide whether to rely on it.

## Write one plain job description

Begin with a sentence that has an input and an observable result. For example: given an approved meeting note, produce draft tasks with the correct owner and due date. That is narrow enough to test. A promise to make the team more productive is useful as an ambition, but it leaves the test writer guessing which behavior is required.

Record the tool version, its connected services, and the account permissions used in the trial. Give the pilot an owner who can decide whether an output is acceptable. The person writing the test should not have to infer the answer from whatever the assistant happened to produce.

## Collect ordinary examples before clever ones

Ask the future users for several requests they would really make. Preserve the shorthand, unfinished sentences, and naming conventions that appear in daily work. Add a small number of unusual cases deliberately, rather than building the whole collection from puzzles. The ordinary examples show whether the workflow is useful; the exceptions show where it needs help.

I learned this with my own terminal assistant. A phrase I had used repeatedly was being silently ignored. Turning the exact request into a test made the problem visible and kept the correction from depending on a conversation I would later forget. The build history is described in the [assistant case study](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/built-with-claude-code/).

## Define the result before running the case

For a draft task, the owner must refer to the right person, an absent date must remain absent or trigger a question, and no live task should be created if the request only asks for a draft. For a summary, separate facts that must be present from wording that can vary. This avoids the easy mistake of approving a convincing answer because it resembles the last convincing answer.

Use the [AI pilot test case worksheet](https://gerriscorp.com/downloads/ai-pilot-test-cases.csv) as a starting point. Its rows describe invented examples. Fill in the expected behavior, the observed result, and the evidence. Keep real client data in the approved project workspace rather than in a public example file.

## Include a few failures on purpose
| Case | Question to settle |
| --- | --- |
| Missing information | Does the assistant ask, preserve the gap, or invent a value? |
| Ambiguous identity | Can it stop before choosing the wrong customer? |
| Duplicate request | Does a retry repeat an action already completed? |
| Unavailable service | Is failure reported without claiming the action succeeded? |
| Instructions inside source material | Does quoted content stay separate from the user's request? |
| Unapproved action | Does the workflow wait at the agreed decision point? |

Exercise service failures in an isolated trial or with a simulated dependency. Do not create a live outage to see how the pilot reacts. The aim is a reproducible example, not a surprise for the people depending on the service.

## Test the permission boundary as behavior

OWASP's discussion of excessive agency recommends limiting tool capabilities and permissions, with human approval for consequential actions. Translate that principle into a case you can observe. If a workflow is allowed to prepare a message but requires approval to send it, inspect both the draft and the sending record. The assistant saying that it waited is only one part of the evidence.

A written instruction helps explain the rules. An account that lacks unnecessary permissions helps enforce them. Review both when the pilot connects to another service. A harmless drafting exercise can become a different system when somebody adds a connection that can publish, delete, or spend.

## Save evidence that outlives the session

Keep the inputs, outputs, timestamps, relevant service records, and the acceptance decision together. When a test runs in GitHub Actions, downloadable workflow artifacts can hold its reports. Set retention deliberately and store sensitive evidence only where the team has approved it. A screenshot of the final answer rarely explains a retry, a hidden error, or a partial action.

My [outreach tracker audit](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/data-cleanup/) is a useful reminder here. The tracker described activity, but checking the actual sending records changed what could honestly be reported. A pilot should make that comparison easier, not bury the trail under a confident paragraph.

## Score separate questions separately

Record correctness, completeness, unauthorized actions, and manual correction effort independently. A mostly useful summary and a message sent to the wrong person should not average into an acceptable score. Decide in advance which failures stop the pilot and which can be tolerated with a documented workaround.

Repeat cases where results vary and retain the individual outcomes. If only one run was observed, say so. A small collection can reveal a repeatable failure without proving a general success rate. The report should state what was tested and the limits of that evidence.

## Keep the collection when the pilot ends

Use the same examples when a prompt changes, a new model is proposed, or a connector gains another permission. Add real failures as the team encounters them. Remove obsolete cases through an explicit decision so the collection continues to describe the job people are actually doing.

I can help define and run that review through [AI workflow testing](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ai-workflow-testing/). For the earlier buying decision, the [AI vendor questions](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-vendor-pitch/) help establish what the supplier should demonstrate before a pilot begins.

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com)

If your company hires through Upwork, you'll find me [there as well](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project: Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/)
- [GitHub Docs: Downloading workflow artifacts](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/download-workflow-artifacts)

# A website handover needs more than a zip file and a password

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 15, 2026

The contractor says the website is yours. Can someone new rebuild it, publish a correction, renew the domain, and restore the data without calling that contractor? Those are practical handover questions, and they can be answered while everyone is still available to help. Here is the inventory I would want before accepting responsibility for an inherited site.

## Start with the account that controls each layer

A domain registration, a DNS zone, a hosting subscription, and a code repository can belong to four different accounts. List them separately. For each, record the business owner, the people with administrative access, the billing contact, and the recovery route. The person who can edit a page is not necessarily the person who can recover the account.

The [website handover inventory worksheet](https://gerriscorp.com/downloads/website-handover-inventory.csv) provides rows for these layers and room to record evidence. Put account identifiers in the private working copy, but keep passwords, recovery codes, tokens, and private keys in an approved secrets manager. The worksheet should say where access is managed, not become another loose credentials file.

## Prove the source matches the site

Ask which repository and revision produced the current deployment. Keep the build instructions, runtime requirements, dependency files, and a list of required configuration variable names with the project. A useful handover lets a new maintainer start from the recorded revision in a fresh workspace and reproduce the intended result.

Try that build before treating the instructions as complete. If it needs a file that exists only on somebody's laptop, an unrecorded account, or a package that cannot be retrieved, the trial has found an unresolved dependency. Record the dependency and its owner rather than quietly borrowing the departing developer's working directory.

## Separate a repository transfer from an access review

GitHub documents that secrets, deploy keys, and webhooks can remain associated with a transferred repository. Receiving ownership therefore does not by itself settle who can still act on the project. Review the actual connections, collaborators, automation accounts, and deployment credentials as part of the handover.

Agree the timing of access changes with the people responsible for the live service. An old key may still be powering the production build. Replace and test necessary connections before withdrawing the previous ones, then record that the old access has been removed. This sequence keeps an ownership improvement from becoming an accidental outage.

## Inventory the things outside Git

A working site may depend on a database, uploaded media, scheduled jobs, a mail provider, search indexes, an external form service, or storage controlled by a different account. Include the dependencies the visitor never sees. A nightly import that stops running can make the site wrong for weeks before anybody notices that a background job was missed.
- **Content and files:** where editable content, original artwork, and visitor uploads live.
- **Recurring jobs:** what runs, on whose service, and who receives a failure alert.
- **Forms and notifications:** where submissions are stored and how delivery is verified.
- **Analytics:** which properties and accounts contain the business's reporting history.
- **Licenses:** which commercial components need renewal or a new owner.

## Restore something before calling it a backup

List what each backup includes, its schedule, where it is stored, and who can retrieve it. Then restore the necessary components into a separate test environment. A repository backup is useful, but the application may also need data and media stored elsewhere. GitHub's backup documentation explains repository backup methods; the running service needs its own inventory around them.

Choose a small, recognizable check after the restore: a particular article, a known uploaded file, or a test record that should exist. Record the backup date and the result. Keep test notifications and outbound integrations disabled while checking the restored copy so a rehearsal does not contact real customers.

## Write down the domain and email dependencies

A website move often shares a DNS zone with the company's email. Save the current records and identify which serve the site, which serve mail, and which verify ownership for other services. A new maintainer needs to know why a record exists before deciding that an unfamiliar entry is obsolete.

Record domain renewal responsibility, certificate handling, redirects, and any old hostnames that still serve files or forward visitors. The domain is not fully handed over if its renewal notice goes only to an address nobody in the business can read. The [email and DNS service](https://gerriscorp.com/services/email-and-dns/) covers that layer when it needs hands on work.

## Ask the receiving person to do one routine job

Have the new maintainer make an agreed harmless change on a preview, inspect the result, and explain the release and rollback process. It is a much better test of the documentation than asking whether the folder of instructions looks complete. The exercise also reveals which decisions still depend on knowledge the departing contractor has never written down.

Record unresolved items, their owners, and the next date to review them. A handover can be accepted with clearly identified followup work, but a missing recovery route should not disappear inside a general statement that everything is finished.

## Keep the inventory useful after handover

Review it when hosting changes, a new supplier joins, or an integration is added. It becomes the starting point for the next contractor and a much calmer starting point for an outage. My [application takeover case](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/app-takeover/) shows the kind of configuration and operational work that an inherited project can require.

If the documentation is incomplete or nobody knows what is running, [project rescue and takeover review](https://gerriscorp.com/services/rescue/) is an existing way to hire me for the inventory and a practical next plan. A second opinion before you accept a supplier's handover also fits [strategic advisory](https://gerriscorp.com/services/advisory/).

# B2B catalog SEO for manufacturers and distributors

Your best customer may be searching for a specific component, a material, or a compatibility answer. I help suppliers make that information findable and useful, then connect the page to a quote request your sales team can act on.

## When this service fits

This is for businesses whose catalog supports a considered purchase: industrial components, technical equipment, specialist materials, or products sold through quotations and repeat accounts. It is especially useful when a site has thousands of items but weak specifications, inaccessible product information, or traffic that rarely becomes a suitable inquiry.

A retail checkout and a supplier qualification process need different content. I review how your customers buy before recommending more pages. Sales conversations, product documentation, Search Console, and a sample crawl establish whether the immediate problem is discovery, missing information, or the route into sales.

## What the diagnostic covers
- Product family and part number discovery, including important identifiers and variant distinctions.
- Specifications, datasheets, selection guidance, and the information buyers need before contacting sales.
- HTML rendering, internal navigation, duplicate URLs, filters, and canonical consistency.
- Product markup checked against the visible information and applicable search requirements.
- Quote forms, product context, confirmation behavior, and the destination of test inquiries.
- A measurement plan that distinguishes total submissions from commercially relevant opportunities.

## A pilot before a catalog rollout

I choose one product family with your commercial and technical reviewers. The first delivery is a written findings list, a page inventory, and a proposed template with acceptance criteria. Each recommendation identifies its evidence, its owner, and what must be checked before it can be published.

Implementation can include editing priority pages, preparing developer specifications, or working in the repository where access permits. I verify the approved changes against the original sample. A pilot report records what shipped, what still depends on your team, and what the early observations do and do not establish.

## What I need from you

Access to the relevant site data, a representative catalog export, approved documentation, and someone who can verify technical claims. Sales needs to define a useful inquiry and identify recurring customer questions. I can organize and explain your source material; an authorized product expert must approve specifications, certifications, and replacement recommendations.

Read the [technical buyer catalog guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/b2b-catalog-seo/) for the selection and measurement method. For a related implementation problem, the [ecommerce rendering case study](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/ecommerce-rendering/) explains how product content can be present visually yet difficult for a crawler to receive. It is evidence of that technical issue, not a forecast of your commercial results.

## Questions before starting

### Does every SKU need a rewritten description?

No. I first identify which pages need distinct information and which problems come from shared templates. A focused product family establishes a standard before a larger editorial commitment.

### Can a quote-only catalog use this service?

Yes. The goal is to help a buyer qualify the product and contact the right person. I do not add fictional prices or promise shopping features for pages that do not meet their requirements.

## Start a conversation

Scope and fees are settled in conversation, once I understand the problem. Choose the route that fits how your company works.

# B2B catalog SEO: help the right buyer choose the right part

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 20, 2026

A catalog can attract visitors while leaving the sales team with the wrong inquiries. The useful question is whether a buyer can establish that a part fits the application, understand the buying terms, and send enough information for a meaningful quote. I start there, then work backward through the content and technical SEO.

## Separate the buyer questions before adding pages

An engineer checking compatibility, a purchasing manager sourcing a known part, and a hobbyist buying one replacement can use similar language. Their needs differ. Review actual inquiries with sales before treating every visit as equally valuable. Record which product families bring repeat business, which requests cannot be served, and which information sales repeatedly has to ask for.

Use that evidence to choose a small pilot family. A list of twenty commercially important parts can teach more than a rewrite of five thousand descriptions. Pick products with reliable source data, a sales owner who can review the copy, and enough existing demand to make observation worthwhile. Do not select solely by search volume.

## Make the specification understandable and inspectable

Put the information needed for an initial decision into readable page text. For a hypothetical fitting, that could include thread standard, connection size, material, dimensions, and the conditions attached to a stated pressure rating. The exact fields must come from the manufacturer's approved documentation. An SEO writer should never infer compatibility or a safety rating from a similar product.

A practical product template includes:
- The manufacturer and exact part identifier, including punctuation that changes the identifier.
- A concise description that distinguishes this item from adjacent variants.
- A labeled specification table with units and the applicable conditions.
- A current datasheet, its revision where available, and any limits on the information shown.
- Ordering information such as pack quantity, minimum order, or the need to confirm availability.
- A quote or purchase route that carries the product context into the next step.

Keep downloadable drawings and PDFs where they help the buyer. Add enough HTML context that someone can understand the item before downloading. Check whether tabs, selectors, or scroll effects hide the essential text from a plain fetch. My [crawler visibility service](https://gerriscorp.com/services/crawler-visibility/) addresses that rendering problem.

## Choose which pages deserve separate addresses

A product, a product family, an application, and a filter combination are different editorial decisions. Give an individual part a useful page when buyers need that item's specific information. Use a family page to explain selection among genuinely related options. An application page should answer a real use question with expert review, rather than repeat a category description under a new heading.

Avoid creating a page for every possible combination of specifications just because the database permits it. Sample filter URLs, identify duplicates, and agree which combinations deserve discovery. Check internal links, canonical signals, and sitemap entries together. See the [faceted navigation guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/faceted-navigation/) for the underlying crawl problem.

For obsolete parts, ask whether the page still helps owners identify an installed component. A discontinued notice and a documented replacement can be useful. Do not redirect to a superficially similar item whose compatibility is unknown. Preserve the distinction between a verified replacement and an alternative that needs engineering review.

## Give technical buyers a usable quote route

A generic contact form can lose the part number the visitor just selected. Test the route from the actual product page. The form should preserve the relevant context and explain what information helps sales respond: quantity, timing, destination, and application details where appropriate. Ask the commercial team which fields are essential rather than making every field mandatory.

State genuine constraints before submission. If the business only supplies trade accounts or has a minimum order, let buyers know. That may reduce inquiry volume while improving fit. A qualification rule should describe how the company actually operates, not discourage an unfamiliar buyer who could become a valuable account.

## Use structured data without inventing a transaction

Structured data should describe the visible product accurately. Google's [product snippet documentation](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/product-snippet) explains eligibility and required properties. Check the applicable requirements before promising an enhanced search appearance. A quote-only catalog must not manufacture prices, reviews, or stock status to satisfy a validator. Valid descriptive markup and eligibility for a particular search feature are separate questions.

## Measure the pilot against commercial fit

Before editing, save the selected URLs, their current content, indexing observations, relevant query groups, and available inquiry counts. Define a qualified inquiry with sales in writing. That might require a supported product, a serviceable destination, and enough quantity or account potential to justify follow-up. Keep rejected inquiries visible in the review so the definition cannot quietly change to flatter the results.

After release, verify the pages, links, forms, and analytics events. Review the same product family over an agreed period that reflects the sales cycle. Compare visibility, inquiries, qualified opportunities, and eventual orders where records allow it. Annotate promotions, stock changes, and seasonal effects. A small sample can indicate a direction without proving that SEO caused every order.

## How I take this on

My [B2B catalog SEO service](https://gerriscorp.com/services/b2b-catalog-seo/) starts with a paid diagnostic and a bounded product family. I map the content gaps, specify template changes, coordinate expert review, and verify implementation. The deliverable is a repeatable page standard and an evidence trail for the pilot, with a decision about whether the rest of the catalog warrants the same work.

# Podcasting as an investment in being found by AI search

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

Most owners who start a podcast treat it as content: record an episode, promote it for a week, move on to the next one. That undersells the asset. Done properly, a podcast is closer to buying a building than to renting a billboard. The recording is a single afternoon of work, but the words attached to it are copied onto hundreds of trusted sites, and those copies are what AI answer engines read when your customers ask questions.

## One recording, hundreds of copies

A podcast runs on a feed, and the feed is a syndication machine. Your host sends every episode to the podcast directories: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, the Podcast Index, Pocket Casts, Castbox, TuneIn, and hundreds of smaller apps and sites that most owners have never heard of. Each directory republishes the episode with its show notes, word for word, exactly as you wrote them. Your business name, your links, and your claims, in your own phrasing, end up living on all of them at once.

That matters more than it used to, because the directories are no longer the only readers. Search engines index those pages, and the AI answer engines, Google's AI answers, ChatGPT, and Perplexity among them, read the same copies when they work out what to say about a business. When a customer asks an AI assistant who to call or what a company believes, the answer is assembled from text like this. An owner who has recorded fifty episodes has fifty topics on which hundreds of sites repeat his own words back to the machines. An owner who has recorded none is quoted from whatever other people wrote about him, or not quoted at all.

## Why it compounds instead of expiring

Compare the asset to the usual alternatives. Advertising stops the day the payments stop. A social post is buried within days. A single article can rank for a season and then slip as competitors publish over it. A podcast back catalog behaves differently: every episode stays listed in every directory, keeps collecting listeners, and keeps standing as a permanent, citable statement of what you know and what you sell. Each new episode adds another page of quotable text and strengthens the catalog behind it.

The production cost is paid once, and it is paid in a currency owners already spend. The raw material of a business podcast is the conversations you have anyway: the questions customers ask every week, the explanations you give on sales calls, the stories you tell about work that went right and work that went wrong. Record those conversations once and they keep answering for you, in your voice, for years. That is what makes the show a citation factory rather than a content chore: the factory runs on talk that was already happening.

## Proof, from my own show

I host a podcast, The Chris Abraham Show, and the mechanism above is not theory to me. On October 24, 2026, a searcher asked Google what Chris Abraham thinks about a television show, the Canadian detective series Private Eyes, and Google's AI answered by quoting my podcast's show notes nearly word for word: the passage where I explained that I came for Jason Priestley and the detective stories and stayed for the patience, the apologies, and the father and daughter relationships. The same notes sit on Apple Podcasts, on Podcast Addict, and on the show's own website, all carrying the same text from the same feed.

Nobody pitched that answer and nobody paid for the placement. The notes were written to be quotable, the feed carried them everywhere a podcast can be listed, and the engine did the rest. Note the subject, too: a question with no commercial value at all, answered from my own words because my words were the ones available to quote. Now run the same machinery on questions in your market, the ones your buyers actually ask before they spend money.

## What doing it right involves

Three things separate a show that becomes an asset from a show that is just audio.
- **Show notes written to be quoted.** Spell out full names of people, companies, and products. Link to the canonical page on your own site. State your claims plainly and completely, because a directory or an AI engine will repeat them exactly as written. Vague notes produce vague answers.
- **An owned show site with transcripts.** Platform pages are thin and platform notes are capped; Spotify cuts show notes off at about 4,000 characters. A site on your own domain carries the full notes and the full transcript of every episode, in text the search and AI crawlers can read completely, and it is the one copy no platform can take away. Here is [how that site gets built](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-website/).
- **Monthly measurement.** Ask the questions your buyers ask, of Google, ChatGPT, and Perplexity, every month, and write down what the answers say. That is how you watch citations arrive, and how you catch a wrong claim early enough to correct it at the source. The method is in [the guide to measuring AI search](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/measure-ai-search/).

The practitioner details, episode pages, schema, and indexing, are in [the podcast SEO guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-seo/). This page is the owner's version of the same argument: the technique is simple, and the returns belong to whoever bothers to set it up properly and keep recording.

## Who should buy this asset

Honesty about the time frame: a podcast is a slow asset. If you need leads this month, advertising buys them faster, and I will tell you so on a call. A catalog pays out over seasons and years, to a business its owner intends to keep. If that is the business you are building, few marketing assets treat you better, because this one gets more valuable the longer you hold it and cannot be outbid by a competitor with a larger monthly budget.

I set up podcast sites, show notes, transcripts, and AI answer measurement for clients, and every engagement starts with a check of what the AI answers currently say about the business. If you want that check on yours, or you want a show of your own working this way, [ask me to look at it](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# Your Google business reports are getting a new scoreboard

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

If you run a local business, your Google Business Profile is the listing that shows your hours, your phone number, your reviews, and your spot on the map when a customer searches nearby. Google is now testing a rebuilt set of performance reports for that listing: five new sections that tell you far more than the old strip of numbers did. I wrote about the news on [my weblog](https://chrisabraham.net/2026/10/google-rebuilds-the-scoreboard.html) the day it broke. This guide is the owner version: what each section means, how to read the numbers without fooling yourself, and what to do about them each month.

## What Google is changing

The old Performance tab was thin: a count of views, calls, direction requests, and website clicks, take it or leave it. The test version, reported by Search Engine Roundtable on October 23, 2026 from screenshots and video sent in by two practitioners who received it early, is a real reporting suite. It arrived one day after Google launched a new home portal for business profiles, which says this is a program, not a stray experiment. The reporter who has covered this beat longer than anyone called it a very big improvement on the current reports.

Calibrate before celebrating: it is a test. It may reach your account next week or next quarter, and Google has retired better ideas than this one. Nobody should rebuild a reporting habit this week on the strength of screenshots. But the direction is unmistakable. Google is investing in telling owners, in detail and with advice attached, what their listings are doing. An owner who learns to read the new scoreboard early gets the benefit of that investment first.

## The five new sections, in plain language

### Overview

The front page of the new reports, and the section to read first. At the top, Google places its own recommendations for your profile: the facts to complete, the photos to add, the details it thinks are costing you customers. Read it as a to do list written by the referee. The referee works for Google, so check the advice against your own judgment, but ignoring homework from the outfit that ranks you is rarely wise.

### Engagement

What people did once your listing caught their eye: the calls placed, the messages sent, the bookings started, the website visits, the direction requests, gathered in one place instead of scattered. This is the section that comes closest to money, because each entry is a customer who moved from looking to acting.

### Reviews

Your reviews, broken out in detail instead of flattened into a single star average. An average hides everything that matters. The detail view shows the recent reviews themselves, the patterns inside them, what customers praise, what they complain about, and whether each one got a reply. Reputation is most of the conversion game for a local business, and this section turns it from a feeling into a ledger.

### Audience

Who is finding you. The audience section describes the people your listing reaches, including the split between people meeting your business for the first time and people coming back to it. Owners ask two questions more than any others: who is finding me, and is it the right crowd? This is the first time the profile reports have tried to answer the first one directly.

### Search trends

The actual words people typed that brought your listing up, and how those words change over time. This is your market describing your business in its own language, which is rarely the language on your sign. If searchers keep finding you under words for work you no longer do, or fail to find you under the words for the work you want, this section shows it before the phone goes quiet.

## Why your clicks and calls can fall while business holds up

Here is the reading skill the new reports demand, because the old habit will mislead you. A customer who asks Google a question increasingly gets the answer from an AI summary at the top of the results: your hours, your phone number, whether you are any good, read straight off your profile and your reviews. That customer got what they needed and never clicked anything. The action happened; it just never registered on your listing.

An analysis published in October 2026 followed three established florists in the United States and found profile interactions down 26 percent against the same period a year earlier, with website clicks down 30 percent, phone calls down 21 percent, and direction requests down 15 percent, on profiles that were active and well kept. Three florists are a signal, not a census, so read those numbers as direction rather than proof. The direction matches what I see across local accounts: the measurable actions on a profile are getting scarcer because the AI answers absorb them first. Your profile now matters as the source the machine reads, not only as the page the customer visits. Judge your marketing by the phone, the bookings, and the till alongside the report, never by one falling line on a chart.

## Fifteen minutes a month: the owner routine
1. **Save the numbers first.** Screenshot or export this month's figures before anything else. Baselines are the first casualty of every dashboard migration, and nobody can prove growth against a number that no longer exists.
2. **Read the Overview recommendations.** Do each one, or hand it to whoever manages your listing with a date attached.
3. **Read every new review and answer each one.** The new detail view is about to make neglected reviews visible to anyone who looks, starting with you.
4. **Compare against the same month last year.** Seasonality makes last month a liar for most local businesses. The honest comparison is a year back.
5. **Read Search trends against your price list.** The words bringing people to your door should match the work you actually want to sell.
6. **Ask the machines about your business.** Once a month, put your name into Google, ChatGPT, and Perplexity and note what the AI answers say. I keep [a guide to measuring AI search](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/measure-ai-search/) for exactly this habit.

## What to ask whoever manages your listing
- Have the new reports reached my account yet, and if so, what do the Overview recommendations say?
- What were my calls, bookings, and direction requests this month, set against the same month last year?
- Has every review been answered, and what are reviewers praising and complaining about this month?
- Which search words are bringing my listing up, and do they match the work I sell?
- What do the AI answers say about my business this month, and is every word of it true?
- What changed on the profile this month, and why?

A manager who can answer those six questions in writing, briefly, once a month, is earning the fee. A manager who sends a screenshot of a views chart is not. That standard is the whole of [my Google Business Profile service](https://gerriscorp.com/services/google-business-profile/): the work reported in writing, with numbers, on a rhythm an owner can hold me to.

## When to worry, and when not to

Worry when the rating slides across several months rather than dipping once. Worry when reviews sit unanswered, when wrong facts surface in the AI answers about your hours, your address, or what you sell, and when Search trends drift toward work you do not offer. Worry most when every section falls at once and the phone goes quiet with them, because that pattern is a business problem and not a measurement problem.

Do not worry when clicks or calls ease downward while bookings and the register hold up: the machine answered on the spot, and the customer still came. Do not worry that your account lacks the new sections yet, since a test rolls out account by account. And do not worry over one soft month in a seasonal trade, which is weather, not climate.

## Questions owners ask about the new reports

### My calls are down. Is my business in trouble?

Not on that evidence alone. AI answers now hand out your phone number, your hours, and your rating before a customer ever reaches your listing, so some calls and clicks simply stop registering. Put the report next to your bookings and your till. If those hold while the chart falls, the likeliest story is that the answers absorbed the actions. If everything falls together, that is a real problem and worth a proper diagnosis.

### Do I have the new reports yet?

Open your profile's Performance section and look for the five sections named in this guide. If they are not there, the test has not reached your account. Google rolls tests out gradually and quietly; even the trade reporter who broke the story did not have it on the day he published. Nothing is wrong with your account.

### What should I do this week?

Three things. Save your current Performance numbers somewhere safe, because the old figures may not survive the migration. Answer any review that is still waiting for a reply. And check that the facts on your profile, hours, phone, address, services, are exactly right, because those facts are what the AI answers repeat.

Your Google Business Profile is a core of my practice at Gerris, and the deal I make with every owner is simple: the work gets reported in writing, with numbers, on a rhythm you can hold me to. A richer scoreboard makes that deal easier to keep and easier to check. If you want the new reports read for your business and the findings put plainly, [ask me to look at it](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# How to vet an influencer or creator before your brand pays them

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

On Edelman's digital public affairs team in Washington, part of my job was checking online voices before a client went anywhere near them. The question was always the same: has this person said what they say now, to real people, for years, before anyone paid them to say it? The tools have changed since then. Follower counts are cheaper to fake, AI can generate a face and a posting history, and the FTC now has a rule with civil penalties attached. The question hasn't changed at all, and it still takes an afternoon of reading to answer.

## What the FTC expects from the brand

Two federal documents set the terms for a US sponsorship.
- **The Endorsement Guides (16 CFR Part 255), revised in 2023.** A creator you pay, or send free product, has a material connection that must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously in each post. The FTC's guidance says advertisers stay responsible for what endorsers say on their behalf, even when an outside agency runs the program, and should have "reasonable programs in place to train and monitor members of their network."
- **The Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule (16 CFR Part 465).** Announced August 14, 2024, published in the Federal Register on August 22, and in force since October 21, 2024. Among other things it bans selling or buying "fake indicators of social media influence, such as followers or views generated by a bot or hijacked account," where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them to misrepresent influence for a commercial purpose.

The fake-followers ban lands on whoever bought them, usually the creator. The Endorsement Guides land on you. A brand that signs a creator with an inflated audience and a habit of unlabeled ads has bought both problems at once, which is why the checking happens before the contract.

## Read the archive first

The single most useful test is time. Scroll back two or three years on every platform the creator uses and read what they posted before your category paid them. A home cook who has been arguing about cast iron since long before any cookware brand called is a different proposition from an account that discovered cast iron the month a sponsor did.
- Check the account's age, its earlier names, and whether it was repurposed from a different topic.
- Look up their website or newsletter in the [Wayback Machine](https://web.archive.org/) to see what it said in earlier years, including anything they've since deleted.
- Search their name and handle with the category terms. Long, specific posts on old forums, Reddit threads, and podcasts are the strongest proof of a real interest.

## Read the audience, not the follower count

Real audiences answer back in particulars. They ask where the jacket came from, argue with the recipe, mention their own kids by name. Bought audiences leave short, interchangeable praise, emoji strings, and comments that would fit under any post on any account.
- Read the comments on a dozen posts, sponsored and unsponsored, and note how many could only have been written by someone who watched or read the post.
- Look for sudden jumps in followers that no viral post explains. Most analytics tools show growth history; ask the creator for screenshots from their own dashboards if you can't see it.
- Ask for audience location and age from the platform's native analytics. A creator pitched to US buyers whose audience sits mostly elsewhere isn't a fit, however large it is.
- Compare views to followers over time. Healthy accounts vary post to post. Numbers that never move are as suspicious as numbers that leap.

## Check who else has paid them

A creator's past sponsorships tell you how they'll handle yours. Find the posts that were clearly paid and see whether each one carried a clear disclosure at the start, where viewers would see it, or a buried tag at the end of a long caption. The FTC's guidance treats a disclosure tucked into comments or behind a "more" link as inadequate. Someone who hid the last brand's ads will hide yours, and your name is the one that ends up in the warning letter.

Note competitors in the list too. A creator who promoted three rival products this year can still be honest, but your audience will notice, and so will you when the next one pays more.

## Read the claims they've made before

The advertiser is answerable for deceptive claims an endorser makes about the product. So read what the creator has said about earlier sponsors: health and weight-loss promises, income claims, "cured my" stories, financial tips. A creator who made unsupportable claims for a supplement brand will improvise about yours. Health, money, and children's products deserve the closest reading, and the FTC's own guidance scales the monitoring it expects with the risk of harm.

## Confirm the person exists

Synthetic personas are cheap now. Run the profile photo and a few post images through a reverse image search to make sure they aren't lifted from someone else or generated. Look for the creator on video, speaking unscripted, in more than one setting. Check that the business details on a media kit, the company name, the address for contracts, the payment details, match each other and match a real registration. Pay a person or a registered company you've identified, never a stranger's account on a payment app.

## See what search and AI already say

Search the creator's name with "scam," "lawsuit," "apology," and "controversy," and read past the first page. Then ask ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Perplexity who this person is, and follow every source they cite. Those answers are what your customers will read when your partnership announcement makes them curious. If an assistant repeats an old controversy, decide now whether you can live beside it, because the announcement will put your brand name in the same answer.

## Write it down

Every creator I check gets a short memo: who they are, how long they've covered the subject, what the audience looks like, how they've disclosed past sponsorships, any claims or controversies, and a plain recommendation. Each finding links to its source, with an archived copy for anything that might be deleted. The memo is the record that shows your brand did its homework, and it makes the next renewal decision a ten-minute read.

## Put the protections in the contract
- Clear disclosure at the start of every sponsored post, in the post itself, on every platform. Name the wording you expect, such as "#ad" or "Paid partnership with."
- Your approval before anything goes live. The FTC's guidance recommends it, and it's the only practical way to catch ephemeral formats like Stories.
- The approved claims, in writing, and a line saying the creator makes no others.
- A statement that the creator hasn't bought followers, views, or engagement, and won't during the term, with termination if that turns out to be false.
- Your right to remove or require edits to sponsored posts, and a clean exit if a past controversy surfaces that the creator didn't disclose.

## How I handle this for clients

I run creator and spokesperson checks for brands, agencies, and communications teams before a contract is signed: archive review, audience reading, disclosure history, identity, and what search and AI assistants say, delivered as one sourced memo per person with a recommendation. The same skills sit behind my [reputation and perception work](https://gerriscorp.com/services/reputation/), and agencies that want a quiet second opinion can use my [agency partner arrangement](https://gerriscorp.com/services/agency-partner/). If there's a name on your shortlist, [send it to me](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# How to freeze an old website as static HTML without losing a single link

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

Plenty of good websites are running on software nobody maintains anymore: Drupal 7 after its January 2025 end of life, Movable Type installs from the 2000s, PHP portals that only run on a host's oldest PHP version. The content still matters, people still link to it, and search engines still send visitors. The owner usually doesn't need a redesign. They need the site to stop being a security liability and a monthly hosting bill, and to keep working. Freezing it as static HTML does both. I did exactly this with my own serialized novel, which ran on Movable Type from 2005 to 2022, and here is the method.

## When freezing is the right call

A frozen site is a set of plain files: no database, no login, no plugins, nothing to patch. It loads quickly, it's close to free to host, and it can sit untouched for years. That makes it right for archives, finished projects, publications that stopped publishing, a business's old site after a rebrand, and documentation for a retired product.

It's the wrong call if people still edit the site every week, or if it depends on logins, shopping carts, or bookings. Those need a real [migration](https://gerriscorp.com/services/migrations/) to a maintained platform. And there's a middle path: a site can be frozen and still be edited occasionally, if the static pages are generated from source files kept in Git. My novel works that way. Corrections still happen; they just go through a build instead of an admin panel.

## Count every address the old site ever published

The single biggest risk is underestimating how many URLs exist. Old blogging and portal software publishes far more than its articles. Movable Type, for example, writes individual entry pages plus monthly, weekly, daily, and category archives, separate feed files, and TrackBack endpoints for every entry. My novel had 309 chapters, and the full count of public addresses came to 953.

Build the list from several sources and merge them, because each one misses something:
- **The database or export.** The most complete list of content, if you can still get a dump. Entry IDs, slugs, and dates let you reconstruct every permalink the software would have generated.
- **The old web root.** If the software published static files, as Movable Type did, the server's folder is a literal inventory of what it served.
- **A crawl of the live site.** Run it before anything changes, and save the export. This also captures what each page looked like, which you'll want for comparison.
- **The Wayback Machine.** The Internet Archive's CDX API returns every URL it has ever captured on a domain, including pages deleted years ago that other sites still link to. When I rebuilt the redirect map for a site that had lived on three platforms, this was where most of the forgotten addresses came from.
- **Search Console and server logs.** Pages with impressions or real visits in the last year or two are the ones you can least afford to lose.

Deduplicate, normalize the protocol and host, and you have the master list. Everything after this point is checked against it.

## Keep the address exactly, redirect only what you must

A redirect works, but the same URL serving the same content works better: no chain, no lost signal, nothing for anyone to maintain. So the goal for each URL on the list is to publish a file at exactly that path. Most static generators let you set the output path per page, so a chapter that lived at `/archives/2005/03/chapter_one.html` can be written back to that exact spot.

For the rest, decide in this order:
1. **Same path, same content.** Entries, main pages, and anything with outside links.
2. **Same path, lighter content.** Date and category archives that only list entries can become small generated listing pages. Mark them noindex, follow so they pass visitors along without competing with the entries they repeat.
3. **Redirect.** Leftovers from moved or merged entries, and dynamic URLs that can't exist as files.
4. **Let it go.** Spam-filled endpoints and admin paths that were never meant to be public can return 404 or 410. Decide this on purpose, with the list in front of you, not by accident.

## The URLs a static host can't serve as files

Some old addresses don't map onto a file at all. Watch for these:
- **Query strings.** Addresses like `/index.php?p=123` or `/node?id=45` are a script plus a parameter. A static host serves the same file no matter what comes after the question mark, so every one of those URLs would collapse into one page. They need redirect rules that match the query string, at the host or at a CDN in front of it.
- **Script extensions.** Paths ending in `.php`, `.cgi`, or `.asp` can be written as files on some hosts but may be served with the wrong content type. Test each one, or redirect them.
- **Feeds.** Feed readers and aggregators subscribed years ago and never updated. If the old site published RSS 1.0, RSS 2.0, and Atom at three different addresses, publish all three again, in their original formats. My novel still serves all three.

Where the redirect lives matters. GitHub Pages can't send a real 301 from a list of rules; it can only serve a page with an instant meta refresh, which Google says it treats as a permanent redirect but other crawlers and tools may not. If a site needs more than a handful of true redirects, put a CDN such as Cloudflare in front and use its bulk redirect lists, or choose a static host that reads a redirects file. I compare the options in my guide to [planning 301 redirects](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/301-redirects/).

## Replace the dynamic parts, or retire them out loud

Every feature that needed the server has to be replaced or retired deliberately:
- **Comments.** Keep the historical comments as part of each page's HTML, since they're often half the value of an old post, and close new ones.
- **Contact forms.** Replace them with a plain email address or a hosted form service. Then send a test message, because a form that silently drops inquiries is worse than no form.
- **Site search.** A static search index, such as Pagefind, builds at publish time and runs in the browser. For a small archive, a good index page by date and topic may be enough.
- **Analytics.** Carry over the same property, so the before and after are comparable.

## Clean up while you're in there, and log it

A freeze is a rare chance to fix things that have bothered search engines for years: give every page a real title and description, make archive pages noindex, generate a sitemap that lists only the pages meant for search, and add a canonical to each page. On my novel, every chapter got a handwritten title and description, and a script checked them. Typos and broken typography got fixed too, each one recorded in a log with the original text, so any correction can be reversed. If you're tempted to "improve" the content more than that, stop. A frozen archive should read like itself.

## Cut over in the right order

The step that most often goes wrong is the last one, because old hosting packages tend to bundle more than the website. Check before you cancel anything:
1. **Find out who runs DNS.** If the old host is also the DNS provider, canceling the account takes the domain's records down with it, including email. Move DNS first, copying every record exactly, especially mail and verification records. My guide to [email authentication](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-authentication/) explains which ones keep mail flowing.
2. **Publish the frozen site on a test address** and check it against the master list: every URL answers, the content matches, redirects land on the right page in one hop.
3. **Switch the website records** to the new host, and confirm https and the www and non-www versions behave.
4. **Run the master list again on the real domain.** For the novel, a script checked all 953 addresses, the redirects, and the canonicals before I told Google and Bing anything.
5. **Submit the new sitemap,** then watch Search Console for a few weeks. Expect a quiet transition. Anything else means something on the list was missed.
6. **Only then cancel the old hosting,** after downloading a final copy of the files and the database.

## What it costs, and what it saves

For a small site, the work is mostly the inventory and the checking, not the conversion. A blog of a few hundred posts is a few days of careful work. The savings are ongoing: no security patches for software that no longer gets any, no emergency when a host retires an old PHP version, and hosting that's often free. The site also tends to get faster, which matters to visitors more than the owner usually expects.

## Questions about freezing a website

### Will I lose my search rankings?

Not if the URLs and content stay the same. Search engines see the same pages at the same addresses, served faster. Rankings drop when addresses change without redirects or when content disappears.

### Can I just use a website copier?

Tools that mirror a site, like wget or HTTrack, are a useful starting point and a good backup. On their own they miss feeds, unlinked pages, and query string URLs, and they copy the old site's problems along with its content. Check their output against the master list.

### Can a frozen site still be updated?

Yes, if it's generated from source files kept in Git. Edit the source, rebuild, publish. No server or database involved.

If you have a site stranded on old software and want it preserved rather than rebuilt, that's [site rescue](https://gerriscorp.com/services/rescue/) work, and I'm happy to look at it. Send me the address on the [contact page](https://gerriscorp.com/contact/).

# Build a website incident timeline before changing code

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 24, 2026

The website lost traffic on Tuesday. Someone remembers a release on Monday. A vendor changed a setting last week. Those facts belong in the same investigation, but their proximity does not establish a cause.

Before changing code, I want a timeline that separates what happened from when someone noticed it. This is a practical way to organize technical forensics: collect dated observations, preserve the evidence, and decide which explanation deserves the next test.

## Define the incident in observable terms

Start with the actual symptom. “Organic clicks to product pages declined” describes a different incident from “product pages return server errors” or “quote requests stopped reaching the sales inbox.” Those events can occur together, but each needs its own evidence.

Record the first confirmed observation and the last confirmed normal state. If a customer reported a failure on Tuesday afternoon, the failure could have begun earlier. Write “first reported Tuesday at 14:10” rather than “began Tuesday at 14:10” unless monitoring establishes the start.

Choose representative URLs and customer actions. Keep a working example alongside the failing examples when possible. A category that still works can help distinguish a shared infrastructure problem from a product template defect.

## Use one time convention

Choose a time zone for the working timeline and write it at the top. Preserve each source timestamp and its original zone in a separate field. A server event recorded in UTC and a release discussed in local time can appear in the wrong order if someone copies the clock values without converting them.

Do not invent precision. If the only record says “Monday morning,” retain that uncertainty. A date without a time cannot establish whether an event preceded an outage by five minutes or followed it by three hours.

For reports summarized by day, retain that reporting granularity. Do not place a daily traffic total beside a second level server event and treat them as measurements with equivalent precision.

## Gather records from different layers

Collect the deployment history, content publication records, DNS and proxy changes, relevant application logs, monitoring alerts, and dated support messages. Ask vendors for their change records when those records are needed to evaluate a theory. A lack of access is an investigation gap, not evidence that nothing changed.

Use Search Console for the search observations it actually supplies. Google's [Search Console introduction](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/monitor-debug/search-console-start) explains its crawl, indexing, and performance reports. Those reports can inform an incident timeline, but they are not a second by second deployment monitor.

Capture the response status, important headers, and visible behavior for selected production URLs. Where caching is involved, record what the public visitor received and what environment was tested. A correct preview page does not establish a correct public response.

Keep the evidence in access controlled storage. The public incident summary should not include customer submissions, tokens, credentials, or identifying log details. Link to a restricted artifact by a descriptive name rather than copying sensitive contents into a shared ticket.

## Maintain a simple evidence table

The following is an invented example. It illustrates the structure and makes no claim about a client incident.
| Time in UTC | Recorded event | What it establishes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monday 09:00 | Product template release completed | A release ran; public output was not recorded |
| Monday 09:20 | Monitor saved a successful category response | That category URL responded successfully then |
| Tuesday 14:10 | Customer reported missing product specifications | The symptom was reported by this time |
| Tuesday 14:40 | Saved product response lacks specification text | The selected public response lacked the text |
| Tuesday 15:05 | Preview includes the specification text | Preview and public behavior differ |

The timeline suggests a useful next question: what differs between preview and production? It does not prove the release removed the specifications. The public response may reflect a different build, stale cache, unavailable data, or a configuration difference.

## Write competing explanations and discriminating tests

List a small number of plausible causes. Beside each one, write the observation that would strengthen or weaken it. “The production release contains different code” can be checked against the deployed revision. “A cache holds old output” requires evidence about the actual response and cache behavior.

Choose a test that separates explanations. Rebuilding everything and clearing every cache may restore service, but it can also remove the evidence needed to understand the failure. When customers are actively blocked, restoration may take priority. Record that choice and capture what is practical before taking action.

Separate confirmed causes from contributing conditions. An old deployment process may make recovery slow without causing the original defect. Both deserve attention, but the prevention work differs.

## Record the intervention and verify the result

Add each repair attempt to the same timeline: the owner, exact change, environment, release identifier, and observed outcome. If two changes ship together, acknowledge that the result may not isolate which one mattered.

Repeat the original failing action on production and check the working comparison example. For a content visibility incident, retain before and after response samples. For an inquiry failure, confirm receipt rather than relying on a success message in the browser.

End the incident record with what is established, what remains uncertain, and the next monitoring check. A repaired product template and a later traffic recovery are separate findings. Do not claim the second from evidence of the first.

This method supports [website rescue and takeover work](https://gerriscorp.com/services/rescue/), [technical SEO diagnosis](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-seo/), and [technical direction](https://gerriscorp.com/services/technical-lead/). For a traffic specific investigation, use the [traffic drop diagnostic guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/traffic-drop/) alongside the timeline. The purpose is to make the next decision better supported than the first guess.

Prepared with OpenAI Codex at Chris Abraham's request. The timeline is hypothetical and contains no client records.

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# The European Accessibility Act for US companies

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

American companies tend to think about web accessibility through the ADA and the demand letters that come with it. If you sell online to consumers in the European Union, a second law has applied since June 28, 2025: the European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882. It reaches past EU borders, it names e-commerce explicitly, and each member state enforces it with its own penalties. Here is what it asks of a US business and how to tell whether yours is in scope.

This is a practitioner's guide, not legal advice. For a specific market or a complaint, talk to counsel in that country.

## Who it covers

The directive defines a service provider as anyone who provides a service on the Union market or makes offers to provide one to consumers in the EU. Location isn't the test. A Delaware company with a Shopify store that ships to France and takes euros is making offers to consumers in the Union.

The services listed in Article 2 include e-commerce services, consumer banking, e-books and the software for reading them, telephony, audiovisual media services, and the websites, apps, and electronic tickets of air, bus, rail, and water passenger transport. E-commerce is defined broadly: services provided at a distance, through websites and mobile apps, by electronic means, at a consumer's request, with a view to concluding a consumer contract. In plain terms, if a European shopper can buy from you online, your storefront is in scope.

The act also covers products, such as computers, smartphones, e-readers, ATMs, and ticket machines, placed on the market after June 28, 2025. Most of my clients are affected by the services side.

## The microenterprise exemption

Microenterprises that provide services are exempt from the accessibility requirements. The directive defines a microenterprise as one employing fewer than 10 people with annual turnover or an annual balance sheet total of no more than 2 million euros. Both parts apply: a nine-person company with 5 million euros in turnover and a 5 million euro balance sheet is not a microenterprise. The exemption covers services only, so a tiny company making a covered product still has to comply.

A company that grows past ten people loses the exemption, and the directive gives no grace period for crossing the line. If you're near it, plan the accessibility work before the hire that tips you over.

## What the standard looks like in practice

The directive's annex sets out functional requirements: content that can be perceived, operated, understood, and used with assistive technology. The annex itself never names WCAG. The European harmonised standard for digital accessibility, EN 301 549, is the usual benchmark, and its web requirements follow WCAG 2.1 at Level AA. Meeting WCAG 2.2 AA, the current W3C version, covers that and a little more.

For an online store, the failures I find most often are the same ones behind US lawsuits:
- Product images with no text alternative, or alternatives that say "image."
- Text with too little contrast against its background, especially prices and buttons.
- Form fields at checkout without labels, so screen readers announce "edit text" and nothing more.
- Menus, filters, and size pickers that can't be used with a keyboard.
- Error messages shown only in red, or not announced at all.
- Pop-ups and cookie banners that trap keyboard focus.

## Beyond the website

The act asks for accessible information about the service itself, not only an accessible interface. Providers are expected to explain in their terms or a similar document how the service meets the requirements. A short accessibility statement, linked from the footer, that says what standard you work to, what's known to be incomplete, and how a customer can get help or report a barrier, does that job and is a sensible habit in any market.

## Transitional periods

Article 32 lets member states allow service providers to keep using products they lawfully used before the deadline to deliver similar services until June 28, 2030. It also lets them keep self-service terminals in use to the end of their useful life, up to 20 years. A website gets no five-year pass from either provision. A store that launches or redesigns today should meet the requirements now.

## Enforcement

Each member state wrote the directive into national law and chose its own enforcement body and penalties, so the consequences differ between Germany, France, Ireland, and the rest. Market surveillance authorities can require fixes and, in some countries, restrict a non-compliant service. Consumers and disability organizations can also complain. A US business with a meaningful share of EU sales should know which countries matter most and how each one enforces.

## Where to start
- Confirm whether you sell to EU consumers and whether the microenterprise exemption applies.
- Test your checkout from product page to confirmation with a keyboard and a screen reader.
- Fix the templates first, because one fixed product template fixes every product page.
- Publish an accessibility statement with a contact route.
- Skip overlay widgets; they don't change the underlying code that the standard measures.

The US side of the same work is in my guide to [ADA website compliance](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ada-website-compliance/). For a store that needs the fixes made, see [accessibility remediation](https://gerriscorp.com/services/accessibility/).

# Domain security: the registrar account comes first

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Every website and every company email address depends on one login at a domain registrar. Whoever controls that account can point the website anywhere, read the mail by changing the MX records, and issue new security certificates in the company's name. In practice that account often belongs to a founder's personal email, a departed employee, or a web designer from years ago, protected by a password and nothing else. This guide covers the protections in the order I put them in place.

## Find out who holds the account

Start with an inventory. For every domain the company uses, record the registrar, the account it sits in, the email address on that account, who can log in, and when the domain renews. Include the domains nobody thinks about: the old brand name that still redirects, the product site from a past campaign, the domain that only sends email. Then check where DNS is hosted, since that can be a different company with a different login.

The account should belong to the company, registered to a shared role address such as domains@ on the company's own domain, with at least two named people able to log in. A domain in a personal account belongs, in every practical sense, to that person.

## Turn on two-factor authentication everywhere

In January 2019, after a wave of DNS hijacking against government domains, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued Emergency Directive 19-01. It required federal agencies to audit their DNS records, change the passwords on every account that could alter them, including registrar accounts, add multi-factor authentication to those accounts, and watch certificate transparency logs for certificates they hadn't requested. CISA recommended phishing-resistant factors and advised against text-message codes.

That list was written for agencies and fits any company. Use a hardware key or an authenticator app on the registrar and the DNS host. Store recovery codes where the company, not one person, can find them.

## Registrar lock

A registrar lock sets status codes at the registry that refuse certain requests. ICANN's explanation of these EPP status codes describes clientTransferProhibited, which tells the registry to reject transfers to another registrar; clientDeleteProhibited, which rejects deletion; and clientUpdateProhibited, which rejects changes. Most registrars switch on the transfer lock by default and show it as a single toggle. Check that it's on for every domain.

You can look up any domain's status codes with a public lookup tool. If clientTransferProhibited is missing on a domain that matters, fix that before anything else on this list.

## Registry Lock for the domains that matter most

A registrar lock can be removed by anyone who gets into the registrar account. Registry Lock goes a level higher. Some registry operators offer it through participating registrars, and it sets server status codes that only the registry can lift, usually after a manual, out-of-band confirmation from named contacts. ICANN notes that server statuses take precedence over client statuses and take longer to remove. That delay is the point. Registry Lock costs money and makes legitimate changes slower, so I recommend it for the primary domain of a company whose revenue or reputation depends on it.

## Auto-renew and a payment card that works

More domains are lost to expired cards than to attackers. Turn on auto-renew, attach a company card that someone watches, and set a renewal of several years for the main domain. Make sure renewal notices go to the shared role address, not to someone who left.

## DNSSEC

DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records so that resolvers can detect forged answers. ICANN describes it as protection against attackers redirecting users to a fake site by tampering with DNS responses. Many DNS hosts now enable it with one setting, and the registrar then publishes the matching record at the registry. It's worth turning on where your DNS host supports it, with one warning: if you move DNS providers later, disable DNSSEC or move the keys first, or the domain can stop resolving.

## Watch for changes

Set registrar notifications for any change to contacts, nameservers, or lock status. Subscribe to certificate transparency alerts for your domains through a free monitoring service, so a certificate you didn't request shows up as an email. Review the DNS records once a quarter against a saved copy, and remove records for services you no longer use, since a stale record pointing at an abandoned service can be taken over.

## The short version
- Every domain in a company-owned account, with two people who can log in.
- Two-factor authentication on the registrar and the DNS host, without text messages.
- Transfer lock on for every domain; Registry Lock on the main one.
- Auto-renew with a monitored card and notices to a shared address.
- DNSSEC on where the DNS host supports it.
- Alerts for changes and for new certificates.

Mail records are covered in my guide to [email authentication](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-authentication/). If a company has dozens of domains spread across accounts, I run the inventory and consolidation as a [domain portfolio audit](https://gerriscorp.com/services/domain-portfolio/).

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.
