# Website restore drills

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Every hosting plan and every WordPress backup plugin promises backups. Few owners have ever restored one. The first restore usually happens during an emergency: the site is hacked, a plugin update breaks the checkout, a developer deletes the wrong folder. That's when people find out the backup excluded the uploads folder, the database export is from March, or the only person with the hosting password is on a plane. A restore drill finds all of that on a quiet afternoon instead.

## What the agencies say

CISA's #StopRansomware Guide tells organizations to maintain offline, encrypted backups of critical data and to regularly test the availability and integrity of those backups in a disaster recovery scenario. It separately advises testing backup procedures on a regular basis. NIST's contingency planning guide for federal systems treats testing and exercises as part of the plan itself. Neither document is written for a small business website, but the principle carries over without change: an untested backup is a hope.

## Decide what you're protecting

List what the site is made of. For a typical WordPress site that's the database, the uploads folder, the theme and plugins, the configuration file, and the DNS records. For a static site in a Git repository, it's the repository, the build settings, the hosting configuration, and DNS. For a store, add product data, orders, customer accounts, and the payment and shipping integrations.

Then set two numbers with the owner. The first is how much recent work you can afford to lose: a day of orders, an hour, none. The second is how long the site can be down before it costs real money. Those two answers decide how often backups run and how fast a restore has to be.

## Restore somewhere safe

Never drill on the live site. Restore to a staging server, a local machine, or a fresh hosting account, on a temporary address blocked from search engines. The point is to rebuild the site from nothing but the backup and the written instructions, the way you would if the original server were gone.

Use the most recent backup, not a specially prepared one. Have someone other than the person who set up the backups run the drill, following only what's written down. Every question they have to ask is a gap in the instructions.

## What to check on the restored copy
- **Completeness.** Every page loads, images appear, downloads work, and the newest content is there.
- **Freshness.** The latest post, product, or order in the restored copy matches what the backup schedule promises.
- **Function.** Forms submit, search works, logins work, a test order goes through in the store's test mode.
- **Settings.** Redirects, robots rules, canonical tags, and the analytics tag are all present, since these live in places backups often skip.
- **Secrets.** API keys, mail settings, and payment credentials can be found and re-entered from a secure store.

## Time it and write it down

Record when the drill started, when the site was usable, and every step in between. Note each problem: a missing file, a version mismatch, a password nobody had, a step that took an hour because nobody had done it before. The record becomes the runbook for the real event and shows how close you are to the downtime the owner agreed to.

## Gaps a drill usually uncovers
- The backup lives on the same server as the site, so it would be lost with it.
- The plugin backs up the database but not the uploads, or the reverse.
- The backup is encrypted, and the key is stored only on the server being protected.
- Backups stopped months ago when a card expired or a storage quota filled, and nobody was told.
- DNS records were never saved, so pointing a new server at the domain means rebuilding them from memory.
- The hosting account, registrar, and DNS host logins belong to someone who has left.

Each of those is easy to fix once seen. CISA's offline-copy advice addresses the first and third: keep at least one copy somewhere an attacker on the server can't reach or erase.

## How often

Run a full drill once a year and after any major change: a new host, a redesign, a new backup tool, a platform migration. Check every month that the latest backup exists and has a sensible size. A backup file that's suddenly much smaller than last month's is often the first sign something has stopped being included.

## The static site advantage

A static site kept in a Git repository carries its own history. Every version of every page is in the repository, and a copy of the repository on any laptop is a full backup. Restoring means pointing a new host at the repository and rebuilding. The drill still matters, because DNS, hosting settings, and form handlers live outside the repository, but the hardest part of the problem is already solved.

When a site needs a fast rebuild after an incident, the record-keeping side is in my guide to [the website incident timeline](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/website-incident-timeline/). Backups and restore drills are part of [WordPress care](https://gerriscorp.com/services/wordpress-care/), and when an old site needs saving outright, see [freezing an old website as static HTML](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/freeze-old-website/).

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

# How to write a company AI use policy

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 26, 2026

Your staff already use AI. Someone pastes a client email into ChatGPT to draft a reply, someone asks Claude to tidy a spreadsheet, someone has an AI note-taker joining calls. Without a policy, each person makes their own rules about what's safe to share and what needs checking. A good AI use policy is short, specific, and written for the people who'll follow it. Here is how I draft one with a client.

## Start from what people already do

Before writing a word, ask. A short anonymous survey or a few conversations will tell you which tools are in use, on which accounts, and for what tasks. You'll find personal free accounts handling company data, browser extensions nobody approved, and a few people doing careful, useful work worth turning into standard practice. A policy that bans what everyone already does gets ignored; one that starts from real use gets followed.

## Approved tools and accounts

Name the tools staff may use and the accounts they must use them through. Business and enterprise plans from the major AI providers generally offer terms that personal accounts don't, such as commitments not to train on your data, admin controls, and data retention settings. Read the terms of the plan you choose and write the result into the policy in one sentence. Personal accounts for company work should be off the list.

Include the AI features built into tools you already pay for: the writing assistant in your email suite, the meeting summarizer in your video platform, the AI in your CRM. Each one sends data somewhere, and staff can't tell which are approved unless the policy says.

## Data that never goes in

This is the section that prevents the worst outcomes, so make it concrete. List the categories: client confidential information, personal data about customers or employees, health or financial records, passwords and API keys, unreleased financial results, and anything covered by a non-disclosure agreement. Give examples from your own business. "Don't paste the client's contract into a chatbot" is clearer than "protect sensitive information."

Say what to do instead: remove names and identifying details, use an approved enterprise tool for confidential work, or ask before using AI at all.

## A human checks before anything goes out

AI tools state wrong facts fluently. Every piece of AI-assisted work that leaves the company, whether a client report, a published article, code in production, or a social post, needs a named person who has checked it and stands behind it. For facts, that means checking against the source, not asking the AI whether it was right. For code, it means review and tests. NIST's Generative AI Profile lists confabulation, its term for confidently stated false content, among the main risks of these systems, and the cure is a human with the time and duty to check.

## Disclosure

Decide when the company tells clients and the public that AI was used. Some industries and clients require disclosure; some contracts forbid AI use on their work entirely. Check client contracts and put the answer in the policy. Never use AI to produce fake customer reviews or testimonials; the FTC's rule on consumer reviews, in force since October 21, 2024, treats AI-generated fake reviews the same as any other fake review.

## Meetings and recordings

AI note-takers raise a question the rest of the policy doesn't: consent. Some US states require every party's consent before recording a call. Set a rule that the host announces any recording or AI note-taker at the start, and that anyone can ask for it to be turned off. Decide where transcripts are stored and how long they're kept.

## Ownership and review

Name one person who owns the policy, answers questions, and approves new tools. Review it twice a year, because the tools change that often. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework, voluntary guidance published in January 2023, organizes the work into four functions: govern, map, measure, and manage. A small company doesn't need the full framework, but the first function, governance with clear ownership, is the part that makes the rest happen.

## Keep it to two pages

A policy people read beats a thorough one they don't. Two pages, plain language, with examples from your own work. Put the approved tools list and the never-share list at the top, since those are what people will look up. Train once, with real examples, and repeat when the policy changes.

## A starting outline
- Purpose, in two sentences.
- Approved tools, plans, and accounts.
- Data that never goes into an AI tool, with examples.
- Review: who checks AI-assisted work before it leaves.
- Disclosure to clients and the public.
- Recordings and AI note-takers.
- How to request a new tool, and who owns the policy.

For companies weighing AI tools before writing the rules, see my guide to [judging an AI vendor's pitch](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-vendor-pitch/) and the one on [running AI pilot tests](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-pilot-tests/). I draft and train on these policies as [AI policy and staff training](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ai-policy/).

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com)

If your company hires through Upwork, you'll find me [there as well](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

- [NIST: AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (Jan 26, 2023)](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)
- [NIST: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, NIST AI 600-1 (July 26, 2024)](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1)

# Website accessibility remediation

Fixing the barriers that stop people with disabilities from using your site, in the templates where they start, with a written record of what was tested and what changed.

Most accessibility problems on a business website come from a handful of templates: the header and menu, the product or service page, the forms, the checkout. Fix those and every page built from them is fixed at once. I test the way people with disabilities actually use the web, with a keyboard, a screen reader, zoom, and a text-only browser, and I hand your developers fixes they can ship, or make them myself.

## What I test
- **Keyboard use** from the home page to the main conversion: every menu, filter, button, and form field reachable and usable without a mouse, with visible focus.
- **Screen reader output** for headings, landmarks, links, images, form labels, error messages, and dynamic content.
- **Color contrast** for text, buttons, and form states against WCAG 2.2 Level AA.
- **Zoom and reflow** at 200 and 400 percent, where layouts break and content disappears.
- **Media**: captions on video, transcripts for audio, and controls for anything that moves.
- **Pop-ups, cookie banners, and chat widgets**, which trap keyboard users more often than anything else on a modern site.

Automated scanners catch only part of the real problems and flag some false ones. I use them to cover ground quickly and then check every template by hand.

## What I fix

Every finding is tied to the template or component that causes it, with the WCAG success criterion it fails and the change that fixes it. On WordPress, static sites, and many Shopify themes I make the changes directly. On custom applications I write developer tickets with acceptance criteria and review the pull requests. Then I retest on the live site and record the result.

Overlay widgets stay off the site. They leave the underlying code as it was, and that code is what a court or regulator examines.

## Documentation

You get a findings report, a record of every fix with the date it went live, and a draft accessibility statement that names the standard you work to, any known gaps, and how visitors can report a barrier. That record is what a lawyer will ask for if a demand letter arrives, and the statement is what EU rules expect a service provider to publish.

## Who needs this

US businesses facing ADA demand letters or wanting to avoid them, which is covered in my guide to [ADA website compliance](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ada-website-compliance/). Companies selling to consumers in the European Union, which has enforced the European Accessibility Act since June 28, 2025, covered in my [European Accessibility Act guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/european-accessibility-act/). And any organization that wants more of its visitors to complete what they came to do.

## The search dividend

Accessible pages are easier for crawlers and AI systems to read. Real headings, labeled links, text alternatives for images, and content that doesn't depend on a mouse all help search engines understand a page the same way they help a screen reader. The work pays for itself twice.

## Common questions

### How long does remediation take?

The testing is quoted from the number of templates and the main user journeys. Fixes depend on who implements them; template changes I make myself usually ship within the engagement.

### Can you certify the site as compliant?

I document what was tested, against which standard, and what was fixed. Compliance is decided by courts and regulators; the documentation is your evidence of good-faith work.

### How is it billed?

An audit first, quoted as a fixed fee. The fixes come second: once the findings are known, they are scoped and quoted as a fixed fee before the work begins.

# AI use policy and staff training

A short, enforceable policy for how your company uses AI tools, built from what your people already do, and a training session that makes it stick.

I use AI tools every working day, for research, writing, code, and the build checks behind my own websites, and I've watched what happens when the checking step is skipped. That experience is what I bring to a client's policy: rules that let people get real value from the tools while keeping client data out of the wrong places and keeping a human accountable for everything that leaves the building.

## How an engagement runs
1. **Discovery.** A short anonymous survey and a few conversations to learn which tools staff use, on which accounts, for which tasks, and where the worries are.
2. **Tool review.** I compare the business plans of the tools you want to keep, read their data terms, and recommend the approved list and account setup.
3. **Contract check.** I list which client contracts restrict or require disclosure of AI use, so the policy matches what you've already promised.
4. **The policy.** Two pages in plain language: approved tools, data that never goes in, who reviews AI-assisted work, disclosure, recordings and note-takers, and who owns the policy.
5. **Training.** A working session with examples from your own business: what's fine, what's off limits, and how to check an AI's output before it goes to a client.
6. **Review date.** The policy carries a review date of its own, because the tools change fast and a dated policy gets revisited instead of quietly expiring.

The method is laid out in my guide to [writing a company AI use policy](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-use-policy/).

## What you get
- The policy, ready to adopt, with a one-page summary for the wall or the intranet.
- An approved tools list with account settings documented.
- A never-share list with examples drawn from your work.
- A review checklist for AI-assisted client deliverables, articles, and code.
- A training session for the team, run on examples drawn from your own work.

## Who it's for

Professional services firms, agencies, nonprofits, and growing companies of ten to a few hundred people, where AI use has spread faster than anyone's rules, and where client confidentiality matters. Companies that also need help choosing what to build or buy should look at [AI agents and automation](https://gerriscorp.com/services/ai-automation/) and my guide to [judging an AI vendor's pitch](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-vendor-pitch/).

## What the policy is built on

NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and its Generative AI Profile, the FTC's rules on endorsements and reviews, the data terms of the tools you choose, and the obligations in your client contracts. For regulated industries, I draft with your counsel, who reviews the final text.

## Common questions

### How long does it take?

The schedule depends on the size of the company and how fast survey answers and contract reviews come back. The timetable is agreed in writing before the work starts.

### Will the policy ban tools people like?

The policy starts from what's working. Tools that handle company data on personal accounts move to business accounts; the work itself usually continues.

### How is it billed?

A fixed fee, quoted from the size of the company and the number of tools involved. How it is paid is settled in conversation before anything begins.

# Domain portfolio audit

A full accounting of the domains your company depends on: where each one is registered, whose account it sits in, who can log in, when it renews, and what it does.

Companies collect domains the way they collect software subscriptions. A founder registers the first one on a personal card. A marketing agency buys three for a campaign. A product launch adds two more, a rebrand adds five, and someone buys the typo versions to keep them from squatters. Ten years later the domains are spread across four registrars and six accounts, some owned by people who've left, and nobody can say which ones still matter. I sort that out, and then I make sure it stays sorted.

## What the audit covers
- **Every domain the company uses or owns**, found from registrar accounts, DNS zones, certificate transparency logs, redirects on the main site, and the memories of long-serving staff.
- **The registrar, account, and account holder** for each, with the email address that receives renewal and transfer notices.
- **Lock status**: transfer, update, and delete locks, and whether Registry Lock is available for the main domain.
- **Renewal dates and payment**, with the domains closest to expiry flagged first.
- **DNS host and records**, including stale records pointing at services the company no longer uses.
- **Purpose**: live site, redirect, email only, defensive, or unused, so each domain gets the right treatment.

## What I fix

Each domain moves into a company-owned account under a shared role address, with two named people holding access and two-factor authentication on every login. Transfer locks go on everywhere. Auto-renew goes on with a card someone watches. Domains that only exist to stop squatters get records that reject all email, so they can't be used for phishing in your name. Domains with visitors or links get permanent redirects to the right page on the main site. Domains nobody needs are allowed to lapse on purpose, after checking that nothing points at them.

Consolidating onto fewer registrars makes all of this easier to keep. I move domains between registrars with the DNS left untouched, so websites and email keep running through the transfer. The step-by-step reasoning is in my guide to [domain security and registrar locks](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/domain-account-security/).

## What you get
- A domain register: one spreadsheet listing every domain with its registrar, account, purpose, renewal date, lock status, and DNS host.
- A written record of what changed, with dates.
- A short procedure for adding, renewing, and retiring domains, so the register stays current.
- A list of anything I couldn't resolve, such as a domain held by a former contractor who must release it, with the steps to recover it.

## When companies call me

After a scare: a renewal notice that went to a departed employee, a phishing email sent from a lookalike domain, a website that vanished because a card expired. Before a sale or an investment, when buyers ask for a list of digital assets. After a rebrand, when the old domains need redirects that keep their search value. And when a new IT or marketing lead discovers nobody can log into the registrar.

## Common questions

### Will moving registrars take the site or email offline?

A registrar transfer leaves DNS where it is. I confirm the nameservers and every record before and after the move, and plan transfers away from busy periods.

### Do you need the account passwords?

I prefer delegated access where the registrar supports it. Where it doesn't, I arrange temporary access and change the credentials when the work is done.

### How is it billed?

A fixed-scope audit, quoted as a fixed fee from the number of domains and accounts. Fixes can be included in that scope or quoted separately, again as a fixed fee.

# Site indexes and glossaries

A hand-built, back-of-the-book index of every topic on your website, and a glossary that defines your field's terms in plain language, both kept current as the site grows.

Search boxes and menus serve people who already know what they're looking for. A good index serves the reader who knows the idea but not the word your site uses for it, and it shows every page where a topic comes up, with the main treatment marked. A glossary does the same for vocabulary. Both are old tools from print publishing, and both turn out to suit search engines and AI systems, which read them as a dense, well-linked map of what the site covers and how its pages relate.

## Who it's for
- Publishers, associations, and nonprofits with years of articles, reports, and resources.
- Professional firms whose sites hold large libraries of guides or insights.
- Documentation and knowledge-base sites where readers search for concepts, not page titles.
- Any site that has outgrown its navigation.

## How it works

I read the site the way an indexer reads a book. Each page gets headings for the topics it treats, people and organizations it names, and the questions it answers, with subheadings where a topic splits, cross-references between synonyms, and the main discussion of each topic marked so readers go there first. The glossary collects the terms a newcomer would stumble on and defines each in a sentence or two, linking to the page that explains it in full.

The index lives as structured data in your site's repository or content system, and the page is generated from it. A build check lists any new page that hasn't been indexed yet, so the index stays complete as content is added. This site carries an index and a glossary built this way, linked from the footer.

## What you get
- An A to Z index page covering every page on the site, with subheadings and cross-references.
- A glossary page, alphabetized, with each term linked to its fullest treatment.
- The underlying data file and a short guide for adding entries when pages are published.
- A check in the build or publishing workflow that flags unindexed pages.

## Why it helps search

An index adds hundreds of descriptive internal links, written as the topic names readers use, pointing at the pages that cover each topic best. That's the kind of linking search engines use to understand a site's structure, and it gives AI systems a clean list of what the site knows about. It also exposes gaps: a topic with one thin mention, or two pages competing for the same subject, shows up plainly in an index.

**Related:** [Internal linking](https://gerriscorp.com/services/internal-linking/) · [Editorial services](https://gerriscorp.com/services/editorial/) · [This site's index](https://gerriscorp.com/site-index/)

## Start a conversation

Scope and fees are settled in conversation, once I understand the problem. Choose the route that fits how your company works.

# Black hat SEO in modern dress: the tactics that end sites

By [Chris Abraham](https://gerriscorp.com/about/) · Published October 27, 2026

Practitioners my age buried black hat SEO a decade ago and attended the funeral in good faith. The corpse changed clothes. Every scheme Google killed between 2003 and 2024 has a living descendant running today, rebuilt for answer engines, and clients arrive at Gerris with the descendants already installed. I keep this taxonomy current because diagnosis starts with naming the thing correctly.

## Tier one: the antiques, still for sale

Keyword stuffing survives as entity stuffing: pages salted with entity names and attribute pairs to impress embedding models, prose no human finishes. Doorway pages survive as programmatic location pages, five hundred city variants of one template with the nouns swapped by script. Article spinning survives as paraphrase networks, the same essay rewritten by a model forty ways and posted across forty domains. Comment spam survives as seeded forum accounts that mention a brand with rehearsed casualness. Tier one wastes crawl budget and calendar time. It rarely kills a site. It reliably marks the operator as an amateur in a field that now reads code.

## Tier two: the plausible failures

Hidden text survives as hidden instruction. Pages now carry passages written for AI crawlers, directives in markup and metadata telling answer engines how to describe the business, invisible to the customer and legible to the machine. Forged expertise survives beside it: author personas with generated portraits, invented credentials, and biographies assembled to simulate the experience signals Google calls [E-E-A-T](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/glossary/#e-e-a-t). Citation stacking rents mentions in listicles built for engines rather than readers. Review velocity gets managed the way link velocity once was, in bursts timed to look like weather. Tier two fails slowly and then publicly. The patterns are statistical, the engines are statisticians, and a fabricated record contradicts itself somewhere crawlable.

## Tier three: the named offenses

Google wrote this tier into policy in March 2024, and practitioners should use the official names. [Scaled content abuse](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials/spam-policies): content generated at volume to manipulate rankings, human or machine authorship irrelevant. Site reputation abuse: third party pages published on a trusted domain to exploit its signals, the coupon directory and the casino review squatting on a newspaper's authority. Expired domain abuse: a lapsed domain with a history, purchased and refilled to inherit trust it never earned. Cloaking completes the set, now aimed at AI crawlers as often as at Googlebot, one text for machines and another for people. Tier three ends in manual actions and removal. Recovery takes quarters, and my guide to [diagnosing a traffic drop](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/traffic-drop/) starts from the wreckage these tactics leave.

## How the descendants get caught

Clients ask why the modern versions fail when the fluent output reads so well. The answer is arithmetic. Schemes must scale to pay, scale leaves distributions, and distributions confess. A paraphrase network shares sentence skeletons across domains. A persona stable shares a biography template, a headshot generator, and a posting rhythm. A parasite section shares a template, a monetization path, and a landlord. Detection no longer reads pages one at a time looking for guilt; it clusters, and the cluster is the evidence. The practitioner who installs a descendant inherits the whole cluster's record, including the parts other operators contributed. That inheritance is the part the sales pitch leaves out.

## The working alternative

E-E-A-T compounds; schemes depreciate. A named expert publishing first hand work on a current site gives the engines evidence they can verify and rivals cannot rent. Currency matters more each quarter, because Google's AI answers from the live index while the chatbots answer from training memory months stale. Fresh, accurate, attributable pages win the live arena outright. The audit trail runs both ways: a clean site's history is visible too, in consistent authorship, corrections made in public, and claims that survived their news cycle. Engines read that history when they choose whose answer to quote. The rebuild Gerris runs after a descendant is found is always the same shape: fewer pages, named authors, current facts, and claims the business can defend in the room. Slow work, honestly labeled, and built to be audited by anyone, including the competition. Retire the antiques, refuse the plausible failures, and treat tier three as a firing offense for any vendor who proposes it.

## Want me to handle this for you?

This guide shows you how to do it yourself. If you'd rather hand it to someone who does this work for clients, I'm glad to help: tell me what's happening and I'll tell you where I'd start.

[Book a 30 minute call](https://calendly.com/chrisabraham/30) [Call +1 202-352-5051](tel:+12023525051) [Email chris@gerriscorp.com](mailto:chris@gerriscorp.com)

If your company hires through Upwork, you'll find me [there as well](https://www.upwork.com/freelancers/chrisjabraham).

- [What Cloudflare's cache leaves exposed on a WordPress site](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/wordpress-behind-cloudflare/): Full-page caching keeps most visitors away from WordPress and MySQL. Here is the traffic that still reaches your server, and how to harden each path it takes.
- [Google Consent Mode v2 for GA4: a practical setup guide](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ga4-consent-mode/): What Consent Mode v2 controls in GA4 and Google Ads, how basic and advanced mode differ, how to set regional defaults, and how to check that it really works.
- [Why business email lands in spam, and how to find the cause](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/email-deliverability/): How to find out why legitimate business email lands in spam or bounces: authentication results, reputation, blocklists, content, list hygiene, and tools.
- [How to use AI coding assistants on a business website safely](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-coding-assistants/): A practical workflow for OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot on business websites: written specs, project context, automated checks, and human review.
- [How to vet an AI vendor's pitch before you sign anything](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-vendor-pitch/): Twelve questions that expose AI washing in a vendor pitch, the SEC and FTC cases that define it, and why a technical skeptic belongs on the sales call.
- [How to hire and manage developers when you can't read code yourself](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/hiring-developers/): A founder's method for hiring web developers: own the accounts first, interview for judgment, pay for a trial task, review pull requests, and manage AI use.
- [Hype or real shift? Eight tests for judging a new technology wave](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/hype-or-shift/): Eight tests for telling a lasting technology shift from a hype cycle, drawn from online communities, blogs, social media, crypto, and the AI wave of 2026.
- [Repositories plus super intelligence: the SEO superpower nobody told you to learn](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/seo-superpower/): Repositories and AI coding assistants help SEOs ship fixes. How Git, OpenAI Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot connect search findings to changes in code.
- [Build a podcast website with Codex or Claude Code, GitHub Pages, and Cloudflare](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-website/): Build a podcast website with OpenAI Codex or Claude Code, GitHub Pages, and Cloudflare: a page for every episode, stable links, and daily feed updates.
- [The state of search in 2026: every Google update so far, and the AI shift behind them](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/search-in-2026/): Every 2026 Google core and spam update with dates, the new spam rule against manipulating AI answers, what Bing and ChatGPT now report, and what to do now.
- [Ranking yourself first in a "best of" list now backfires in AI answers](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/self-ranking-lists/): How self-ranked best agency lists came to steer AI answers, why Google, Anthropic, and the data now push back, and what earns a real AI recommendation instead.
- [SEO 101: a first principles primer for any website](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/seo-101/): SEO from first principles for absolute beginners: how search works, people-first content, E-E-A-T, titles, links, alt text, speed, and accessibility.
- [Podcast SEO: get every episode found in Google and AI search](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-seo/): How to make podcast episodes findable in Google, Bing, and AI answers: episode pages on your own domain, transcripts in the HTML, schema, and alt text.
- [Starting a podcast to build your brand: what it really takes](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/podcast-for-your-brand/): What a podcast does for a personal or business brand, the commitment behind it, and the cheap gear and AI tools that take the friction out of every episode.

- [ADA website compliance for businesses: lower risk, better SEO](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ada-website-compliance/): What the ADA expects of business websites, the six fixes that cover most of the risk, what to skip, and why the same work improves search, AI answers, trust.

- [Test an AI pilot with the work it is supposed to do](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/ai-pilot-tests/): Turn an AI demonstration into a testable pilot: real examples, expected results, permissions, retries, failure records, and a decision your team can explain.

## Case studies
- [Magento store: product content Googlebot never saw](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/ecommerce-rendering/): How Chris Abraham traced a Magento and Hyvä store's falling traffic to Alpine.js sections that never rendered for Googlebot, and kept two problems apart.
- [WordPress media site: a consent banner hiding every article](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/consent-blocking/): A bilingual WordPress review site indexed on Bing but barely in Google: Chris Abraham traced it to consent blocking that left article tabs empty.
- [React event platform: 2,000 pages Google couldn't reach](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/react-event-platform/): A Create React App event platform with 2,000 pages Google never found: Chris Abraham wrote a 13 page developer spec ranked P0 to P3 and verified the fixes.
- [Clinical practice: WordPress to Netlify, with search intact](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/netlify-migration/): Migration oversight for a clinical practice leaving WordPress: redirect decisions for every URL, an AI-assisted repository analysis, and a careful disavow.
- [Local service business on Sanity and Vercel: SEO in the repository](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/sanity-vercel/): A local service business on Sanity and Vercel: Chris Abraham set SEO priorities, merged metadata changes through GitHub, and verified the prerendering.
- [Specialty retailer: cleaning up after Squarespace to Shopify](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/shopify-migration/): A premium fly fishing store moved from Squarespace to Shopify and left 3,400 404s and duplicate URLs behind: a four part audit and theme schema work.
- [Consumer brand: taking over a stalled React application](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/app-takeover/): A consumer skincare brand's React application changed hands after an outage. Chris Abraham inventoried code, hosting, and DNS and fixed the server over SSH.
- [Programmatic site: managing crawling and indexing at scale](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/programmatic-indexing/): A trading card price site of 20,000+ pages on an expired domain lost indexing after a strong start. How Chris Abraham manages crawling at scale.
- [Health-testing store: recovering after an SEO plugin outage](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/indexing-recovery/): A WooCommerce health testing store lost indexing, traffic, and AI referrals after its SEO plugin was briefly disabled: how the recovery was checked.
- [Multi-location brand: untangling the parent from its first location](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/multi-location-entity/): A custom closets brand with locations in several states and one website: Chris Abraham separated the parent brand from its first location in schema.
- [Seasonal retailer: a staged plan around the peak](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/seasonal-retailer/): A multi store seasonal retailer with related sites and profiles: audit findings and a staged plan that keeps risky changes away from the peak season.
- [Therapy practice: a suspended Google Business Profile reinstated](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/gbp-reinstatement/): A hypnotherapy practice's suspended Google Business Profile, reinstated in February 2025 after Chris Abraham reviewed the listing and built a documented appeal.
- [Two B2B companies on Umbraco: publishing and technical operations](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/umbraco-operations/): Two B2B companies on Umbraco: 54 city landing pages and steady publishing for one, and a homepage overhaul with cache and template fixes for the other.
- [AI company: search visibility for recruiting engineers](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/ai-recruiting/): An AI company recruiting engineers in the Bay Area wanted to appear in AI answers about jobs. Chris Abraham audited its footprint and planned the fix.
- [Contact data: three cleanups and an AI audit](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/data-cleanup/): Python pipelines that cleaned an 88,900 contact list, merged two 28,800 record exports at 94% email coverage, and caught an AI tracker inventing its data.
- [A founder's public record: tracing AI errors to the pages behind them](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/founder-record/): AI answers about me got a founding year wrong, invented a company rename, and doubted a real award. Each traced to a page, and the archive settled the rest.
- [Four static sites: a speed and AI crawler pass in one afternoon](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/four-site-speed-pass/): Four static sites I own, measured with mobile Lighthouse, fixed in one afternoon, and measured again: analytics deferred, images resized, robots rules verified.
- [Built with Codex and Claude Code](https://gerriscorp.com/case-studies/built-with-claude-code/): How Chris Abraham directs OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, with original Claude Code builds of a tested assistant, a legacy blog migration, and this website.

# Index

Reference books end with an index, and so does this site. I went through every page, from the services to the case studies, and recorded each person, company, tool, standard, and problem it discusses: 526 headings drawn from 129 pages. A locator is a page's short name; bold marks the page that treats the subject in full, and hovering shows the page's whole title.

Names of people run surname first, and "See also" leads to neighboring headings. Short definitions live in the [glossary](https://gerriscorp.com/guides/glossary/), and the [site map](https://gerriscorp.com/sitemap/) lists every page by section.
